CSES Module 5 Coding of Parties/Coalitions & Leaders CSES codes parties/coalitions in its dataset numerically and alphabetically. Below we provide explanations of both of these coding schemes. The details of each party/leader classification are available in Part 3 of the codebook. CSES Numerical Party/Coalition Coding Each party is assigned a unique numerical code which consists of two components and six digits in total: the first three digits indicate the numerical country UN code the latter three digits indicate the numerical party code within the given election study. All parties/coalitions or presidential candidates, where applicable, participating in the election or the previous election receive a numerical code. These codes are used to identify the following: who respondents feel best represented by (variable E3010_2). who a respondent voted for in the current election (variable E3013). who the respondent voted for in the previous election (variable E3015). the respondent's party identification (variable E3024). The numeric coding is also used to identify macro level information about the parties/coalitions, namely: numeric party code identifiers for Parties A-I (E5000) which party/coalition held the presidency before and after the elections (variable E5009 and E5013). which party/coalition held the prime ministership before and after the elections (variable E5010 and E5014). Numerical codes assigned to parties/coalitions are consistent for the current and previous election. CSES Alphabetical Party/Coalition Coding Parties A through F are the six most popular parties/coalitions, ordered in descending order of their share of the popular vote in the parliamentary election (unless otherwise stated). Thus Party A is the party/coalition that received the most votes in the election, party B the second most votes, etc... Parties/coalitions who achieve at least 1% of the vote nationally are eligible for an alphabetical A-F assignment. In countries with multiple electoral tiers and where one vote is cast, parties are ordered according to their vote share in tier 1 (the lowest tier), unless otherwise stated. In countries where voters have two votes (i.e.: a constituency and a list vote) simultaneously, for example Germany, parties are ordered by the national share of the party list vote (tier 2) unless stated otherwise. Parties G, H, and I are supplemental parties. They may, but do not have to, accord with how parties A-F are ordered, that is ordered on the popular share of the vote in a country. More often, they are codified in no particular order. These parties are voluntarily provided by each country's election study and often reflect important or notable parties within a country. Numerical codes assigned to parties/coalitions are consistent for the current and previous election. CSES Alphabetical Party/Coalition Coding Parties A through F are the six most popular parties/coalitions, ordered in descending order of their share of the popular vote in the parliamentary election (unless otherwise stated). Thus Party A is the party/coalition that received the most votes in the election, party B the second most votes, etc... Parties/coalitions who achieve at least 1% of the vote nationally are eligibl e for an alphabetical A -F assignment. In countries with multiple electoral tiers and where one vote is cast, parties are ordered according to their vote share in tier 1 (the lowest tier), unless otherwise stated. In countries where voters have two votes (i .e.: a constituency and a list vote) simultaneously, for example Germany, parties are ordered by the national share of the party list vote (tier 2) unless stated otherwise. Parties G, H, and I are supplemental parties . They may, but do not have to, accord with how parties A-F are ordered, that is ordered on the popular share of the vote in a country. More often, they are codified in no particular order. These parties are voluntarily provided by each country's election study and often reflect important or n otable parties within a country. For Presidential elections, the United States use an electoral college system, a system which sees the Presidential candidate who wins in a state awarded its electoral college votes (except for Maine and Nebraska where electoral votes are awarded on the basis of who wins congressional districts within the state). Hence, the first three digits of electoral district codes above refer to the state the respondent resided in. Together with the first three digits, the last two digits specify Congressional Districts, which are also listed after the state name. U.S. states, the geographical level E4001-E4007 refer to, are provided in E2020 (REGION OF RESIDENCE). Table of Contents Important Note Regarding Advance Releases List of Tables in Codebook Part 4 Overview of “Codebook Part 4: Primary Electoral Districts” Part 4 of the CSES Codebook presents the primary electoral districts by polity, which refer to the constituency/riding/district in which an individual respondent in a survey votes. These value labels refer to coders reported in variable E2021 "PRIMARY ELECTORAL DISTRICT" detailed in CSES Codebook Part 2. These districts are sometimes identified "indirectly," through postal codes, etc... by the CSES Secretariat with the assistance of the national collaborators. Where postal codes, etc., were ambiguous, cases are coded missing. Wherever possible, CSES uses the labels used by each country's electoral commission. Only districts where respondents are in the CSES data are listed (see second column of Table below). Polities are listed in alphabetical order. How to Navigate the CSES Module 5 Codebook In the CSES Module 5 dataset, all variables begin with the letter "E" (E being the fifth letter of the English alphabet and thus signifying Module 5). The CSES codebook is especially extensive and users are advised that the best way to navigate it is electronically. It is produced in two formats, a plain text .txt format and a PDF format to allow for easy accessibility. As such, the Codebook can be read into a variety of programs. The two formats differ in style, but not in substance. These districts are sometimes identified "indirectly," through postal codes, etc... by the CSES Secretariat with the assistance of the national collaborators. Wyoming - WY01 United States (2016): Primary Electoral Districts District data given in E4001 -E4007 refer to the U.S. 2016 Presidential election, while codes listed above indicate Congressional Districts. For Presidential elections, the United States use an electoral college system, a system which sees the Presidential candidate who wins in a state awarded its electoral college votes (except for Maine and Nebraska where ele ctoral votes are awarded on the basis of who wins congressional districts within the state). Hence, the first three digits of electoral district codes above refer to the state the respondent resided in. Together with the first three digits, the last two d igits specify Congressional Districts, which are also listed after the state name. U.S. states, the geographical level E4001 -E4007 refer to, are provided in E2020 (REGION OF RESIDENCE).

Election Summary – Portugal 2019 The 2019 Portuguese lower house election took place on Sunday, October 6, 2019. All 230 seats of the Assembly of the Republic, Portugal's unicameral legislature, were at stake. The turnout rate among registered voters was 48.6%, a historic low for lower house elections. Incumbent Prime Minister Antonio Costa (Socialist Party, SP) contested for re-election. Before the election, Costa headed a minority government and relied on external support from the Left Bloc (BE), the Portuguese Communist Party (PCP) and the Greens (PEV). Costa's governing Socialist Party surpassed the Social Democratic Party (PPD/PSD) to become the strongest party, winning 36.4% of the vote and 108 seats, a plus of 22 seats. In second, the Social Democrats suffered a significant defeat by securing 79 seats (27.8%), thereby losing ten seats. text: Power Party (PPRP). Elections were held under the new 2017 constitution, introducing changes to the electoral system. For the 2019 election, 350 of the 500 parliamentary seats were elected by plurality vote in single-member constituencies, with the remaining 150 seats being elected through closed-list proportional representation. Voters cast a single fused vote counting towards both segments. Further, the constitution specified that the new Prime Minister was to be elected by the full parliament, i.e., by joint members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, consisting of 250 members appointed by the military. Hence, candidates were required to win 376 out of 750 votes from the combined houses to win prime ministership. In adapting to the newly introduced rules that were perceived as disadvantaging opposition parties, the Pheu Thai party led by Sudarat Keyuraphan decided to coordinate campaigns with the affiliated Thai Raksa Chart Party (TRC) to compete against Prayut's PPRP. To increase the chances of winning party-list seats, Pheu Thai ceded candidacies in 100 constituencies to TRC, with prominent members of PTP competing on TRC tickets. The TRC nominated Thai Princess Ubolratana Rajakanya, the King's sister, as their candidate for prime minister. At the beginning of March, TRC was dissolved by the Constitutional Court for allowing a Royal Family member to enter politics, following a condemnation of the Princess's candidacy by the King. Prayut Chan-o-cha's State Power Party came out as the strongest party in the election, obtaining a vote share of 23.7% and 116 seats. Although Pheu Thai came only second with 22.2%, it became the strongest group in the lower house by winning 136 district candidate seats. The newly founded Future Forward Party (FFP), also campaigning on an anti-junta stance, came in third with 17.8% of the vote, thereby gaining 81 seats. The conservative Democrat Party (DP), the oldest party in Thailand, became the fourth-strongest party with 11.1% and 53 seats, a disappointing outcome for the party leading to the resignation of its chairman and former Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva. In the aftermath of the election, Thailand's Electoral Commission, the country's electoral management body, was criticized for announcing official results only weeks after the election. The constitution provided no strict guidance for allocating party-list seats, hence granting the EC some leeway in calculating seat shares. Eventually, the EC decided to reduce the minimum threshold for a parliamentary seat from approximately 71,000 votes as announced initially to around 35,000 votes, thereby increasing the number of parties represented in parliament to 26 at the expense of anti-junta coalition parties. Forging a coalition of 19 political parties, Prayut Chan-o-cha was re-elected as Prime Minister on June 5, 2019, also supported by all members of the Senate. Sources For Further Information

The TRC nominated Thai Princess Ubolratan a Rajakanya, the King's sister, as their candidate for prime minister. At the beginning of March, TRC was dissolved by the Constitutional Court for allowing a Royal Family member to enter politics, following a condemnation of the Princess's candidacy by th e King. Prayut Chan -o-cha's State Power Party came out as the strongest party in the election, obtaining a vote share of 23.7% and 116 seats. Although Pheu Thai came only second with 22.2%, it became the strongest group in the lower house by winning 136 district candidate seats. The newly founded Future Forward Party (FFP) , also campaigning on an anti -junta stance, came in third with 17.8% of the vote, thereby gaining 81 seats. The conservative Democrat Party (DP) , the oldest party in Thailand, became the fourth -strongest party with 11.1% and 53 seats, a disappointing outcome for the party leading to the resignation of its chairman and former Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva. In the aftermath of the election, Thailand's Electoral Commission, the country's electoral management body, was criticized for announcing official results only weeks after the election. The constitution provided no strict guidance for allocating party -list seats, hence granting the EC some leeway in calculating seat shares. Eventually, the EC decided to reduce the minimum threshold for a parliamentary seat from approximately 71,000 votes as announced initially to around 35,000 votes, thereby increasing the number of parties represented in parliament to 26 at the expense of an ti-junta coalition parties. All 230 seats of the Assembly of the Republic, Portugal's unicameral legislature, were at stake. The turnout rate among registered voters was 48.6%, a historic low for lower house elections. Incumbent Prime Minister Antonio Costa (Socialist Party, SP) contested for re-election. Before the election, Costa headed a minority government and relied on external support from the Left Bloc (BE), the Portuguese Communist Party (PCP) and the Greens (PEV). Costa's governing Socialist Party surpassed the Social Democratic Party (PPD/PSD) to become the strongest party, winning 36.4% of the vote and 108 seats, a plus of 22 seats. In second, the Social Democrats suffered a significant defeat by securing 79 seats (27.8%), thereby losing ten seats. While the Left Bloc retained its position as the third-largest party (9.52%, 19 seats), the Unitary Democratic Coalition (Communists and Greens) lost five of the previously held 17 seats with a vote share of 6.3% (12 seats). However, the worst defeat was experienced by the People's Party (CDS-PP), which came fifth with a vote share of 4.2% (5 seats), losing almost three-quarters of their representatives in parliament. The 2019 election also resulted in three new parties gaining representation in parliament with one seat each: Enough (CH), Liberal Initiative (IL) and Free (L). Short of a majority in parliament, Antonio Costa (SP) formed a single-party minority government without any formal cooperation agreements, after turning down a proposal from the Left Bloc. Overview of Study Design and Weights – Portugal 2019 Study Design The 2019 Portuguese post-election study was administered between October 12 and December 15, 2019, as a face-to-face survey. Fieldwork was conducted by GfK Portugal, starting six days after the Portuguese legislative election held on October 6, 2019. Interviews were conducted in Portuguese. The sample is meant to be representative of individuals aged 18 years or older residing in continental Portugal. Portuguese citizenship was not required to participate in the interview. The two autonomous regions Madeira and the Azores were excluded from the sample frame (5 percent of the eligible population). The same holds for institutionalized persons (less than 1 percent of the eligible population). The study is based on a multistage stratified random sample. The sample was stratified according to locality size ("habitat") and EU NUTS II regions; a hierarchical geocode standard subdividing the territories of EU member states. The NUTS II regions North, Centre, Lisbon, Alentejo, and Algarve were also the primary sampling unit. In a first step, the random selection of localities within each of the five listed NUTS II regions was carried out following the General Index of INE's Population Census, based on the sample matrix of NUTS II regions and habitat. In each designated locality, sample points were then again sampled randomly. Afterward, households were selected through random route. From within each household, the adult who had the most recent birthday was selected for the interview in the last step. From within each household, the adult who had the most recent birthday was selected for the interview in the last step. If the selected person was not available, up to three more revisits were made to reach the potential interviewee on different days (week and weekend) and throughout different times of the day. After a fourth unsuccessful visit, the selected individual was replaced by another person with similar characteristics (sex, age group and location) from a different household. The sample consists of 1,500 completed interviews. Polity Weights The Portuguese Election Study includes a DEMOGRAPHIC WEIGHT and a POLITICAL WEIGHT. Both weights were created through iterations in Marktab software. The demographic weight (E1010_2) adjusts the sample to known population characteristics regarding gender, age, and educational attainment. Population estimates were taken from the Portuguese National Institute for Statistics INE 2017 Estimates and Eurostat 2017 Schooling. The political weight (E1010_3) is a combined weight that adjusts the sample to match the 2019 legislative election results on top of the demographic weight. Overview of Study Design and Weights – United States 2020 Study Design The election and the fieldwork for the study took place during the COVID-19 pandemic. The American National Election Study (ANES) 2020 Time Series study has a pre and post-election panel design in which 4,779 respondents were interviewed twice: Once before the election and once after the election. Another 2,670 were sampled for the 2016 ANES time series study and were re-interviewed in 2020 before and after the election. The CSES sample includes respondents sampled in 2016 and 2020 who took part in both rounds of the 2020 interviews. Post-election interviewing featuring the CSES module started on November 8, 2020 - five days after the General election on November 3 - and continued until January 4, 2021. As the pandemic made face-to-face interviewing unfeasible, the 2020 ANES implemented a contactless, sequential mixed-mode design. This design combined self-administered online surveys, live video interviews, and telephone interviews. Respondents were assigned to modes and did not switch modes between interviews. Westat, Inc. administered the study in either English or Spanish. The fresh 2020 cross-sectional sample is meant to represent eligible voters in the 2020 presidential election, as defined by being age 18 as of election day and being a U.S. citizen. Institutionalized persons were excluded from the sampling frame. Further details on the sampling process with which panelists from 2016 were recruited are available in this part of the Codebook ("Overview of Study Design and Weights - United States (2016)"). Further details on the sampling process with which panelists from 2016 were recruited are available in this part of the Codebook ("Overview of Study Design and Weights - United States (2016)"). The 2020 fresh cross-sectional sample is based on a simple random sample drawn from the computerized delivery sequence file (C-DSF) provided by the U.S. Postal Service. All included residential addresses across the 50 states and Washington DC had an equal probability of selection. Selected addresses were sent a series of letters, asking one household member to go online to complete a survey. That survey contained a screening instrument to randomly select one person from all eligible household members for the final interview. Upon completion of the screener, the selected individual was randomly assigned to one of three sequential mode conditions: web-only, mixed web, and mixed video. Cases assigned to the web-only group were released in two replicates for the pre-election survey and solely interviewed online. The first replicate was released in mid-August 2020 with the other sample groups. The second replicate was released on September 11, 2020, after the Republican and Democratic conventions, roughly corresponding to the field period of previous ANES Time Series studies. Respondents in the mixed web group were initially invited to complete the survey online. Non-responding persons and refusals were shifted to the telephone at the case level in the final weeks of the pre-election period. Finally, upon completing the web screener, respondents in the mixed video group were invited to complete the survey by live video interview via Zoom. Following the invitation link, respondents were instructed to wait briefly to connect with an interviewer or set an appointment. In case of refusal or non-response, respondents were shifted to the web. At the final stage, non-respondents to web were subsequently pushed to the phone. Similar to the mixed web group, this shift occurred at the case level in the final weeks of the pre-election period. All panelists from the 2016 ANES Time Series study completed the 2020 survey online. Invitations were made by e-mail and mail. Respondents from all groups completed the post-election survey in the same mode as the pre-election survey. Before the pre-election interview, selected addresses were sent invitation letters including 10 USD in cash that promised an additional 40 USD for completing a survey online. Among all groups of the fresh 2020 sample, non-responding households were offered escalated incentives of 100 USD for completing the screener later in the field period. Additionally, individuals from under-represented groups with a low response rate were offered 200 USD as part of a targeted, adaptive design approach in the mixed-web group and for panelists from 2016. Likewise, to counter initial non-response, 200 USD escalations were offered to respondents from the mixed video group for completing interviews by video. For the post-election survey, pre-election respondents were offered the incentive amount they received previously. The pre-election re-interview rate for the 2016-2020 panel cases was 77.9%. Of these, post-election re-interviews were conducted with 94.0% of panelists. The cumulative 2020 re-interview rate was thus 73.2%. The weight adjusts for unequal probability of selection, non-response, age by gender, marital status by gender, race/ethnicity by educational attainment, race/ethnicity by Census region, nation of birth, home tenure by metropolitan status, population density, household income, and early voter status. The weight deposited with CSES (variable V200010b in the ANES 2020 Time Series data) is targeted to the full post-election dataset, namely all three mode conditions from the 2020 fresh cross-sectional sample and sample members from the 2016 ANES Time Series Study. Users interested in conducting analyses with a subset of these sample components only are referred to the ANES 2020 Time Series Study, which provides individual weights for selected components. Weights were calculated following a complex multistage procedure involving raking and the trimming of large weights. Users interested in the detailed step-by-step approach for creating weights are referred to the Design Report for the United States 2020, available for download on the CSES website. List of Tables in Codebook Part 6 Weights CSES provides users with up to three original weights from each national election study (see variable E1010_) namely: SAMPLE WEIGHT (variable E1010_1): intended to correct for unequal selection probabilities resulting from booster samples procedures for selection within the household, non-response, or other sample design features DEMOGRAPHIC WEIGHT (variable E1010_2): intended to adjust sample distributions of socio-demographic characteristics to more closely resemble the characteristics of the population. POLITICAL WEIGHT (variable E1010_3): intended to reconcile discrepancies in the reported electoral behavior of respondents vis-a-vis official electoral counts. Users are advised to read carefully about the different weights in CSES to ascertain whether their analyses should be subjected to weighting and if so which kind. The CSES project does not provide advice as to which weights are appropriate to use in particular circumstances. This is best left to analysts to decide based on their detailed knowledge of the research question under investigation. We advise analysts to consult each Polity's Design Report on the CSES Module 5 Study Page (see https://cses.org/data-download/cses-module-5-2016-2021/ ). For information on derivative weights calculated for the Cross-National Dataset, users should consult Parts 1 and 2 (variables E1011-E1014) of the CSES Codebook. text: the Azores were excluded from the sample frame (5 percent of the eligible population). The same holds for institutionalized persons (less than 1 percent of the eligible population). The study is based on a multistage stratified random sample. The sample was stratified according to locality size ("habitat") and EU NUTS II regions; a hierarchical geocode standard subdividing the territories of EU member states. The NUTS II regions North, Centre, Lisbon, Alentejo, and Algarve were also the primary sampling unit. In a first step, the random selection of localities within each of the five listed NUTS II regions was carried out following the General Index of INE's Population Census, based on the sample matrix of NUTS II regions and habitat. In each designated locality, sample points were then again sampled randomly. Afterward, households were selected through random route. From within each household, the adult who had the most recent birthday was selected for the interview in the last step. If the selected person was not available, up to three more revisits were made to reach the potential interviewee on different days (week and weekend) and throughout different times of the day. After a fourth unsuccessful visit, the selected individual was replaced by another person with similar characteristics (sex, age group and location) from a different household. The sample consists of 1,500 completed interviews. Polity Weights The Portuguese Election Study includes a DEMOGRAPHIC WEIGHT and a POLITICAL WEIGHT. Both weights were created through iterations in Marktab software. The demographic weight (E1010_2) adjusts the sample to known population characteristics regarding gender, age, and educational attainment. Population estimates were taken from the Portuguese National Institute for Statistics INE 2017 Estimates and Eurostat 2017 Schooling. The political weight (E1010_3) is a combined weight that adjusts the sample to match the 2019 legislative election results on top of the demographic weight. Overview of Study Design and Weights – United States 2020 Study Design The election and the fieldwork for the study took place during the COVID-19 pandemic. The American National Election Study (ANES) 2020 Time Series study has a pre and post-election panel design in which 4,779 respondents were interviewed twice: Once before the election and once after the election. Another 2,670 were sampled for the 2016 ANES time series study and were re-interviewed in 2020 before and after the election. The CSES sample includes respondents sampled in 2016 and 2020 who took part in both rounds of the 2020 interviews. Post-election interviewing featuring the CSES module started on November 8, 2020 - five days after the General election on November 3 - and continued until January 4, 2021. This dataset and all accompanying documentation is the " Fourth Advance Release " of CSES Module 5 (2016 -2021). By definition, an Advance Release is a preliminary version of a dataset , and thus lacks some of the checking, cleaning, processing, documentation, data, and variables that are usual to the Full Release of a dataset. Many election studies that will eventually be present in the CSES Module 5 Full Release are not available in this file. Advance Releases are provided as a service to the CSES user community, for those analysts who find it valuable to work with pr eliminary versions of the dataset. We would appreciate being notified of any errors in the dataset or documentation by email to " cses@umich.edu ". Users should expect future changes and improvements to the naming, data, and documentation of variables and election studies that appear in an Advance Release file. If users wish to re -use their programming code on a future release of the file, the code should be written in a way that is flexible and can be accomm odating of these future changes. Users of the Advance Release may also wish to monitor the errata for CSES Module 5 on the CSES website, to check for kn own errors which may impact their analyses. To view errata for CSES Module 5, go to Data Download on the CSES website, navigate to the CSES Module 5 download page, and click on the Errata link in the white box to the right of the page. We hope that until such time as the Full Release of CSES Module 5 is available, users will find this and future CSES Module 5 Advance Releases to be helpful in their work. CSES Module 5 AR4 Codebook Part 6 | 8 COMPARATIVE STUDY OF ELECTORAL SYSTEMS (CSES) MODULE 5 Fourth Advance Release, March 1, 2022 Codebook Part 6: Study Design s and Weights Overview of Study Design and Weights – Portugal 2019 Study Design The 2019 Portuguese post -election study was administered between October 12 and December 15, 2019, as a face -to-face survey. Fieldwork was conducted by GfK Portugal, starting six days after the Portuguese legislative election held on October 6, 2019. Interviews were conducted in Portuguese. The sample is meant to be representative of individuals aged 18 years or older residing in continental Portugal. Portuguese citizenship was not required to participate in the interview. The two autonomous regions Madeira and the Azores were excluded from the sample frame (5 percent of the eligible population). The same holds for institutionalized persons (less than 1 percent of the eligible population). The study is ba sed on a multistage stratified random sample. The sample was stratified according to locality size ("habitat") and EU NUTS II regions; a hierarchical geocode standard subdividing the territories of EU member states. The NUTS II regions North, Centre, Lisbo n, Alentejo, and Algarve were also the primary sampling unit. In a first step, the random selection of localities within each of the five listed NUTS II regions was carried out following the General Index of INE's Population Census, based on the sample matrix of NUTS II regions and habitat. In each designated locality, sample points were then again sampled randomly. Afterward, households were selected through random route. From within each household, the adult who had the most recent birthday was selected for the interview in the last step. If the selected person was not available, up to three more revisits were made to reach the potential interviewee on different days (week and weekend) and throughout different times of the day. After a fourth uns uccessful visit, the selected individual was replaced by another person with similar characteristics (sex, age group and location) from a different household. The sample consists of 1,500 completed interviews. Polity Weights The Portuguese Election Stu dy includes a DEMOGRAPHIC WEIGHT and a POLITICAL WEIGHT . Both weights were created through iterations in Marktab software. The demographic weight (E1010_2)

The 2020 fresh cross -sectional sample is based on a simple random sample drawn from the computerized delivery sequence file (C -DSF) provided by the U.S. Postal Service. All included residential addresses across the 50 st ates and Washington DC had an equal probability of selection. Selected addresses were sent a series of letters, asking one household member to go online to complete a survey. That survey contained a screening instrument to randomly select one person from all eligible household members for the final interview. Upon completion of the screener, the selected individual was randomly assigned to one of three sequential mode conditions: web-only, mixed web, and mixed video. Cases assigned to the web -only group were released in two replicates for the pre-election survey and solely interviewed online. The first replicate was released in mid -August 2020 with the other sample groups. The second replicate was released on September 11, 2020, after the Republican and Democratic conventions, roughly corresponding to the field period of previous ANES Time Series studies. Respondents in the mixed web group were initially invited to complete the survey online. Non - responding persons and refusals were shifted to the telephon e at the case level in the final weeks of the pre -election period. Finally, upon completing the web screener, respondents in the mixed video group were invited to complete the survey by live video interview via Zoom. Following the invitation link, responde nts were instructed to wait briefly to connect with an interviewer or set an appointment. In case of refusal or non -response, respondents were shifted to the web. At the final stage, non - respondents to web were subsequently pushed to the phone. Similar to the mixed web group, this shift occurred at the case level in the final weeks of the pre -election period. All panelists from the 2016 ANES Time Series study completed the 2020 survey online. Invitations were made by e -mail and mail. Respondents from all groups completed the post -election survey in the same mode as the pre - election survey. text: Design s and Weights Before the pre -election interview, selected addresses were sent invitation letters including 10 USD in cash that promised an additional 40 USD for completing a survey online. Among all groups of the fresh 2020 sample, non -responding households were offered escalated incentives of 100 USD for completing the screener later in the field period. Additionally, individuals from under -represented groups wit h a low response rate were offered 200 USD as part of a targeted, adaptive design approach in the mixed -web group and for panelists from 2016. Likewise, to counter initial non -response, 200 USD escalations were offered to respondents from the mixed video g roup for completing interviews by video. For the post -election survey, pre -election respondents were offered the incentive amount they received previously. The pre -election re -interview rate for the 2016 -2020 panel cases was 77.9%. Of these, post -electio n re-interviews were conducted with 94.0% of panelists. The cumulative 2020 re -interview rate was thus 73.2%. For the fresh 2020 sample, 87.9% of respondents from the pre -election survey also completed the post -election interview (88.1% in web -only, 88.7% in mixed web and 84.6% in the mixed video group, respectively). The resulting combined post -election sample consists of 7,449 completed interviews. Polity Weights The American National Election Study includes a combined DEMOGRAPHIC and SAMPLE WEIGHT . The weight adjusts for unequal probability of selection, non -response, age by gender, marital status by gender, race/ethnicity by educational attainment, race/ethnicity by Census region, nation of birth, home tenure by metropolitan status, populati on density, household income, and early voter status. The weight deposited with CSES (variable V200010b in the ANES 2020 Time Series data) is targeted to the full post -election dataset, namely all three mode conditions from the 2020 fresh cross -sectional sample and sample members from the 2016 ANES Time Series Study. Users interested in conducting analyses with a subset of these sample components only are referred to the ANES 2020 Time Series Study, which provides individual weights for selected components. Weights were calculated following a complex multistage procedure involving raking and the trimming of large weights. Users interested in the detailed step -by-step approach for creating weights are referred to the Design Report for the United States 2020, available for download on the CSES website.

text: Guidelines for formatting the PDF-Version of the CSES Module 5 Codebook The PDF-Drafts follow some stylistic guidelines, described in this document, and preceded by some general introductory remarks on the CSES Module 5 Codebook. The CSES Module 5 Codebook – An Overview Over the Six Parts The CSES Module 5 Codebook is the primary documentation component accompanying the dataset. As of now, it is provided in six separate .txt files, i.e., six parts, namely: Part 1: Introduction (file name: cses5_codebook_part1_introduction.txt) Part 1 provides an overview of the CSES study and data, information about how to use the files, election study descriptions, information on the CSES data file, the checks the CSES Secretariat conducts on the data file and information on the national collaborators of the CSES project for each polity. Part 2: Variables Description (file name: cses5_codebook_part2_variables.txt) Part 2 is the variable description file and includes the survey questions, code frames, general notes, election study notes, and details about sources for macro data. Part 3: Parties and Leaders (file name: cses5_codebook_part3_parties_and_leaders.txt) Part 3 details the party/coalition and leader numeric and alphabetical coding for each polity included in the CSES Module 5 dataset. Part 4: Primary Electoral Districts (file name: cses5_codebook_part4_primary_electoral_districts.txt) Part 4 details the primary electoral district by polity for each respondent included in the CSES Module 5 dataset. Part 5: Election Summaries (file name: cses5_codebook_part5_election_summaries.txt) Part 5 contains short summaries of each election included in CSES Module 5. It also provides analysts with details of additional sources they may wish to consult to understand the elections included in CSES in greater detail. Part 6: Study Design And Weights (file name: cses5_codebook_part6_designs_and_weights.txt) Part 6 contains overviews of the design of each election study included in CSES Module 5. It also provides analysts with details regarding the polity weights provided by each election study. All Parts of the CSES Codebook are provided in plain text format and are machine-readable, such that they are parsable by computers. Furthermore, as the CSES documentation is extensive, the information presented in the files is structured in a way that facilitates navigation. Originally designed to aid users, we imagine that these structures may also be exploited to parse and format texts from the .txt files according to the PDF style templates provided by the CSES Secretariat. In what follows, we provide further details on stylistic edits applied to the PDF-templates. Whenever available, we describe how navigation features in the .txt files may be exploited for implementing the styles included in the PDF: 1. text: Study Design and Weight Overview Guidelines As adopted by Steve Quinlan and Dave Howell in April 2018 6 April 2018 The Study Design and Weight Overviews included in the CSES codebook should be formulated in the following way: Structure: There will be two separate sections to the overview, namely a study design overview and weights overview. Format: Both sections of the overview should be written in a paragraph style (see below example). The Study Design Overview section should contain the following information: Start date of fieldwork and end date of fieldwork and how this relates to the election date (e.g., when does interviewing begin vis a vis the election date). Please include an estimate of the number of days between election date and the beginning of fieldwork. Days can be calculated here: https://www.timeanddate.com/date/duration.html The mode(s) of the interview. Mention if study part of panel design. If so, mention attrition rate information. The organization the conducted the Fieldwork/Data Collection. Language(s) survey administered in. The age range of those eligible for selection (e.g., aged 18 years +). Other eligibility criteria such as citizenship/voter register requirements. Were any group excluded from the sampling frame (e.g., institutionalized or military personnel). Only mention when applicable. The default assumption is no exclusion. Sample selection procedures – e.g., what kind of sample (systematic random sample, stratified random sampling) and the primary sampling unit (constituencies). Total sample size. Incentives to participate (e.g., payment or gift to the respondent). Only mention when applicable. The Weights Overview section should contain the following information: Which CSES weights are applicable (sample, demographics, or political). Explain what weight is intended to control for. Explain how weight was constructed. Word Count: Study Design Overview: no more than 400 words. Weights Overview: no more than 200 words The introduction to this segment of the codebook will advise users that more specific information regarding the study design and the weights are available in the design reports. The purpose of this overview is to provide a quick understanding to users about each study’s design. When writing these overviews, please consult the design report for the country in question where most of this information can be found. text: 2013 and 7 January 2014. The mode of interview was a mail-back questionnaire. The fieldwork period began one day before the Federal Election on 7 September and in total took 123 days. The questionnaire was administered in English and the fieldwork was carried out by the Survey Research Centre Pty Ltd. The study collected information from voters, that is Australian adults aged 18 years or over who were enrolled on the electoral register, and eligible to vote. A stratified random sampling procedure was used to compile a sample of respondents from the Australian Electoral Register which is administered by the Australia Electoral Commission (AEC). Initially, 15,000 records were provided, 100 from each electorate. The sample was provided by the AEC for use only for this study. Due to budget considerations, only 12,200 of the original sample was selected for the initial mail-out. The following strategy was used for sub-selection: 1) Randomly select 81 voters from each electorate (totally 12,150) 2) After Step 1, randomly select 1 additional voter from 50 randomly selected electorates. Sample records with an overseas mailing address were removed from the mailing sample. A total of 3,955 Surveys (3,379 via mail-back and 576 online) were received. 2) WEIGHTS The Australian Election Study provides a DEMOGRAPHIC WEIGHT. This weight was calculated to correct for the following: the disproportionate probability of selection, non-response in the survey, and to match known demographic characteristics of the population. This weight was calculated using rim weighting adjusting to four benchmarks. Figures for age, gender, and the state of residence were obtained from the AEC enrollment data for the 2013 election. Figures for voting came from the AEC Final Election Vote Tallies. For the category "(Voted Informal)/Did not vote," "Voted informally" is bracketed as this response is included in the dataset but not in the benchmark. The numbers represent only the number of enrolled voters who did not vote, i.e., the difference between the vote tally and the number of enrollments). Counts of invalid votes were obtained. However, it was impossible to ascertain how many invalid votes were deliberate (in which the case the respondent would give the "invalid vote" response) and how many were unintended (in which case the respondent would most likely not realize their vote was invalid and respond with their voting intention).

text: [Slide 1] CSES Secretariat Training: Education and ISCED Andrei Artimof GESIS Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Mannheim Mannheim, 3-5 February 2015 [Slide 2] Presentation Outline What is ISCED? From ISCED ‘76 to ISCED ‘97 ISCED 2011 CSES implementation of ISCED CSES difficulties in data harmonization Conclusions [Slide 3] What is ISCED? 1 [Slide 4] What is ISCED? I The International Standard Classification of Education It was developed in 1976 and is continuously revised by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS). WHAT? An advanced and systematic framework for gathering, compiling and analyzing cross-nationally comparable statistics and indicators on education. (p.6) HOW? An abstract classification system for harmonizing national education systems, their programmes and related qualifications into internationally comparable and transparent categories. http://www.uis.unesco.org/Education/Documents/isced-2011-en.pdf [Slide 5] What is ISCED? II It does not strive to provide a comprehensive definition of what education is. Rather, it is a comparative classification system of national education systems. Classification, not evaluation of each category: German PhD vs. Romanian PhD they are not weighted against each other in terms of quality The unit of classification is educational programmes and their related qualifications (more on this later). http://www.uis.unesco.org [Slide 6] Why do we need ISCED? Education as an institution varies strongly between countries. Education varies across time as new qualifications are introduced (MOOC degrees). As educational systems and their evaluations may vary to a large extent both across time and countries. WHY? education is a variable of interest in social research and is both consistently used as a dependent variable and more often an independent variable  we need a means to compare systems cross-nationally. [Slide 7] What is ISCED? III ISCED is the response! ISCED was designed in the early 1970s as a statistical instrument for representing education both within individual countries and internationally. The first version, ISCED 1976, was approved by the International Conference on Education (Geneva, 1975). It was developed for internal use and provided a basic classification of education levels by fields of study The second version, ISCED 1997, was approved by the UNESCO General Conference at its 29th session in November 1997 as part of efforts to increase the international comparability of education statistics. It measured education and training in more detail within the different levels of education. http://www.uis.unesco.org [Slide 8] What is ISCED? IV The third version, ISCED 2011, was adopted by UNESCO’s 36th General Conference in November 2011. It allows even more differentiation at the lowest and tertiary levels; it distinguishes between educational enrollment and educational attainment. http://www.uis.unesco.org [Slide 9] From ISCED ‘76 to ISCED ‘97 2 [Slide 10] ISCED – ‘76 I “The first drafts in preparation for ISCED were produced in 1958 when UNESCO presented a conceptual framework for describing four core areas of education (institutions, educational finance, illiteracy, and the educational attainment of the population).” (p.24) Before that, “an early pioneer of comparative education research named Nicholas Hans proposed in 1933 the development of an <<artificial terminology>> that should be implemented by all the states for comparative purposes.” (p.24) https://www.wbv.de/pdf/BWP_SE_EN_2013_Web.pdf#page=23 [Slide 11] ISCED – ‘76 II ISCED ‘76 had a very limited scope in defining education ISCED ‘97 was designed to improve the basic ISCED ‘76 guidelines [Slide 12] ISCED ‘76 educational categories http://unstats.un.org/unsd/iiss/International-Standard-Classification-of-Education-ISCED.ashx [Slide 13] Example of ISCED ‘76 codes [Slide 14] ISCED – 1997 I MOTIVATION: ISCED ‘76 was too crude of a classification to account for changes in educational systems, and it was not ideal for comparative statistical analyses  ISCED ‘97 ISCED ‘97 saw: the inclusion of guidelines on how national collaborators should go about classifying their educational programmes according to ISCED; ISCED ‘76 codification of educational programmes was done at a very basic level. ISCED ’97 allows for more sophistication; accordingly, comparisons between countries’ systems are more accurate because we are measuring equivalent concepts. [Slide 15] ISCED – 1997 II The biggest change between ISCED ‘76 and ISCED ‘97 is the introduction of a multi-dimensional classification framework which includes: 1. the type of subsequent education or destination to which the programme leads 2. the programme orientation general education – (gen/A) pre-vocational education – (prev/B) vocational education – (voc/C) 3. the programme’s cumulative duration (short, medium, long) 4. position in the national degree and qualification structure [Slide 16] ISCED – 1997 III The basic unit of classification of the ISCED ‘97 is the educational programme. In ISCED ‘97, a new category introduced to cover programmes: “post-secondary, non-tertiary”. Also, a new category combining some previous separate categories to cover tertiary education. The highest category is now reserved for programmes leading to advanced research qualifications only (PhDs). [Slide 17] ISCED – 1997 IV comparison ISCED ‘76 to ISCED ‘97 [Slide 18] Structure of ISCED 1997 e.g.: ISCED 3C would cover trainings which would allow unskilled laborers to get their worker’s permit e.g.: ISCED 5A are higher education programmes that are largely theoretically based (university studies) e.g.: ISCED 5B encompasses practical courses (technical schools, vocational colleges) [Slide 19] ISCED 2011 3 [Slide 20] ISCED – 2011 Changes I MOTIVATION: ISCED 2011 was an organic improvement over ISCED

text: ISCED 3C would cover trainings which would allow unskilled laborers to get their worker’s permit e.g.: ISCED 5A are higher education programmes that are largely theoretically based (university studies) e.g.: ISCED 5B encompasses practical courses (technical schools, vocational colleges) [Slide 19] ISCED 2011 3 [Slide 20] ISCED – 2011 Changes I MOTIVATION: ISCED 2011 was an organic improvement over ISCED ‘97 meant to reflect developments in education systems across the world and over time it clarified concepts and definitions: takes into account the education programmes of very young children clearly distinguishes between formal and non-formal education though it acknowledges informal learning (learning STATA at GESIS), it explicitly excludes it as a valid form of education tertiary education categories have been reworked and extended a more logical classification by giving more information (i.e.: collapsing categories further) [Slide 21] ISCED – 2011 Changes II ISCED 2011 now distinguishes between educational programmes and educational attainment. educational programmes (ISCED-P) educational attainment (ISCED-A) [Slide 22] ISCED – 2011 Variants I This distinction was introduced because the statistics collected via ISCED ’97 could not track programme attendance over time or programme completion. For scholars interested in the comparison of educational systems across countries it is now easier to assess the ‘performance’ of certain education programmes by measuring completion rates. For the users of CSES data, ISCED-P and ISCED-A has no relevant meaning. [Slide 23] ISCED – 2011 Changes II ISCED 2011 now distinguishes between educational programmes and educational attainment. educational programmes (ISCED-P) educational attainment (ISCED-A) ISCED 2011 introduced the concept of completion of ISCED levels  educational attainment. ISCED 2011 introduced a new coding systems both for educational programmes and for educational attainment. [Slide 24] ISCED – 2011: direct mappings ISCED mappings: “provide clear guideposts on how to report national education data for international purposes.” are currently under development and have yet to be finalized. The available national level mappings are based on ISCED ‘97 (at the present time). This means that when CSES micro-coders receive data that doesn’t correspond to ISCED, they first have to check degree equivalency with ISCED ‘97 before recoding that to ISCED 2011. http://www.uis.unesco.org/Education/ISCEDMappings/Pages/default.aspx [Slide 25] ISCED – 2011 Definitions I in ISCED 2011 the unit of classification is the national education programmes and the related recognized educational qualifications; ISCED 2011: “An education programme is defined as a coherent set or sequence of educational activities or communication designed and organized to achieve pre-determined learning objectives or accomplish a specific set of educational tasks over a sustained period.” (p.7) ISCED 1997: “An array or sequence of educational activities which are organized to accomplish a pre-determined objective or a specified set of educational tasks.” (p.11) http://www.uis.unesco.org [Slide 26] ISCED – 2011 Definitions II

[…] it is complementary to formal education within the process of lifelong learning of individuals.” (e.g.: literacy, life and work skills, specializations) (p.11) informal education: “is defined as forms of learning that are intentional or deliberate, but are not institutionalized.” (e.g.: within the family, at the workplace, community, social interactions) (p.12) [Slide 29] ISCED – 2011 Tertiary categories I Key difference for CSES Where the ISCED ‘97 scale had seven sorting categories in total, ISCED 2011 now has nine categories of education differentiation ISCED 2011 now has 4 instead of 2 levels of tertiary education classifications: ISCED 1997 distinguished between first stage and second stage of tertiary studies ISCED 2011 distinguishes between: Short-cycle Tertiary Bachelor’s Master’s Doctoral Studies [Slide 30] ISCED – 2011 Tertiary categories II [Slide 31] ISCED – 2011 overview [Slide 32] CSES implementation of ISCED 4 [Slide 33] CSES and ISCED The CSES doesn’t impose on its collaborators the manner in which demographic data is collected. Instead, the goal was to standardize the coding of each socio-demographic variable to a common, cross-national scheme. CSES Modules 1 through 3 used the same schema for coding education. It was not based on any existing standardized schema for clasifying educational attainment (such as ISCED ‘97). CSES Module 4 was the first one to use ISCED 2011 to code education  focus on economic issues. [Slide 34] CSES: measuring education M1-M3 01.

For this, we used the ISCED 2011 specifications about the duration of each education level to approximate placement of respondents into the different ISCED categories (code in next slide). We are awaiting validation of our coding decisions by the national collaborators. We’ve also separated the ‘don’t know’ and ‘missing’ answers into the appropriate categories. Given the limited scope of its implementation within the CSES (we use only the highest level of aggregation) and its standing as a comparative framework, ISCED should be kept in future modules. A revision of ISCED in the near future is highly unlikely. ISCED actually has the flexibility to account for future educational developments (such as informal learning). If in the future CSES would require even more precision in estimating a respondent’s educational level, ISCED can provide that. [Slide 50] ISCED – Conclusions II In essence, no matter how the collaborators might gather the data, ISCED 2011 will provide the conceptual correspondence. [Slide 51] Thank you for your attention!

text: Dear Theodore, I trust you are well. I’m Steve Quinlan, the new co -manager of the CSES project along with Dave Howell. It is very nice to make your acquaintance. I am writing to you in respect of the CSES Greek data deposit which you provided us with in the Autumn. We have a number of questions and clarifications that we are seeking with respect to both the micro data (see questions AA1 -AA7) and the macro data (see question ZZ1) for Greece listed below. To enable us to include Greece in the next advance release of CSES Module 4, which is due for release in early spring 2015, we would appreciate your answers to the above questions by 1 February 2015 . Can you give me a sense if this is possible? If I can be of any assistance to you in responding to these questions, please do n ot hesitate to contact me. text: CSES Project Manager June 27, 2025 Core Role The CSES Project Manager co-leads the CSES Secretariat, the project’s organization hub (in conjunction with the Director of Studies of the project). Their goal is to ensure the project is delivered on time, within scope and aligns with stakeholder expectations, user needs, and ethical standards. Key Responsibilities PROJECT PLANNING & DELIVERY Define the project scope, objectives, timelines, and deliverables for each year (In conjunction with the Director of Studies). Develop an annual detailed project plan, including milestones/deliverable and risk assessments (In conjunction with the Director of Studies). Set up systems and processes to track project against deliverables and timelines. Draft progress reports, updates, and documentation for internal and external stakeholders. STAKEHOLDER LIAISON, EXTERNAL COMMUNICATION, & PUBLIC DISSEMINATION Serve on the CSES Planning Committee (PC, the project’s governing board) in an ex-officio capacity. Serve as one of the two primary points of contact between the CSES Secretariat and the CSES PC and CSES Collaborators. Maintain ongoing communication with stakeholders to ensure alignment with project goals, address emerging issues, and report on progress, including Liaising with CSES project collaborators globally on implementing the CSES survey in national election studies and ensuring data quality guidelines. Contribute to project’s public engagement strategy, including the organization of public events (e.g., Klingemann Prize Award), academic panels at scientific conferences, and project meetings (PC meetings) and Conferences (Plenary). Principal coordination contact point between the project and GESIS ensuring compliance and collaborative efforts with one of our custodians. Support preparation of presentations about CSES to conferences and policy roundtables. SECRETARIAT CO-ORDINATION & OPERATIONS MANAGEMENT Assign and oversee tasks across the CSES Secretariat Team. Conduct regular 1on1 meetings with CSES Secretariat Team to track progress, address challenges, and mentor team members toward achieving project goals. Organize and facilitate team meetings, document outcomes, and follow up on action items. Organize the CSES Secretariat Annual General Meeting (AGM). Spearhead internal documentation guidelines and workflows to ensure consistency and multifunctionality of the team. Monitor human resource allocations, including contracts for researchers or assistants. Procure necessary services or tools for CSES Secretariat to function (e.g., software; student assistants; consultants). PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT Serve on the CSES Planning Committee (ex-officio) and co-devise the CSES Module survey, a comparative post-election study fielded in over fifty states. Develop project policies and procedures. Oversee data management, harmonization workflows, anonymization procedures, and version control ensuring accuracy, consistency, and alignment with the project’s policies. Devise scripts for & oversee Cross-National Phase (CNP) of data processing including setting out key milestones on the Road to Release. Facilitate reproducibility and transparency, by documenting methodologies, and processes and organizing the internal project repository (i.e., Dropbox). Central role in shaping the product’s documentation ensuring all documentation

text: 1 Adding COVID -19 Macro Data to CSES Module 5: Rationale, Parameters, and Recommendations Memorandum prepared by Steve Quinlan July 7, 2022 Memorandum Purpose This memorandum discusses the CSES Module 5 approach to classifying the COVID -19 pandemic, specifically macro data classifying COVID -19 contextual conditions. The note’s chief function is to recommend that the CSES Secretariat collect several variables to capture the context of the COVID -19 pandemic – circumstances potentially pertinen t to some studies that implemented CSES Module 5 partially or fully during the pandemic and include these additional variables in the full release of the CSES Module 5 product . The memo advances as follows: first, I outline the rationale for COVID -19 macr o data to be incorporated in Module 5 . Next, I provide an overview of the CSES Module 5 studies impacted by the pandemic and go on to outline the parameters ( and constraints) in which CSES Module 5 operates for the studies in question , and how t hese circum stances guide the recommendations for addition al variables. Finally , the note details the proposed COVID -19 macro variable additions for CSES Module 5 , before concluding with a summary of the proposals and the conditions in which the recommendations apply. A Rationale for including COVID -19 Macro Data in CSES Module 5 At the time of writing, COVID -19 was first discovered in Novembe r 2019 before eventually being declared a global pandemic on March 11, 2020 by the World Health Organization.1 The COVID - 19 pandemic could be described as an epoch – a memorable fundamental event of our times that has had profound implications for citizen health, economics, global food supply, education, medicine, societal norms and lifestyle, and individual freedom and democracy. Specifically, for CSES, several Module 5 studies were conducted partially or entirely duri ng the pandemic , impacting the implementation of these studies in various guises .2 Given its profound effect on 1 It is possible human -to-human transmission of th e disease was occurring before this discovery. This variable relates not only to the election timing but also to the fieldwork of the post -election study. Macro Data Collection in CSES : Parameters and COVID -19 dat a addition strategy CSES’ prime function is to collect data that will help in understanding turnout and vote choice from a comparative perspective. This mission opens the possibility of CSES collecting an unending plethora of contextual data. CSES has been a pioneer in developing micro -macro designs in social science surveys (e.g., Fortin -Rittberger et al., 2016; Howell, 2010) . As of CSES Module 5 Advance Release 4 (March 1, 2022), there are over 100 different variables measuring contextual conditions . While collecting macro data is a core dimension of the project, CSES has adop ted three criteria to determine its choice of which macro data to collect. If either of the three criteria is met, CSES consider s the inclusion of macro data indicator s. The benchmarks are: 1. If the macro data is deemed relevant in helping to understand turnout and vote choice in a comparative context. 2. If the macro data is particularly pertinent to the theme of a CSES Module. 3. If the macro data would be unavailable where CSES did not collect it (e.g., expert ideological classifications of parti es included in CSES). So how to approach collecting COVID -19 macro data within these parameters? While there is evolving evidence that COVID -19 impact s turnout and vote choice (e.g., Constantino et al., 2021; Giommoni & Lourneau, 2020; Haute et al., 2021; Picchio & Santolini, 2022) , and is linked to wider questions on democracy (e.g., misinformation, conspiracy theories) and election administration (see Birch et al., 2021; Engler et al., 2021; Pennycook & Rand, 2021; Uscinski et al., 2020) , this research area is embryonic, especially from a comparative perspective. And while the evidence of meaningful impacts is admittedly promising, given that most of the studies within CSES Module 5 were not subject to a COVID -19 intrusion, the relevance an d value of collecting a large plethora of information on COVID -19 is questionable. Additionally, Module 5’s theme is not

Regarding data availability, there are several organizations providing data on COVID -19. But the three most promising databases from a comparative perspective and with their temporal scope of data are the following: • Oxford COVID -19 Government Response Tracker (OXCGRT) – see https://ourworldindata.org/ • World Health Organization ( WHO) Coronavirus Database – see https://covid19.who.int/ • John Hopkins Coronavirus Resource Centre – see https://coronavirus.jhu.edu/map.html The OXCGRT provides a systematic comparative and temporal dataset of how government responses have evolved during the pandemic and aggregate data on all the aforementioned variables are provided free of charge.5 Consequently, it is proposed that this data set provide the first go to source for any of the recommended additions. If the data is not available from the OXCGRT, the other two databases offer alternatives. 5 In their mission statement, they maintain that “data is a public good” – see https://ourworldindata.org/about (Accessed: July 5, 2022). 5 Methodological issues COVID -19 vaccinations were not widely available or distributed until 2021. COVID -19 data is no different, with many of the abov e variables the subject of competing definitions and counting strategies (SDG Plus UNCTAD, 2021) . There is also the matter of data availability with time lags in reporting; and some polities report some kinds of information, while others do not. This latte r problem is particularly the case with hospitalization and testing information with the availability of data patchy across the potential applicable cases in CSES Module 5. Thus, it is recommended not to include these indicators in Module 5. Societal restrictions were prominent in the fight against COVID -19. While comparative data appears plentiful, there is a plethora of available data covering issues like face coverings, travel constraints, and school closures, among other things. Consequent ly, it is unclear what data capturing societal restrictions should be collected and what shouldn’t. One alternative to this issue would be to incorporate composite measures such as the Government Stringency Index or Containment Health Indexes .6 While such indices are compiled by reputable organizations and appear to be in sync with open science principles, and are thus promising, these are relatively new measures and at the time of writing, their validation and reliability is unknown. Consequent ly, it is suggested these measures not be included in the CSES Module 5. Nor are any individual societal measures recommended for direct inclusion. Instead, it is proposed to include an additional administrative variable to ensure that these data can be “b ridged” to CSES Module 5 by users directly should they wish to and that these databased be highlighted to users on the CSES Data Bridging webpage.7 6 The Government Stringency metric is produced by the Oxford Coronavirus Government Response Tracker (Oxford Coronavirus Government Response Tracker (OxCGRT), 2022) . The nine metrics used to calculate the Stringency Index are school closures; workplace closu res; cancellation of public events; restrictions on public gatherings; closures of public transport; stay -at-home requirements; public information campaigns; restrictions on internal movements; and international travel control . COVID -19 data is most often reported daily. This raises the question of what time horizon is relevant to measure . The premise of retrospective voting is that voters hold their representatives accountable based on looking back at their performance - specifically rewarding or punishing governments based on their management of issues like the economy, crises, etc. (Fiorina, 1981; Key, 1966) . In economic voting studies, the conventional retrospective horizon is usually one -year (e.g., Lewis -Beck, 1988; Lewis -Beck & Stegmaier, 2000) , but research has shown voters are attentive beyond that (e.g., Stiers et al., 2020) . At t he time of writing, there is no consensus on the appropriate time horizon for COVID - 19 retrospective judgments. Indeed, borrowing a time horizon of one year will not fit most of the studies CSES Module 5 has at its disposal. Given the lack of clarity on a particular time horizon, it is proposed to offer users three different measures based on the timing of the election: T -14 days from the election; T -28 days from the election; T -91 days from the election. These time horizons are admittedly somewhat arbitrar y. Nevertheless, it would ensure CSES users are offered three different time points that fit with the data CSES Module 5 has at its disposal and time points on the same measurement scale (corresponding to two weeks, four weeks, and 13 weeks from the electi on). It will offer users sufficient variety and empower them to decide what time horizon is most suitable for their analysis. text: [Slide 1] CSES Secretariat Training Macro Data STEVE QUINLAN AND BOJAN TODISJEVIC Nashville, October, 23-4, 2025. [Slide 2] Presentation Outline Macro Data: What and why? The CSES and Macro Data: Our USP and Module 6. CSES & Macro Data: Some conventions & standards. Collecting and Processing CSES Macro Data. Common Challenges with CSES Macro Data. [Slide 3] Macro Data: what and why? 1 [Slide 4] What is macro data? Big picture data: Information that describes whole systems/populations or aggregates information. Aggregated data: Combines information about lower units into a higher unit. This information summarizes the properties of the lower units (Diez-Roux 2002). E.g.: GDP/Unemployment stats/Government spending stats. Aggregation of traits of a geographical unit. System level data: Measures properties of the state/politicial system (i.e.: characteristics of the higher units themselves). Institutional variables: Electoral System Regime Indices: Democracy (e.g.: Freedom House/Polity IV). [Slide 5] Substantive advantages of macro data Allows us to disentangle causal heterogeneity (i.e.: are relationships influenced by context?) Allows us to test the generalizability of our findings (Pzeworski & Teune 1970). New research frontiers can be opened. Enables temporal analysis of change. Policy: Decisions in regards to electoral system reforms can benefit from knowing the associations between system features and public attitudes and behaviors (e.g.: Gallagher 1998; Bowler & Donovan 2012; Karp 2013). [Slide 6] Methodological advantages of macro data Model specification: Allows for multi-level modelling. Data is highly clustered by country and consequently violates assumption of observational independence underestimates standard error estimates (Hox 2002; Gelman and Hill 2007; Arceneaux and Nickerson 2009). Model specification: Reduces omitted variable bias. Offers standardization: enhancing cross-national comparability. Transparency & replication: a gold standard is greatly enhanced by the inclusion of contextual variables in cross-national surveys. [Slide 7] The Rationale for the CSES I Rokkan (1970): Co-ordinated cross-national research to explore ways “through secondary analysis of independently conducted surveys the strucutral contexts of the individuals reactions to politics” There is wide variations across countries of… Electoral rules. Presidential or parliamentary systems. Federalism vs. unitary governments. Lines of political conflict …and more. How do these variations impact individual attitudes and behaviours, especially voting and turnout? [Slide 8] The Rationale for the CSES II CSES objective is to heed Rokkan‘s call to investigate the impact of system level variables cross-nationally on citizen behaviour: “We want to make theoretical and substantive advances in our understanding of how variation in the institutional arrangements that govern the conduct of elections affect the nature and quality of electoral choice in democratic Polities. Through comparative analysis, where citizens are observed in different settings, the impact of institutions can be established.” (“Guiding Principles”, Final Report of the 1995-96 Planning Committee)  Need for macro level data to be collected. [Slide 16] CSES: Freedom Status of Elections Majority of studies that comprise CSES are collected in polities that have free or partly free elections. However, sometimes a Collaborator will include the CSES module in a study of a polity that is a developing democracy or that is considered “not free”. If the data collection is judged to be of sufficiently high quality, the study is included in CSES datasets even if the polity is considered to be “not free”. CSES products: Freedom House; Polity IV; V-Dem (M6). Only studies that would be deemed free are eligible for funding under the CSES seed funding initiative. [Slide 17] Party Coding in CSES: Instructions Each party/coalition appearing in CSES receives a unique numerical code. These codes are used to identify who R voted for in current & previous election & Party ID (if applicable). Top 6-9 party/coalitions applicable also receive an alphabetical code for relational data purposes. Guideline on Dropbox provides information on how to classify parties/coalitions numerically and alphabetically under various conditions: CSES Secretariat II/CSES Guidelines & Policies/CSES - Coding of Party_Coalition & Leader_Classification Schemes & Documentation/Party & Coalition Alphabetical and Numerical Classification Macro coder determines allocation of numerical and alphabetical party/coalition codes in accordance with policy above. If micro coders work ahead of macro coder, they send their proposed table to the macro coder. [Slide 18] Party/Coalition Codes – Numerical Since CSES M5, numerical party codes have six digits. Numerical party codes have the following structure: Germany 2021 276001. DEU – Social Democratic Party (SPD) 276005. DEU – Left Party UN country code. Number of studies from the same country in the module (0 usually; but 1 if polity appears in CSES Module more than once). Party code (01=highest vote share, 05= fifth highest, etc.). [Slide 19] Party/Coalition Codes – Alphabetical Alphabetical codes are assigned to the six most popular parties/coalitions, ordered in descending order of their share of the popular vote in the parliamentary election (unless otherwise stated). Alphabetical codes are required so respondent data can be linked to party/coalition assessments: R likeability of the party/coalition. R left-right placement of the party/coalition. The said party/coalition's share of the seats in the election. The said party/coalition's share of cabinet portfolios before and after the election. Alphabetical party codes have the following structure – Denmark 2022 example: 208001. DNK – Social Democratic (SD) PARTY A 208002. DNK – Liberal Party (V) PARTY B

text: [Sheet: Overview and Instructions] Template to Recode Parties from CSES Module 4 Dataset to IMD Party Codes based on IMD Party Table by: CS (Jan.29, 2018) Explanation & Instructions: Based on the template below, IMD coders can generate the STATA commands to recode the party codes used in CSES Modules into the IMD party codes that are consistent across time. There are six columns that need to be filled in. All of these information can easily be obtained from the IMD Party Table by sorting the codes of the respective CSES Module that is recoded and then, copying and pasting the information that needs to be filled in. After filling in the information, the lines can be copied and pasted in the IMD processing Stata DoFile. This file contains separate sheets for each of the variables for which party codes are used. CSES IMD processors must enter the information thats required and can then go on to copy and past the code based in the template into their STATA DoFiles in the appropriate places. The table below is an EXAMPLE of how information would need to be filled in by IMD processors to recode the party codes for Austria 2013 and Norway 2013 into IMD party codes for variable IMD3002_LH_PL (CURRENT LOWER HOUSE ELECTION: VOTE CHOICE - PARTY LIST). Use grey shades to highlight the codes for different countries in this template and leave one blank row in between countries when creating the code for the different variables. Enter the party codes by variable in alphabetial order, following the first letter of the country name. Also, leave an empty row between pary codes for different countries and add the Country Name and Year with "* COUNTRY". This will make both the template and the code in the STATA DoFile clearer. Finally, when copying and pasting the code in STATA, note that it will create tabs that STATA cannot handle when running the code. See the processing guidelines for tipps and tricks on how to eliminate these tabs. Good luck. These are listed in separate columns in the IMD Party Table next to the Module to which they refer. text: 1 CSES IMD: Phase I V – Proposed Plan and Outstanding Issues Memorandum prepared by Steve Quinlan and Katharina Blinzler September 2022 Memorandum Purpose This memorandum sets out the key goals of Phase IV of the CSES IMD release . The memo briefly summarizes CSES IMD releases' current status and the unifying principle underlying the data product . It then sets out the two key objectives of Phase IV and a tentative calendar of delivery . Next, w e provide an o verview of the work involved in a chieving these goals . We briefly outline our proposed recommendation and rationale for not including district data in CSES IMD Phase IV . Finally , we conclude with a workflow proposal as to how CSES IMD can be delivered by the Secretariat. CSES IMD: The Story So Far As of September 2022 CSES IMD has had t hree releases: • December 2018: Phase I – Launch of the dataset including harmonized numerical coding of parties/coalitions over time. 137 variables; 174 election studies; 281,083 respondents; 55 polities; 600+parties. • October 2019: Phase II – addition of substantial segment of macro data to IMD. 137 variables added to the dataset (total number of variables: 276). Most eligible survey variables now incorporated into CSES IMD.1 Also improved documentation. • December 2020 : Phase III – addition of substantial segment of macro, demographic, and administrative variables in addition to derivative and data bridging variables . 113 variables added to the dataset (total number of variables: 389). Also improved documentation. With these three phases of CSES IMD, we estimate approximately 85% of the product has been delivered to users. 1 The Unifying Principle of the CSES IMD is the 3 and 1 Rule . The 3 refers to the variable level and specifies that a variable must appear in at least three modules (up to an including Module 5) for eligibility for inclusion in CSES IMD. The 1 refers to the polity level and stipulates that any study that appears in CSES is eligible for inclusion in the IMD. This unifying principle was adopted at the CSES Planning Committee (PC) Meeting in Mannheim in November 2017 and re -affirmed by acclamation at the CSES PC Meeting in Göteborg in June 2018. 2 CSES IMD: Phase IV – Key objectives and Calendar of Delivery The focus of the Phase IV Release of CSES IMD is to deliver 97% of the planned CSES IMD product to users . Hence, Phase IV has two central objectives: 1. To add Module 5 observations to the IMD and harmonize to CSES IMD standards. 2.
