To add Module 5 observations to the IMD and harmonize to CSES IMD standards. 2. To add outstanding eligible administrative , survey, and macro data to the CSES IMD. An additional su pplementary objective is to potentially include additional weights data , but this a matter for discussion at the A GM. Phase IV of CSES IMD involves a hybrid approach compared to Phases I -III as we will be adding both observations (the principal goal of Phase I) and variables (the principal goal of Phases II -III respectively) simultaneously. Work on Phase IV would primaril y be conducted in 2023, with substantial work beginning upon the Full Release of Module 5 (anticipated between April -August 2023). Given current CSES resources, we expect Phase IV would require 5-6 months of work, with an anticipated release potentially oc curring between October 2023 and March 2024.2 Post Phase IV, an update of the IMD would not be required until the Full Release of Module 6 (anticipated in 2028). The Key Features of CSES IMD Phase IV The first key objective of Phase IV is the addition of Module 5 observations to the IMD and harmonization of the variables to CSES IMD standard. We anticipate this will involve approximately 105,000 observations and 260 variables in total.3 From a cursory analysis, we anticipate that approximately 60% of these variables could be classified as low intensity resource variables – variables that are straightforward and can be coded with relative ease. Of the remaining variables, we anticipate about 20% could be classified as high resource intensive variables and these are listed in Table 1. The remaining variables are medium resource intensive. The second objective of Phase IV is to add outstanding eligible administrative, survey, and macro data to th e CSES IMD. We list these variables in Table 2. In total, there are approximately 30 variables here eligible for inclusion. Most are low intensity resource wise, but there are a few, marked in ORANGE which are complicated. 2 This assumes CSES r esources and experiences are ceterus paribus, perhaps ambitious. 3 Currently, there are 76,123 observations in CSES M5 AR4. District Data and Phase IV Currently, there is no district data included in CSES IMD. In early internal discussions, there was an expectation that district data would be included in IMD in line with the "3 and 1 rule". Yet the stimulus paper, launched with phase 1 of CSES IMD in 201 8, makes no explicit mention of district data , and their inclus ion have never been publicly promised. While the recent Planning Committee has endorsed district data's continued inclusion in CSES, there are some harmonization challenges with the inclusion of district data. First is harmonizing the respondent's primary electoral district across time (e.g., en suring a respondent in London Ruislip is consistently allocated to this district across CSES Modules). Of course, this does not consider boundary changes, which is beyond the power of CSES. Of course, this does not consider boundary changes, which is beyond the power of CSES. Second is the lack of consistency in the district data in specific polities due to electoral changes (e.g., Romania). Table 3 details the eligible district variables eligible for inclusion in CSES IMD according to the “3 and 1 rule”. 6 Table 3 District data variables eligible for inclusion in CSES IMD under the “3 and 1 rule” Variable Description No. Primary Electoral District 1 Number of seats in district 2 Number of seats in district: nationwide district 3 Number of candidates in district 4 Number of candidates in district: nationwide district 5 Number of party lists in district 6 Number of party lists in district: nationwide district 7 Number of party lists in district 8 Percent vote in district Party A -I 9-17 Percent vote in district Party A -I: nationwide district 18-26 Turnout in district 27 Turnout in district: nationwide district 28 Note: The nationwide district variables would be eligible as pre -CSES Module 4, we did not make a distinction between nationwide and non-nationwide electoral districts. To ensure CSES IMD is in line with the latest CSES products, we would incorporate the national and non-nationwide distinction. While these challenges are not insurmountable, the resources available to us to achieve these goals in Phase IV are limited. Focusing on including district data at this stage would distract from Phase IV 's critical goals. It would also likely contribute to delays in delivering this product and CSES Module 6. As the demand for district data among users is limited, it is proposed not to include district data in Phase IV. Instead, the inclusion of district d ata should be determined at the next release of CSES IMD (scheduled for 2028). text: CSES IMD: Phase IV – Proposed Plan and Outstanding Issues Memorandum prepared by Steve Quinlan and Katharina Blinzler September 2022 Memorandum Purpose This memorandum sets out the key goals of Phase IV of the CSES IMD release. The memo briefly summarizes CSES IMD releases' current status and the unifying principle underlying the data product. It then sets out the two key objectives of Phase IV and a tentative calendar of delivery. Next, we provide an overview of the work involved in achieving these goals. We briefly outline our proposed recommendation and rationale for not including district data in CSES IMD Phase IV. Finally, we conclude with a workflow proposal as to how CSES IMD can be delivered by the Secretariat. CSES IMD: The Story So Far As of September 2022 CSES IMD has had three releases: December 2018: Phase I – Launch of the dataset including harmonized numerical coding of parties/coalitions over time. 137 variables; 174 election studies; 281,083 respondents; 55 polities; 600+parties. October 2019: Phase II – addition of substantial segment of macro data to IMD. 137 variables added to the dataset (total number of variables: 276). Most eligible survey variables now incorporated into CSES IMD. Also improved documentation. December 2020: Phase III – addition of substantial segment of macro, demographic, and administrative variables in addition to derivative and data bridging variables. 113 variables added to the dataset (total number of variables: 389). Also improved documentation. With these three phases of CSES IMD, we estimate approximately 85% of the product has been delivered to users. CSES IMD: Phase IV – Key objectives and Calendar of Delivery The focus of the Phase IV Release of CSES IMD is to deliver 97% of the planned CSES IMD product to users. Hence, Phase IV has two central objectives: To add Module 5 observations to the IMD and harmonize to CSES IMD standards. To add outstanding eligible administrative, survey, and macro data to the CSES IMD. An additional supplementary objective is to potentially include additional weights data, but this a matter for discussion at the AGM. Phase IV of CSES IMD involves a hybrid approach compared to Phases I-III as we will be adding both observations (the principal goal of Phase I) and variables (the principal goal of Phases II-III respectively) simultaneously. Work on Phase IV would primarily be conducted in 2023, with substantial work beginning upon the Full Release of Module 5 (anticipated between April-August 2023). Given current CSES resources, we expect Phase IV would require 5-6 months of work, with an anticipated release potentially occurring between October 2023 and March 2024. Post Phase IV, an update of the IMD would not be required until the Full Release of Module 6 (anticipated

The Key Features of CSES IMD Phase IV The first key objective of Phase IV is the addition of Module 5 observations to the IMD and harmonization of the variables to CSES IMD standard. We anticipate this will involve approximately 105,000 observations and 260 variables in total. From a cursory analysis, we anticipate that approximately 60% of these variables could be classified as low intensity resource variables – variables that are straightforward and can be coded with relative ease. Of the remaining variables, we anticipate about 20% could be classified as high resource intensive variables and these are listed in Table 1. The remaining variables are medium resource intensive. The second objective of Phase IV is to add outstanding eligible administrative, survey, and macro data to the CSES IMD. We list these variables in Table 2. In total, there are approximately 30 variables here eligible for inclusion. Most are low intensity resource wise, but there are a few, marked in ORANGE which are complicated. Table 1 Module 5 variables to be added in CSES IMD Phase IV which are high intensity A potential supplementary objective of Phase IV could be to add additional weight data to the CSES IMD: Currently, CSES includes the three original weights from each national election study (conventionally variable _1010 in Standalone CSES products), namely: Sample weight: intended to correct for unequal selection probabilities resulting from booster sample procedures or other sample design features Demographics weight: intended to adjust sample distributions of socio-demographic characteristics to resemble the features of the population more closely. Political weight: intended to reconcile discrepancies in the reported electoral behavior of respondents vis-à-vis official electoral counts. Open questions to be discussed at AGM: Should we add a fourth slot for the existing weights to distinguish weights which include mixtures of the above three? Should we have factor mean weights? Should we have polity weights? Should we have dataset weights? At the time of writing, there are plans for CSES to revisit its weighting approach for Module 6. Consequently, it may be prudent to take a minimalist approach at this stage and not do any follow ups until the Module 6 data is added. District Data and Phase IV Currently, there is no district data included in CSES IMD. In early internal discussions, there was an expectation that district data would be included in IMD in line with the "3 and 1 rule". Yet the stimulus paper, launched with phase 1 of CSES IMD in 2018, makes no explicit mention of district data, and their inclusion have never been publicly promised. While the recent Planning Committee has endorsed district data's continued inclusion in CSES, there are some harmonization challenges with the inclusion of district data. First is harmonizing the respondent's primary electoral district across time (e.g., ensuring a respondent in London Ruislip is consistently allocated to this district across CSES Modules). Of course, this does not consider boundary changes, which is beyond the power of CSES. Second is the lack of consistency in the district data in specific polities due to electoral changes (e.g., Romania). Table 3 details the eligible district variables eligible for inclusion in CSES IMD according to the “3 and 1 rule”. Table 3 District data variables eligible for inclusion in CSES IMD under the “3 and 1 rule” Note: The nationwide district variables would be eligible as pre-CSES Module 4, we did not make a distinction between nationwide and non-nationwide electoral districts. To ensure CSES IMD is in line with the latest CSES products, we would incorporate the national and non-nationwide distinction. While these challenges are not insurmountable, the resources available to us to achieve these goals in Phase IV are limited. Focusing on including district data at this stage would distract from Phase IV's critical goals. It would also likely contribute to delays in delivering this product and CSES Module 6. As the demand for district data among users is limited, it is proposed not to include district data in Phase IV. Instead, the inclusion of district data should be determined at the next release of CSES IMD (scheduled for 2028). text: 1 “It’s Time ” for a CSES Collaborator Pack Memorandum prepared by Steve Quinlan September 2022 Purpose This brief memorandum sets out the motivation for the development by the CSES Secretariat of a CSES Collaborator Pack. It is a maximum 4 -5 page brochure explaining to collaborators (potential or recognized) what the CSES is and how it oper ates, how to administer CSES in their study, the benefits and responsibilities as CSES collaborators, and provides a quick guide to CSES jargon. It also sets out a “road to publication” for Collaborators. The note advances as follows: First, I put forward the advantages of developing such a pack. Following this, I list items proposed for inclusion in the first draft of the Pack and the structure and style it might take. I conclude with a proposed Launch Timetable for the Pack. Why develop a CSES Collaborator Pack? Providing a CSES Collaborator Pack has many potential benefits and ad vantages, including: • Responsibility: Fulfilling our integral responsibility to Collaborators to provide them with the necessary information to ensure quality standards are adhered to. Even experienced stakeholders could benefit by using the Pack to refresh their memories on a feature of CSES they aren't as familiar with. • Brand Promotion : A potential valuable resource in attracting new Collaborators to CSES. • Education: This would improve stakeholders (Collaborators, Planning Committee) understand ing of the CSES's operation. Also potentially beneficial to users who may refer to this to understand CSES without traversing various website segments. • Transparency & Sustainability: Ensures pellucidity of CSES processes (including change in procedures an d standards) and avoids knowledge of the project's operations being invested in one or few persons. • Diversity: Potential for the product to diversify the CSES offering as the Pack could be offered in several languages besides English (e.g., German, French , Spanish). What should be included in a CSES Collabor ator Pack? The key objective of the Collaborator Pack would be to provide Collaborators (and other Stakeholders – e.g., Planning Committee) with a quick guide as to the CSES and to provide a guide through the series of steps for CSES to be administered correctly and comprehensively in a study. The following topics could be included in the brochure: • Brief s ummary of what CSES , its history , and its funding (4-5 lines) • Who the main CSES Stakeholders are? (E.g., Secretariat, Collaborators, Plenary). 2 • Benefits of being a CSES Collaborator (bullet point form).1 • Demys tifying CSES jargon: ❖ What is the Design Report ? ❖ What is the Macro Report ? ❖ What are Collaborator Questions ? ❖ What is the Plenary & Planning Committee ? ❖ CSES position

Structure & Style The Pack should be a maximum of 4 /5-A4 pages (1.5 -spaced), concise, accessible, and bright – readers should want to read it and should be able to find information quickly. Long blocks of text and pages tightly packed with written and graphic content can make user guid es or manuals feel intimidating and unfriendly. The design should be inviting. Launch Timetable , Location of the Pack, and Distribution to Collaborators The Pack should be no later than Spring 2023 and be designed in line with Module 6 guidelines. text: Data Playground David Howell October 25, 2023 CSES Secretariat Annual Meeting Belgrade, Serbia Funding Three innovations funded through a grant from the U.S. National Science Foundation: 1.Data Playground * 2.Curriculum Tools * 3.Seed Grants * David Howell and outgoing CSES chair Liz Zechmeister will work on the resourcing and day - to-day implementation of these two initiatives under the guidance of the Planning Committee. Data Playground Data Playground Goal: Innovate on data dissemination Data access is a core CSES principle. •CSES seeks to extend data access by developing a Data Playground •A Data Playground is an interactive point- and- click means that junior scholars and non- specialists can use to create visualizations •Many Data Playgrounds exist; some examples are… Data Playground: ANES Data Playground: BES Data Playground: LAPOP Progress so far Liz and Dave have begun thinking about: •The target audience(s) for the tool •The user interface and experience •Limiting variables and functions by design •What visualizations would be most useful •Documentation and advice about the tool, variables, weighting, and analysis •Helping users understand/evaluate data quality Progress so far Liz and Dave have begun thinking about: •The timeline for the effort and deliverables •A RFP to hire professionals to implement it •What platform to program it on •Graphic design •How to import updated data into the tool •How to maintain the system thereafter There is a lot to think through!

text: Summary of Module 7 Proposals Received October 9, 2023 CSES Module 7 Planning Committee Lisbon, Portugal Proposal 1 Broken Connections? Voters' Perceptions of Political Parties in Unstable Times Authors : Jacob R. Gunderson and Ann- Kristin Kölln Proposal 1: Gunderson and Kölln Broken Connections? Voters' Perceptions of Political Parties in Unstable Times Summary: •Summarize existing research on voters ’ perceptions ofpolitical parties and suggest a battery ofquestions for inclusion in the seventh module of the (CSES) thatwould enable scholars to more thoroughly understand thevoter- party linkage in both established andyoung democratic systems . •what voters think about thecorrect role thatparties play in their democracies •thedegree to which voters believe parties succeed in those tasks •howvoters perceive parties to differ from oneanother •howvoters perceive andevaluate intraparty divisions . Proposal 1: Gunderson and Kölln 17-42 Questions Proposed : •(1) Parties –necessary vs. not needed •(5) Importance of each of five party functions •(1) Parties –single stance vs. set of strong views •(3) Driving factors of disagreement within parties •(1) How should engage with disagreement •(1) Differences of choice options •(1) Last election parties different/similar issues Proposal 1: Gunderson and Kölln 17-42 Questions Proposed : •(1-9) Each party: extent internally divided •(1-9) Each party: what divided on (open- ended?) •(1-2) Parties represent your views / which best •(1-9) Each party: difficulty placing left -right Proposal 2 Partisanship and affective polarization around the world Authors : Eelco Harteveld, Luana Russo, Markus Wagner Proposal 2: Harteveld et al Partisanship and affective polarization around the world Summary: •Revisiting partisanship andaffective polarization. •Runa set ofadditional items thatmeasure partisanship , both positive andnegative, as wellas affective polarization, bothactual andperceived . These measures willbe useful in providing important descriptive analyses ofhowvoters relate to parties , theirsupporters andtheparty system , as wellas in generating answers concerning thelink between polarization andvote choice , social group membership , anddemocratic attitudes . Proposal 2: Harteveld et al 13-43 Questions Proposed : •(1-9) Each party: Like -dislike supporters •(2) Positive partisanship —insult at criticism of party; connected with supporters •(4-26) Negative partisanship —Party feel most distant from, more distant from —Each party [less one]: disconnection, feel good about criticism of, could never vote for due to party values Proposal 2: Harteveld et al 13-43 Questions Proposed : •(2) Ideological polarization —divided on values, agree on steps to improve lives •(2) Affective polarization —supporters of different parties dislike each other strongly, get along well in everyday life •(2) Social avoidance [behavioral affective polarization] —I avoid time with people with different opinions, don’t mind talking to Proposal 2: Harteveld et al Core Questions Required : •Vote choice and turnout •Satisfaction with democracy •Political efficacy •Socio- demographics Macro Variables Required: •Party positions •Level of democracy •Macro challenges:

The Political Implications of a Novel Typology of Trust Author : Michael Hunter Driggers Proposal 5: Driggers How Do We Trust? The Political Implications of a Novel Typology of Trust Summary: The author proposes to introduce items to study the sources of trust. A new typology of the sources of trust –one that borrows from literatures on trust, economic voting, and democratic satisfaction. The author proposes that trust is based on competence and may be general, retrospective, prospective, egotropic or sociotropic. Understanding trust in this way brings insight for understanding political behaviour and legitimacy. The sources of trust are shaped by contexts, which should be measured. Then, how much time on each. •(4-8) Whether heard of four pieces of misinformation specific to their country. Then, degree to which they think misinformation piece is correct. The macro data, compiled from surveys completed by our collaborators, include: (1) electoral returns (votes and seats); (2) variables pertaining to the s tructure of the party system, including the classification of parties according to their ideological families and international organization memberships); (3) data about the election itself, including turnout, alliances, candidates, and the most influenti al issues; (4) variables characterizing the electoral rules, institutions and voting procedures; and general significance of these elections are included in the macro study documentation. The CSES district level data will allow our researchers to evaluate the impact of "local" factors on voting behavior. These data report: (1) district level vote returns; (2) turnout at the district level; (3) the number of seats contested in each district; and (4) the number of candidates standing for election in each district. These data have been added to the CSES micro (individual survey) level data that include items on the following topics, in addition to the usual social and economic battery: (1) satisfaction with democracy; (2) candidate and party evaluations; (3) left -right rankings of parties; (4) retrospective economic evaluations; and (5) vote choice. The Second Wave of Data Collection: Module 2, 2001- 2006 The second wave of data collection is intended to span 2001-2006. The planning committee and collaborators have finalized the design to pursue two broad goals: a) A new focus on representation and accountability. Two broad functions of electoral democracy are (1) to allow the electorate to hold officials accountable, ousting them if they are not performing well and replacing them with others who they think will perform better; and (2) to allow the electorate to put in place a broad government representing the full electorate, who will give all voters a sense that they are included in the process, and who may also be expected – because of the need for coexistence in the government – to develop patterns of cooperation and consensus -based decision making that arguably produce better policies. These two functions obviously coexist i n some tension with each other. An important question about voters is, to what extent do they make their choices in light of each of these functions? Although multi-national data collections that enhance the comparative study of public opinion had since been carried out, Rokkan’s plea for research that would illuminate how electoral systems constrain and condition the beliefs and behaviors of citizens had gone unheeded. In response, the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES) was born. A 1994 conference sponsored by the International Committee for Research into Elections and Representative Democracy (ICORE) established the effort in an official way. A decade later we find over 50 countries participating, hundreds of international scholars having been involved, and the third module in progress. In the past three years, persons have registered nearly 5,000 times to download data from the CSES website. Rokkan, Stein. 1970. Governance CSES Module 2 CSES Module 1CSES Module 2 (2001-2006) focuses on representation and accountability via three key theoretical questions. First, it examines the contrasting views of the logic of elections — to what extent are elections a mechanism to hold government accountable, as opposed to a means to ensure that citizens’ views are properly represented in the democratic process? Second, the module adds a new set of items on citizen engagement and cognition across democratic polities. Third, the module expands the analyses of the first module to examine how voters’ choices are affected by the institutional context within which those choices are made. The fourth advance release of Module 2 contained 32 election studies and was made available for download in April of 2006. The full release is expected to be available CSES Module 3 CSES Module 3 (2006-2010) continues some measures from previous modules, but shifts the substantive theme to that of “meaningful choices” — how electoral motivations and decisions vary with the choice set available. The theme was developed in a stimulus paper prepared by Hermann Schmitt and Bernhard Weßels and available for download from the CSES website. As described in the stimulus paper, from a normative perspective, the module seeks to examine to what degree different supply patterns allow meaningful choices to be made in an election, and thereby make democracy work. From a theoretical perspective, the module examines how the choice sets, or limits thereof, affect electoral motivations and decisions, in order to help to refine our models of electoral choice. Nearly 50 countries have already expressed their interest in participating in Module 3.

Cualquier persona puede descargar nuestras bases de datos completas desde nuestro sitio Web: http://www.cses.org ACERCA DEL CSES Hace más de tres décadas, Stein Rokkan invitó a desarrollar un proyecto de investigación coordinado y comparado entre países que permitiera explorar “los contextos estructurales de las reacciones de los individuos hacia la política, proyecto no realizable por medio del análisis secundario de encuestas conducidas en forma independiente” (1970, p.15). Si bien se han desarrollado desde entonces proyectos multinacionales de recolección de datos que realzan el estudio comparativo de la opinión pública, la invitación de Rokkan a realizar investigación acerca de como los sistemas electorales condicionan las creencias y el comportamiento de ciudadanos ha sido desatendida. Como respuesta a este vacío nació el Estudio Comparado de Sistemas Electorales (CSES). En una conferencia de 1994 auspiciada por el Comité Internacional para la Investigación de Elecciones y Democracia Representativa (ICORE), se estableció el esfuerzo de manera ofi cial. Una década después encontramos a más de 50 países participando de la iniciativa; cientos de académicos internacionales se han involucrado en el proyecto, y el tercer Módulo ya está en progreso. Durante los últimos tres años contamos con cerca de 5,000 registros de personas que descargan los datos desde el sitio Web del CSES. Rokkan, Stein. 1970. Nueva York: McKay.ORIGEN El CSES es un programa de investigación cooperativo y multinacional de estudios electorales alrededor del mundo. Las bases de datos del CSES contienen un Módulo común de preguntas de encuesta de estudios pos-electorales de cada país -que incluyen ítems sobre voto y variables demográfi cas, entre otros-, resultados electorales a nivel de los distritos electorales y datos macro sobre los sistemas políticos. La potencia del diseño de estudio reside en su habilidad para realizar avances teóricos y sustantivos en nuestro entendimiento acerca de cómo variaciones en los arreglos institucionales que gobiernan las elecciones afectan la naturaleza y calidad de las decisiones democráticas. A través del análisis comparado, donde los ciudadanos son observados en diferentes contextos, se puede establecer el impacto de las instituciones. De primera prioridad son aquellos conceptos que nos ayuden a comprender el impacto que tiene las propiedades de los sistemas políticos sobre las evaluaciones políticas y decisiones de voto de la personas. DESCRIPCIÓN DEL ESTUDIOGOBIERNO El Módulo 1 del CSES (1996-2001) concentró la atención en tres grandes temas: el impacto de instituciones electorales sobre la cognición y comportamiento político de los ciudadanos (parlamentarismo versus presidencialismo, impacto de leyes electorales que regulan la forma de votar y su proceso de conteo, y los partidos políticos); segundo, la naturaleza de los clivajes y las alineaciones políticas y sociales; y tercero, la evaluación de las instituciones democráticas y su desarrollo. El lanzamiento completo de la base de datos del Módulo 1 se realizó en julio del 2002, e incluye información acerca de 39 estudios electorales conducidos en 33 países diferentes. El Módulo 2 del CSES (2001-2006) concentra la atención en representatividad y responsabilidad a través de tres preguntas teóricas claves. Primero, examina el contraste entre la visión de las elecciones como mecanismo que asegura un gobierno que rinde cuentas y aquella que enfatiza en las elecciones como un medio para asegurar que las visiones e intereses de los ciudadanos sean representados adecuadamente en el proceso democrático. Segundo, se agrega al módulo un nuevo conjunto de preguntas acerca del compromiso ciudadano y la cognición de las personas en los distintos sistemas democráticos. Tercero, este módulo también expande el análisis del primer módulo acerca de cómo las decisiones de los votantes están afectadas por el contexto institucional en el cual están insertos los ciudadanos. El cuarto lanzamiento de datos preliminares del Módulo 2 -que contiene 32 estudios electorales- se encuentra disponible para descarga desde abril de 2006. Se espera que el lanzamiento completo del Módulo 2 se realice durante el 2007. MÓDULO 2 - CSES MÓDULO 1 - CSES Folleto versión Marzo 2007

Globalization increases electoral fairness. Voters are not only concerned about party positions, but also policy outcomes. Inequality undermines public goods provision. Adverse economic conditions motivate political participation. By exposing divisions, open party nomination processes decrease political participation. The wealthy turn out to vote more when the public wants — and the state can deliver — redistribution. Ideologically distinct options make it easier for citizens to vote according to their interests. Political polarization increases political engagement. Public attachment to political parties facilitates political representation. People vote less on the economy when multi-level governance makes it hard to identify who is in charge. Corruption and human rights problems decrease the importance voters place on the economy. The voting public is more tolerant of poor national economic performance when the global economy is also lackluster. APPENDIX A – STUDY DETAILS AND VARIABLE OPERATIONALIZATIONS A1.1 GLES 2021 post-election study details Fieldwork conducted by Kantar Public started on September 27, the day following the 2021 Bundestag election, and ended on November 21, 2021. The sample was devised as a multistage probability study, based on population registers to represent all German citizens aged 16 and older residing in Germany, with oversampling for Eastern Germany. Respondents could choose between completing the questionnaire online or completing a mail-back questionnaire. A1.2 GLES 2021 RCS details The GLES 2021 Rolling-Cross Section (panel) is based on a dual-frame telephone survey (60% landline, 40% mobile phone numbers), with respondents interviewed twice - once before the election and once after. Data collection by Ipsos took place between August 2 and September 25, before the election, and between September 27 and October 31, 2021, after it (election: September 25). Of the 7,068 respondents from the pre-election survey, 4,446 (62.9%) were re-interviewed post-election. The sample is designed to represent eligible German-speaking voters living in private households in Germany with a landline or mobile telephone connection. Data are arranged so that each observation in the dataset classifies one respondent – with answers at different time points being saved in separate variables. In what follows, we refer to interviews from the pre-election survey as t-0 and interviews from the post-election panel as t-1. In the RCS, respondents were not asked to evaluate the economic situation retrospectively, but to assess Germany’s current general economic situation. Further, information on whether respondents’ obtained a university degree was not available in RCS, as respondents only provided their highest level of general education (with the highest level being upper secondary). Therefore, we include a four-category ordinal variable on education, ranging from (0) no school leaving certificate, to (3) upper secondary qualification. Coding of all variables are detailed in Appendix A.2, including information on the time of data collection (t-0 vs. t-1). A3 – 2021 Panel-Data (GLES 2021 Rolling-Cross-Section) A.3.1 Key Dependent Variable: Vote Choice A.3.2 Party and Leader Likability A.3.3 Control Variables APPENDIX B – CODING OF VOTER TYPES FOR 1998 – 2021 TIME SERIES DATA B.1 – Coding Procedure Voter types for the 1998 – 2021 times series analysis were created following the typology introduced by Quinlan and McAllister (2022). Data was coded in STATA Version 16.1 based on the following steps: Identifying the maximum value a respondent assigned to any of the six parties CDU, SPD, GRUENE, FDP, PDS/LINKE (1998 – 2021) and AfD (2017 - 2021). Creating binary variables for each of the parties indicating whether the respondent assigned the party the maximum value (from Step 1) or not for all respondents that rated at least one party. Identifying to how many parties the maximum value was assigned. Excluding straightliners and “don’t know” responses from binary variables by coding them to missing (i.e., respondents who assigned all parties the same value.) Coding all binary variables to 0 for respondents who assigned their highest score to more than two parties. Repeating steps 1 to 5 for leader likability scales of CDU, SPD, GRUENE, FDP, PDS/LINKE (1998 – 2021) and AfD (2017 - 2021). Generate the types of voter variable based on binary party and leader favorite variables and vote choice (“Zweitstimme”). Specifically, for the party a respondent voted for… Leader-inclined vote: Leader-Favorite = 1 & Party-Favorite = 0 Leader-leaning vote: Leader-Favorite = 1 & Party-Favorite = 1 & higher maximum score for leader than party Party and leader inclined vote: Leader-Favorite = 1 & Party-Favorite = 1 & identical maximum scores assigned to leader and party Party-leaning vote: Leader-Favorite = 1 & Party-Favorite = 1 & higher maximum score for party than leader Party-inclined vote: Leader-Favorite = 0 & Party-Favorite = 1 Incongruent vote: Leader-Favorite = 0 & Party-Favorite = 0 B.2 – Some Examples Illustrating Voter Types Imagine three hypothetical voters (V1, V2, and V3) who cast their party-list vote (Zweitstimme) for the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in 2021. text: Paper draft subject to minor modifications – please do not circulate without the authors‘ consent. 1. INTRODUCTION Meine Damen und Herren, Bundeskanzler Olaf Scholz. It was not the scriptwriters’ original intent and arguably represented one of the greatest surprises in German electoral history. Olaf Scholz, Finance Minister in the outgoing Merkel-led Grand Coalition (and the man who had ignominiously failed to win his party leadership in 2019), was not seen as a frontrunner. Structural forecasts four months out from polling day implied a Christian Democrat-led administration and electoral disaster for the SPD (e.g., Graefe 2022; Quinlan et al. 2022; Gschwend et al. 2022). The Greens, buoyed by favorable polling, were inspired to nominate a Chancellor candidate for the first time and were expected to be the Union’s primary challenger for leading government. However, the SPD defied the pundits, emerging as the largest party. While achieving a momentous high, the Greens fell below the expectations of spring 2021, and the Union scored their worst-ever result. So how did it happen? Some commentators highlighted leadership (e.g., Der Tagesspiegel 2021a; Heescher 2021; WDR 2021). Leadership was salient in 2021 with the retirement of long-standing popular Chancellor Angela Merkel, the rumblings over who would succeed her as the Union’s standard bearer, the Green Party’s nomination of a Chancellor candidate, and the late vote surge of the SPD, credited supposedly to the steady Olaf Scholz. Nonetheless, the academic evidence of leaders’ effect on the vote – in the academic taxonomy – demand-side behavioral personalization - is modest. While there is a consensus leaders are not unimportant to the vote, the extent, circumstances, and pathways for what we call leader-inclined voting (Quinlan and McAllister 2022), independent of party popularity, takes root, is still debated. It primarily rests on whether leaders are the essential (and increasingly more critical) ingredient for electoral success (leaders’ matter school) or whether their impact is undoubtedly there but modest and conditional on context and party (leaders’ minimalist school). Germany and the 2021 contest offer an interesting test case to explore demand-side behavioral personalization. The character of the election allows us to separate incumbency from personality, given Mrs. Merkel’s retirement. Germany also offers a contradiction on personalization. On the one hand, the country’s fascist past has meant less emphasis on individual politicians. Little wonder copious research has cast doubt on behavioral personalization (e.g., Kaase 1994; Faas and Maier 2017; Anderson and Brettschneider 2003; Weßels and Wagner 2013; Schoen 2014; Jungmann et al. 2022). Conversely, at least in German campaigns, the focus on Chancellor candidates highlights the individual, creating a pseudo-presidential contest. text: Kaase 1994; Faas and Maier 2017; Anderson and Brettschneider 2003; Weßels and Wagner 2013; Schoen 2014; Jungmann et al. 2022). Conversely, at least in German campaigns, the focus on Chancellor candidates highlights the individual, creating a pseudo-presidential contest. And with some pundits suggesting leader effects were especially important in 2021 (e.g., Der Tagesspiegel 2021b; Heescher 2021; WDR 2021), the question as to whether 2021 marked a new departure in terms of the importance of leaders to the vote is unresolved. Our contribution has two goals. First, based on German post-election studies included in the CSES between 1998-2021 and in the vein of Quinlan and McAllister (2022), we create a descriptive index disentangling leader and party popularity and its association with individuals’ reported vote. It puts the impact of demand-side behavioral personalization into a historical context, allowing us to establish if the 2021 election marked a crossroads, to quantify the proportion of voters aligning their vote with their favorite leader vis-à-vis their favorite party. For the 2021 contest, if leaders were essential, as some commentators have assumed, we would expect more citizens to have lined up their vote with their favorite leader compared to previous contests. Second, and more innovative, we disentangle the distinct effect of leader popularity from party popularity in the 2021 election with the descriptive index, providing a solid test of the observable implications of demand-side behavioral personalization. Yet, while this index advances our understanding of the leader-vote association, it does not allow us to tease out the reciprocal or temporal dynamics of the relationship between party and leader evaluations and the vote. Attempts to unravel this have been few and far between, primarily hampered by a lack of relevant panel data. In response, we leverage the German Longitudinal Election Study (GLES), which includes repeated measures of respondents over time, capturing respondents’ attitudes towards party and leaders at multiple and separate intervals, allowing us to delve into the associations in more depth. First, we measure citizens’ assessment of leader and party popularity and their vote choice at different points, circumventing the challenge of simultaneous measurement of variables. Specifying reported vote at time t as a function of leader popularity at t-1 allows us to mimic an essential prerequisite for causality – for x to cause y, it must occur before y. Second, we tackle the likelihood of reciprocity between the leader and party evaluations. Some leaders’ matter proponents contend failure to consider this has resulted in underestimating leader-inclined voting (e.g., Garzia, 2014). Consequently, we employ an instrumental variable procedure. This three-pronged approach: using a descriptive index, using panel data with temporal separation for the measures of interest, and using instrumental variables, enables us to quantify demand-side behavioral personalization

Personalization – the idea that the individual, the candidate, or the leader has a strong impact on political dynamics, perhaps even trumping the party brand, was born. Such enthusiasm for the concept seems plausible considering that some institutional rules privilege individuals over the party, swelling leader power within parties, greater media focus on party leaders, and increasingly leader and candidate-centered election campaigns more common (e.g., Rahat and Sheafer 2007; van Aelst et al. 2012; Webb and Poguntke 2013; Renwick and Pilet 2016). Little wonder conventional wisdom, largely driven by media, is that leaders are essential for electoral success today. Despite this prevailing narrative, the impact of leaders on electoral outcomes and citizen vote choice – demand-side behavioral personalization, is mired in debate. There is consensus leaders can be influential, but academic deliberations center on how, for whom, and when they matter, the extent of their influence, and whether their impact exceeds that of the party brand. There are various ways leaders could influence elections: personality traits, appearance, television debates, or popularity more generally, with existing studies exploring a wide facet of these dynamics. There are also two types of leader effect: direct versus indirect (King 2002). Direct effects assume the leader themselves – their popularity, competence, personal characteristics, or performance in TV debates directly correlates with the vote. Indirect effects assume the leader’s impact is transmitted to the vote through another variable. Think of a leader’s impact on shifting party policy, like Tony Blair’s transformation of British Labor or how the media present leaders in their coverage – the effect on the vote is channeled (mediated in the nomenclature of social sciences) through the policy shifts and the media coverage. The most enthusiastic strand of literature, the leaders matter school invokes both types of effect, although arguably, there is a greater reliance on indirect effects. Proponents claim leaders’ impact on the vote is substantial (Hayes and McAllister 1997; Bittner 2011; Costa-Lobo and Curtice 2015; Garzia 2011, 2014; Garzia and De Angelis 2016). Taking stock of the demand-side behavioral personalization literature above, two prominent questions emerge. First, a novelty was three candidates for Chancellorship, all of whom could win (Horst 2021; Infratest dimap 2021). We know in times of volatility, leaders can become more prominent in the vote choice calculus of voters (e.g., Dassonneville 2016; Quinlan and McAllister 2022). Fourth, the 2021 election was held during the COVID-19 pandemic. Fewer in-person campaign events were scheduled, with campaigning principally via the media: both traditional and social – heightening the saliency of the leaders, with more television debates than usual. Most behavioral personalization studies come at popularity from the positive side of the ledger, focusing on the general popularity of leaders or deciphering who is the favorite (most popular) leader. But there is a potential adverse side, too, with the dislike of actors conceivably motivating vote choice (Garzia & Ferreira da Silva 2021; Alexiadou and O’Malley 2022). Our starting point for testing demand-side behavioral personalization is the descriptive index that established whether voters aligned their vote with their favorite party or favorite leader. Overall, the results are in line with the bivariate analyses. The predicted likelihood of voting SPD is highest among the group of leader-inclined voters (0.56), dropping among each other category, with the predicted probability of voting SPD among party-inclined voters being 0.10. However, this association needs to be set into context. While there is evidence of a connection between leader-inclined voters and support for the SPD, leader-inclined voters constitute a relatively small share of the general electorate, the smallest of the other six classification groups in 2021. Even including leader-leaning voters, whom the SPD did well with, this is still the case. That said, the election was close between the SPD and Union (1-point difference), and even these small differences could have been decisive. The exceptional unpopularity of Armin Laschet documented earlier is worth bearing in mind. Had he been less unpopular, the Union might have been able to make inroads among other voter groups, including among those who aligned their vote in some way with their favorite leader. As it was in 2021, support for the Union among these groups was relatively low, and significantly less probable considering other potential influences. As alluded to earlier, the key challenge in quantifying leader evaluations’ impact on the vote is to isolate them from party evaluations. Our earlier analyses go some way to do this, separating party and leader effects and alignment with reported vote. Notwithstanding this, cross-sectional data cannot deal with the endogeneity challenge, and detractors could charge us with drawing a premature conclusion on the evidence thus far. To stand on firmer footing, we must deal with two challenges: simultaneous measurement of the vote and leader and party evaluations and the potential reciprocity of leader and party appraisals and voter behavior. Thankfully, the 2021 GLES boasts a rolling cross-section study (2022b) where participants are interviewed at two different time points – before and after the election. It allows us to evade this simultaneous measurement challenge to a certain degree. To explore this, our modeling approach takes inspiration from Garzia and De Angelis (2016). It contends leader and party evaluations should be measured at separate time points and advocates that voters’ views of leaders are best measured before reported vote (our dependent variable) is captured to reduce bias and provide a “more exogenous (although not fully exogenous) measure of causal effects” (Garzia and De Angelis 2016: 610). So, we measure whether vote at t1 (post-election) is a function of leader evaluations at t0 (pre-election) and party evaluations at t1, thereby providing a strong test of behavioral personalization and giving it the maximum opportunity to overcome the supposed biases it faces from simultaneous measurement approaches. We follow the same modeling strategy and retain the same control variables for the panel as we did with the 2021 post-election analyses, and they are broadly operationalized similarly. We detail our models in Table E2.1 in Appendix E. We can see leader and party popularity both matter to vote choice. The more popular a respondent found the leader of a party, the more likely they were to report voting for that party, with the same pattern exerted for party likeability. We estimate the same models as Garzia and DeAngelis (2016) for completeness for each party (see Table H1, Appendix H). For these analyses, we implement a logit model strategy as our interest is solely the impact of party and leader-likeability on the likelihood of supporting that particular party. While leader likeability and party popularity directly influence the likelihood of supporting all parties, party likeability has stronger sway than leader evaluations for the Union, SPD, and the FDP, albeit the differences are small (see Figure H1, Appendix H). For the Greens, the pattern is more nuanced, but party evaluations are still more likely to yield more votes in real terms than leader popularity. Recall that this is a strong test given the myriad controls, so the fact party evaluations emerge as having a stronger association with the vote, albeit by a small margin, and is likely to result in greater aggregate-level gains, is noteworthy. Critics may charge such a conclusion remains premature as arguably the issue of reciprocity between leader and party evaluations and the vote has not been fully addressed with the leader and party evaluations, be it at t0 or t1, theoretically still contaminated by bias. Such potential presents challenges for conventional regression techniques. Statistically, leader and party popularity could correlate with the error term in the regression model, resulting in biased estimates. So how to approach this? An instrumental variable method offers a solution by pseudo-exogenizing the offending endogenous variables. Some in the leaders’ matter school assume the offending variable is attitudes (e.g., likeability) or attachment to a party. Yet, there is cause too to think leader evaluations could be endogenous. To provide a comprehensive test of behavioral personalization, partly exogenizing both party and leader appraisals may be necessary. We take up this challenge by partially exogenizing party evaluations measured at t1 and leader evaluations at t0. To partially exogenize, the likely endogenous measures (leader and party likeability, respectively) are regressed on a set of exogenous parameters – in simple terms, the characteristics and preferences of the respondent, which are relatively fixed. Sociodemographic characteristics (age, female, church attendance, employment status, education level) and certain political attitudes and expectations (e.g., political interest, expectations regarding the election result, and sentiments regarding electoral integrity and the debt break) achieve such status. CONCLUSION The unlikely ascent of Olaf Scholz to the Chancellorship and the seismic shifts in the German political landscape have prompted questions as to whether Wahl 2021 marked a “Crossroads.” In this vein, our paper unpacks this focusing on behavioral personalization with two objectives. First, to quantify demand-side behavioral personalization in Germany to establish its extent and impact on the 2021 election. Second, and with relevance to the broader debate, we tease out the distinct impacts of leader and party popularity on the vote in several different ways. There are three takeaways. First, concerning 2021 as a “Crossroads” contest, some divergences from the traditional conventions are observable, most notably the exceptional unpopularity of Armin Laschet. Nevertheless, the idea this alone represents a significant departure concerning demand-side behavioral personalization is underwhelming. Only 1 in 6 voters in 2021 aligned their vote with their favorite leader - the lowest proportion in 23 years—nearly three times as many citizens in 2021 aligned their vote with their favorite party (46%) – the highest proportion in our study. This pattern – more voters aligning their vote with their favorite party rather than their favorite leader – is a consistent trend in recent German elections. The message is that traditionally more voters sync their vote more with party than leader. Thus, regarding leader-inclined voting, we conclude 2021 does not stand out, contrary to what some may have expected given the saliency of leaders in the election. However, that is not to say leaders were unimportant in 2021. Although present among a minority of voters, there is evidence demand-side behavioral personalization was active. Voters who aligned their vote with their favorite leader reported voting in greater numbers for the SPD in 2021, a shift from previous elections, and this group was more likely to have done so, even considering other correlates. Meanwhile, voters who aligned their vote with their favorite party reported voting for the Union and the Greens in greater numbers, a conclusion sustained by the multivariate analysis. Given the closeness of the 2021 election, where less than two percentage points separated the SPD and the Union, it would be remiss to say that leader popularity was unimportant, although, in a contest this close, a multitude of factors conceivably could have made the difference. Our third and perhaps most important discovery is while leader evaluations directly and meaningfully correlate with the vote, the balance of evidence implies that party evaluations more often hold stronger sway than leader assessments. The cross-descriptive index, which teases out the observable implications of demand-side behavioral personalization, finds few citizens align their vote with their favorite leader solely. Instead, far more do so with their favorite party. While this evidence is consistent across elections, the finding broadly holds when considering temporal measurement concerns and acknowledging potential reciprocal effects, which few studies have been comprehensively able to explore. Party evaluations tend to have stronger connections to the vote than leader evaluations when temporal measurement challenges are overcome. When potential reciprocal feedback from previous vote choices is considered, party popularity emerges as having a stronger association. True – when party evaluations are pseudo-exogenized, leader evaluations become more critical, especially in explaining support for the Greens and FDP. But under this specification, party evaluations still hold considerable influence, especially for the Union. When leader evaluations are exogenized, the results are more consistent – party evaluations outweigh leader popularity. Our results imply both party and leader evaluations are essential in understanding the German voter. But the balance of evidence suggests while similar in scope, they are not equivalent, with party evaluations demonstrating a stronger connection to the vote. Our finding aligns more closely with the leader minimalist school interpretation and infers a more nuanced interpretation of the extent and sway of demand-side behavioral personalization could be wise. text: =========================================================================== COMPARATIVE STUDY OF ELECTORAL SYSTEMS (CSES) www.cses.org MODULE 6 (2016-2021) METHODOLOGICAL GUIDELINES - January 25, 2022 - =========================================================================== Collaborators in the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems shall adhere to the following standards of data quality: a. Mode of interviewing: Interviews should be conducted face-to-face, unless local circumstances dictate that telephone, Internet, or mail surveys will produce higher quality data. Mixed-mode surveys are acceptable to increase response rates and/or compensate for undercoverage associated with particular survey modes. In cases of mode variation as well as in cases of within-mode variation (e.g. adaption of Internet surveys to multiple devices) presentation of questionnaires to respondents should be as similar as possible. All variation within surveys shall be documented in detail, and technical information on survey mode and, where appropriate, device used shall be identified in the data set for each respondent. National studies should seek to keep mode changes to a minimum to maximize comparability of their data sets across modules. b. Timing of interviewing: We strongly recommend that collaborators in the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems conduct their interviews in the weeks following their national election. Interviewing should not start later than six months after the election. Out of concern for data quality, data collection should be completed in as timely a fashion as possible. In the event of a runoff election, interviewing shall be conducted after the first round election. The date of interview shall be provided for each respondent. c. Placement of module in post-election questionnaire: The questionnaire module should be asked as a single, uninterrupted block of questions. We leave it to each collaborator to select an appropriate location for the module in their national survey instrument. Collaborators should take steps to ensure that questions asked immediately prior to the questionnaire module do not contaminate the initial questions in the module. Collaborators are also free to select an appropriate place in their survey instrument to ask the turnout, vote choice, and demographic questions. d. Population to be sampled: National samples should be drawn from all age-eligible citizens. No sampling frames with systematic undercoverage of significant population groups (such as citizens without access to the Internet) are acceptable. When non-citizens (or other non-eligible respondents) are included in the sample, a variable should be provided to permit the identification of those non-eligible respondents. When a collaborator samples from those persons who appear on voter registration lists, the collaborator should quantify the estimated degree of discrepancy between this population and the population of all age-eligible citizens. Studies based on panels or access panels are acceptable if dictated by local circumstances. In such cases the collaborator should seek to minimize the time lag between initial sampling and the CSES survey and quantify the estimated degree of discrepancy to the population of all age-eligible citizens and provide weights. Details about initial sampling must be documented. e. Sampling procedures: We strongly encourage the use of random samples, with random sampling procedures used at all stages of the sampling process. Collaborators should provide detailed documentation of their sampling practices for all stages. f. Sample Size: We strongly recommend that no fewer than 1,500 age-eligible respondents be interviewed, and under no circumstances should fewer than 1,000 age-eligible respondents be interviewed. g. Interviewer training: Collaborators should pre-test their survey instrument and should train interviewers in the administration of the questionnaire. The Planning Committee will provide each collaborator with documentation that clarifies the purposes and objectives of each item and with rules with respect to probing "don't know" responses. h. Field practices: Collaborators should make every effort to ensure a high response rate. Investigators should be diligent in their effort to reach respondents not interviewed on the initial contact with the household and should be diligent in their effort to convert respondents who initially refuse to participate in the study. Data on the number of contact attempts, the number of contacts with sample persons, and special persuasion or conversion efforts undertaken should be coded for each respondent. i. Strategies for translation (and back-translation): Each collaborator should translate the questionnaire module into their native language(s). To ensure the equivalence of the translation, collaborators shall perform an independent re-translation of the questionnaire back into English. Collaborators engaged in translation of the questionnaire module into the same language (e.g., Spanish, French, English, German, and Portuguese) should collaborate on the translation. //END OF DOCUMENT

text: [Slide 1] An Analysis of the 2023 Montenegro National Election Study: Voter Opinions and Electoral Behavior in the Aftermath of Snap Parliamentary Elections Slaven Živković CSES & DeFacto Consultancy [Slide 2] Montenegro National Election Study (MNES) Fourth wave in 2023 MNES 2012 (included in CSES Module 4) MNES 2016 (included in CSES Module 5) MNES 2020 (pre-test for CSES Module 6) / not a representative sample MNES 2023 includes CSES Module 6 questions & Montenegrin context questions Nationally representative sample (multi-stage random probability) 1200 respondents Face-to-face, CAPI mode of data collections App. 35% response rate Currently: 870 interviews completed [Slide 3] What is the main political cleavage in Montenegro? The cleavage is dead? General orientation towards the independent Montenegrin state and acceptance of Montenegrin national identity Oversimplified version – political cleavage mirrors ethnic division Reality – Ambiguity among Orthodox population [Slide 4] What is the main political cleavage in Montenegro? Highly ethnically heterogeneous polity Relevant nations: Montenegrins, Serbs, Bosniaks, Muslims, Albanians and Croats No national group holds demographic majority (Montenegrins 44% and Serbs 29%) Ethnic tensions - Disputed statehood/nationhood Narrow independence vote in 2006 (55.5%) Active calls for unification with Serbia and contested state symbols Politically highly polarized (Serbs vs. the Others) Civic state vs. ethno-federalism (”homeland nationalism”) [Slide 5] What is the main political cleavage in Montenegro? ”Malleability” of ethnic identity within Orthodox population in MNE (Morrison 2009; Dzankic 2013; Jenne and Bieber 2014; Komar and Živković 2016; Kapidžić and Komar, 2021; Batrićević, 2023) “Montenegrin paradox” - contrary to the literature, the nation building seem not to follow the state building and modernization Main actors in boundary change: The Government (pre-2020 regime change) - Strengthening boundaries Serbian Orthodox Church (SOC) - Blurring lines and stimulating dual identity as interim solution [Slide 6] Why would war in Ukraine matter? Historical sympathy for Russia and Russian politics within Orthodox population on both sides of the cleavage Foreign policy formally aligned with NATO and EU’s Contested identity and asymmetry of power Language, religion, statehood… West vs. East division NATO membership as a issue [Slide 7] Who is to blame for the war in Ukraine? 53.3% [Slide 8] How to “pinpoint” the cleavage? How would you vote on Referendum for independence if it was held tomorrow again? (71.33% in favor) Do you stand up when national anthem is played? (81% yes) Do you celebrate Statehood day May 21st? (69.18% yes) Do you support introduction of two new letter to the alphabet? (43.57%) Do you believe that Montenegrins are in fact Serbs? (51.56% no) [Slide 9] “UNIONISTS” “INDEPENDISTS” [Slide 10] t statistics in parentheses * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001 Analysis [Slide 11] Conclusions The main political cleavage

text: On Mon, Jul 3, 2023 at 3:41 PM CSES <cses@umich.edu> wrote: Dear Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES) User Community, Now is the time to begin our work on identifying a substantive theme for CSES Module 7, for which data collection will start sometime in 2026. To that end, the CSES Planning Committee has established a Subcommittee to identify gaps in existing research that CSES Module 7 might address. As part of their work, the Subcommittee is to canvas possible substantive themes for the new module and questions to include in the resulting survey. With this note, we are asking the CSES user community to propose themes and questions that the Task Force should consider for CSES Module 7. Proposals should be ten pages or shorter and single- spaced. Appendices are not allowed. Hyperlinks to external materials are also not allowed. While we will accept your ideas in any format, proposals should ideally include as many of the following items as possible: 1. Title of proposal 2. A brief overview of the proposal 3. A brief discussion of the theory and broader literature that the proposal would contribute t o 4. A summary and links to previous national or comparative studies and findings 5. A brief discussion of methodological issues, for instance, regarding equivalence across countries 6. A CV for each of the proposers 7. Suggesting specific survey questions relevant to the proposed theme is not required, but it is strongly encouraged. If your proposal suggests particular questions, please include evidence from any previous testing and validation of the questions, as prior testing will make for a stronger application. Please remember that CSES questions appear in post -election surveys - that is, surveys conducted after the election in each participating nation. 8. Please also suggest any contextual/macro variables necessary to include in the dataset to address the proposed t heme Proposals should address as many of the following evaluation criteria as possible: • The potential of the theme and questions to significantly advance science and answer “big questions” that need to be studied. • The theme and questions take advantage of the unique design of the CSES - that is, through examining differences in individual behaviors and attitudes across various nations and electoral systems. • The associated questions are specifically useful within the context of elections and in understanding turnout and voting behavior. • The suitability of the theme for cross -national comparison and to be run in all participating nations, not just for established democracies; for a list of nations that have previously participated in CSES, please visit t he following link. https://cses.org/data -download/download- data- documentation/election- studies/ • The theme is of broa d interest to the scientific community,

A CSES module can be up to 10- 15 minutes in length. Of this, 5 - 8 minutes of questions in each module are core content and likely to be automatically repeated. T herefore, up to 7- 10 minutes of new questions are available to address the theme of the new module. Demographic and administrative questions do not typically count against this total. However, if specific questions from past CSES modules (administrative, demographic, or otherwise) are required to address the proposed theme, they may count against the available minutes. For a list of variables and questions which have appeared in past CSES modules, please visit the CSES website. The CSES is a collaboration of election studies from around the world who volunteer time and space on their surveys for our modules. Participating election studies must be willing and able to implement all the content in a CSES module. Therefore, any proposal containing specialized designs – for instance, experimental components – should address how the procedure is possible and feasible to implement across all election studies in a comparative, multi -mode, international setting, in addition to meeting the above- mentioned criteria. Please direct your proposals for consideration by the CSES Module 7 Task Force to the following email address: cses@umich.edu Proposals received on or before September 20, 2023, will be presented for feedback and discussion at a CSES Module 7 Planning Committee meeting. Please be aware that the CSES Planning Committee may adapt and modify proposed themes and questions while developing the Module. For instance, on past occasions, the Planning Committee has integrated multiple proposals into a single theme. Selected proposals may be adapted in full or in part. Proposals that influence the theme and questionnaire will be acknowledged in the stimulus paper for the Module. For more in formation about CSES, please visit our website at: http://www.cses.org/ To review questionnaires from past CSES Modules, please visit: https://cses.org/questionnaires/ Thank you in advance for your ideas, and thank you for your support of the CSES project! text: [Slide 1] M6 AR1 Debrief – First Insights Katharina Blinzler GESIS Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Köln December 17, 2024 [Slide 2] M6 AR1 CNP – Overview I [Slide 3] M6 AR1 CNP – Overview II [Slide 4] M6 AR1 CNP Overview – Micro vs. Macro [Slide 5] M6 AR1 CNP Overview – Micro vs. Macro [Slide 6] M6 AR1– Issue Types [Slide 7] Issue Types – Micro vs. Macro [Slide 8] M6 AR1 Issue Types – Content-Wise [Slide 9] M6 AR1 Issue Types – Content-Wise [Slide 10] Issue Types - Conceptualization Miscodes (coding errors) Irregularities in the Data (wild codes, missing data or new variables added/dropped in cross-national phase, misbehaving correlations, inconsistencies, miscellaneous, etc.) Labels (Misspecified labels, the addition of missing labels and label checks) (Display) Formatting (Updating display formats for decimals, changing variable types) Collaborators (Awaiting and addressing responses) Documentation (Improvements to documentation such as adding ESNs or clarifications, issues spotted in formal checks) [Slide 11] Takeaways M6 is the first documented release for which micro- and macro issues roughly occur in a ratio of 1:1 (previously 3:1 up to 4:1 micro vs. macro) Having fewer studies in a release does not seem to decrease the number of issues spotted (M6 AR1 with fewest studies but highest N of issues per study) The amount of data issues (& miscodes) decreased considerably for microdata – both compared to M5 AR1 and to other M5 Releases  We seem to get better at both documenting and spotting Codebook issues, as evidenced by the increasing amount of Codebook-related issues overall [Slide 12] M6 AR1 Debrief – First Insights Katharina Blinzler GESIS Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Köln December 17, 2024

Takes about 20-30hrs. Duplicates Check: Classification of respondents with corresponding answers to all questions. Inconsistency Checks: Identifies sets of variables which are inconsistent, or could be perceived as inconsistent (e.g., strange skip pattern, incompatible answers to related questions). The CSES convention is not to change data. Instead, inconsistencies are noted in the CSES codebook, allowing users to make the final determination. Irregular code checks: Sometimes these irregular codes are legitimate in the sense that they may be accounted for by a polity deviation on a particular variable. [Slide 31] Data Quality Controls III Variable and value label checks. Theoretical Checks: Explore theoretically expected relationships between variables (e.g., correlation between Political Efficacy and Satisfaction with Democracy; turnout and age; religiosity and religious service attendance). Examine distributions, correlations, and undertake regression analysis. Relatively unique to CSES to our knowledge. Multilevel Models: on turnout (age, education, gender, presence of a party attachment, efficacy) on incumbency vote (age, education, gender, party ID, state of economy, left-right self, satisfaction with democracy) [Slide 32] Data Quality Controls IV Derivative Variable Checks: Further checks on variables created by the CSES Secretariat that are popular within the field: Turnout and Vote Switchers Vote for a Left/Right Party, Vote for Ideological Party Family (Social Democrats, Conservatives, Liberals, Greens etc.) Additionally: Free Style Checks No syntax templates, conducted by each staff member individually according to expertise, research interests, etc. [Slide 33] How to Assess Whether Something is Odd? text: Center for Global Democracy Advancing Scientific Research for a More Democratic World Noam Lupu, Director Strategic Focus Our core research projects, including our flagship LAPOP Lab, examine how mass publics perceive, experience, and support democratic development. We strive to drive policy innovation to strengthen democracy and good governance globally. Mission Deepen the understanding of how democracies emerge, function, and decline globally through research that adheres to the highest standards of scientific rigor. W hy CGD? In an era of democratic backsliding and declining trust in institutions, CGD serves as a critical hub where cutting-edge research informs evidence-based policies to protect and advance democracy worldwide. We bring together top-tier researchers and practitioners to generate knowledge, build capacity, and inform decision-making that strengthens democratic institutions and practices across the globe. Cutting-Edge Research Generating knowledge on democracy Global Impact Advancing democracy worldwidePolicy Innovation Developing evidence-based solutions Expert Collaboration Connecting researchers and practitioners Democracy is at a Crossroads Around the world, democracies face mounting challenges—from declining public trust to rising authoritarianism. These threats undermine the foundations of democratic governance and create instability in political systems globally. Yet policymakers often lack high-quality data on citizen attitudes and experiences to design effective, responsive interventions that can strengthen democratic institutions and practices. We need better data—and better insight—to protect and strengthen democratic systems.Declining Trust Eroding confidence in democratic institutionsDemocratic Backsliding Regression in democratic norms and practicesRising Authoritarianism Increasing autocratic tendencies globally Data Gaps Insufficient evidence for policy decisions Our Solution CGD is a global leader in democracy research. Our high-quality, policy-relevant work provides the empirical foundation for democratic development and reform. Our comprehensive approach combines methodological rigor with practical applications, ensuring that research translates into actionable insights for policymakers and practitioners working to strengthen democratic institutions. Rigorous international survey design and implementation Collecting reliable data across diverse contexts Longitudinal and comparative analysis Longitudinal and comparative analysis Innovative tools to assess democratic resilience Advancing survey methods and insights on democratic processes Publicly available datasets Driving transparency and evidence-informed decision-making Ongoing Projects Our portfolio of projects addresses critical aspects of democratic governance through innovative research methodologies and practical applications. From our flagship AmericasBarometer to specialized studies on migration, we generate insights that inform policy and practice. Our interactive Data Playground makes complex survey data accessible to diverse users, while our training programs build research capacity across the region. text: [Slide 1] CSES Training & Mentorship Overview of the 3-Stages Training Program for New Employees Katharina Blinzler & Steve Quinlan Comparative Study of Electoral Systems [Slide 2] Why have a training and mentorship program I? Demonstrates investment in colleagues & commitment to seeing them develop. Assists with the integration of colleagues into the project. Improves colleagues' skills and knowledge of the project's policies and processes. Prepares our colleagues for higher responsibility. Fosters an inclusive, equitable atmosphere in the project: everyone receives same training. [Slide 3] Why have a training and mentorship program II? Efficient use of resources: allows for functional diversity so Secretariat members are not constrained to fixed roles, thus requiring reduced supervision. Project knowledge, processes, & policies are communicated to all. Not invested in particular people. Facilitates personnel changes. Supports Adaptive Project Management: we‘re agile and responsive. [Slide 4] CSES Training Program – Overview I Formal training, mentorship, and development program since 2015. To be completed by new colleague(s) within the first six months of joining the project. Core assumption: “learning is not a spectator sport” (Chicerking and Gamson 1987, 4) & is in part experiential (Baume and Scanlon 2018; Kolb 1984; Rogers 1969). Initial 3-stage-onboarding program: Project overview, micro-data processing, and communication skills. Hands-on Coding Experience & Feedback. Review of preceding stages, cross-national phase, and beyond. Participants engage in various learning activities mapping to four of Laurillard’s (2002; 2020) six learning types (acquisition, practice, discussion, production). Afterward: Ongoing training and support over the course of a CSES career. [Slide 5] CSES Training Program – Overview II A mix of transmission & active forms of knowledge exchange Scaffold knowledge framework as a series of building blocks facilitates learning. [Slide 6] Principles of CSES Training I Instructor-led formal training - making learning active, engaging, and fun. CSES assumes no new colleague has every attribute to the level the project might like when joining. Starting point is colleagues grow in the role. Explain (with examples) and repeat! Ongoing review of content and staff exposure to training is continuous. Active learning: hands-on experience & testing. [Slide 7] Principles of CSES Training II Positive feedback, encouragement, and timely reviews. Social enterprise responsibility to our employees: nurturing environment where colleagues can grow and evolve for the future. Everything is written down. Weekly team meetings (and 1-on-1s). text: 1 2-3 day meeting. Usually within 2-4 weeks of the new employee's start (10-12h in total). Transmission focus: presentations and discussion. Inspired by Bruner’s Spiral Curriculum (1960) reinforcement idea. Starts with Project Overview (Welcome, who we are, our goals; How does CSES operate). Micro Processing: STATA processing. Extensive documentation training – including internal replication, how to communicate information and with international collaborators. Confidentiality and data usage. Project communication and tools. Practical examples of how to handle complex variables. District data: collation and issues. [Slide 9] CSES Training Program – Stage 2 Hands-on trial: Employee asked to code and document a dataset – given four weeks to do it. Encouragement to consult stage 1 material & reach out to experienced colleagues. The dataset is blind-coded and reviewed by an experienced coder. One day of 1-on-1 training going through the dataset and documentation in detail. New colleague then incorporates feedback into second round of coding. Not considered to be a test! The goal is to practice & learn. [Slide 10] CSES Training Program – Stage 3 1-2 days. Usually within 3-6 months of the new employee's start (8-10hrs).
