text: CSES Module 6 Advance Release 1: Review of CNP with a Comparison to M5 Memorandum prepared by Katharina Blinzler May 2, 2025 Memorandum Purpose & Executive Summary This memorandum serves as a review of CSES Module 6 First Advance Release, released in December 2024, in comparison with the five previous iterations of the CSES Module 5 (released between 2019 and 2023), with a special focus on Module 5 AR1, i.e., the last first advance release product from spring 2019 (i.e., the release most comparable to the December 2024 release). The key takeaway points from the memo are as follows: With 103 issues discovered at Cross-National Phase, M6 AR1 came third regarding issues discovered (M5 AR1 = 111, M5 FR = 105). This confirms the pattern from M5 that the first advance and full releases are the heaviest in terms of workload. Having fewer studies in a release does not appear to decrease the number of issues spotted (M6 AR1 with the fewest studies but the highest N of issues per study). We are discovering and documenting Codebook issues earlier compared to Module 5, as evidenced by the increasing number of codebook-related problems overall – remarkable for a first advance release. Hence, the previously assumed release cycle (data issues predominate early on, followed by a consolidation phase in later releases) does not fit the M6 AR1 experience. Instead, staff experience with releases seems to have carried over from M5 to the new CSES product. The number of data issues (& miscodes) decreased considerably for microdata, compared to M5 AR2 and other M5 Releases, a success! M6 is the first documented release for which micro- and macro issues roughly occur in a ratio of 1:1 (previously 3:1 up to 4:1 micro vs. macro). The trend is driven by micro coders’ performance, and a slight increase in miscodes and other data-related issues for macro. The memo advances as follows: First, the memo provides an overview of M6 AR1 and all M5 releases in terms of checking periods, resources, and the number of studies added. Next, it details the number and type of identified issues for each Release individually, followed by an analysis of the issues' contents for M5 AR2-M6 AR1. It concludes with a reflection on the key takeaway points from past audits based on Module 5 in light of the first experiences with Module 6. text: CSES: Secretariat Operational Philosophy Prepared by Steve Quinlan June 2025 Memorandum Purpose This memorandum provides a brief overview of the CSES Secretariat's Operational Philosophy. The Operational Philosophy is the principles and values that underpin how the CSES Secretariat operates. CSES Operational Philosophy Zweck des Memorandums Dieses Memorandum gibt einen kurzen Überblick über die Arbeitsphilosophie des CSES-Sekretariats. Die Arbeitsphilosophie umfasst die Grundsätze und Werte, die die Arbeit des CSES-Sekretariats bestimmen. Operative Philosophie von CSES General | “Bottoms Up”: Project & Secretariat adheres to a non-hierarchical structure and atmosphere. General | Focus on Project’s Core Objectives: “We do not try to be everything to everyone.” General | Research and Service are of equal importance. General | Emphasis on Big Pebbles: “We don’t sweat the small stuff.” Stakeholders | Respectful, productive, and responsive relationships with CSES Planning Committee and Collaborators. Stakeholders | Empower users by being responsive to feedback and the market. We do not take away power from user to make choices regarding contestable analytical/coding decisions. Members | Crucial to our success is the fostering of Secretariat members’ job satisfaction and personal wellbeing. Members | Recognize Secretariat members’ contribution and give them “a voice”. Members | Formal Training Program for all Secretariat members. Members | Support Secretariat members’ advancement through mentorship, upskilling, encouraging research, and development of transferable skills, especially communication expertise. Members | Functional diversity: Secretariat members not constrained to fixed roles or tasks but can take on most roles. Data & Documentation | Transparency about data and its potential drawbacks: “Expose our warts.” Data & Documentation | Extensive documentation internally for Secretariat members and externally through CSES Codebooks and the CSES Website. Data & Documentation | All Data Processing is reproducible through detailed comments of scripts and processes: “Replication, Replication.” Data & Documentation | It’s Ok To Make Mistakes. Perfection is not the goal. Mistakes are an opportunity. Allgemein | "Von unten nach oben": Das Projekt und Sekretariat hat eine nicht-hierarchische Struktur und Atmosphäre. Allgemein | Konzentration auf die Hauptziele des Projekts: "Wir versuchen nicht, alles für jeden zu sein." Allgemein | Forschung und Dienstleistung sind gleich wichtig. Allgemein | Die Betonung liegt auf "Big Pebbles": "Wir lassen uns nicht von Kleinigkeiten vom Ziel abbringen." Interessen- vertreter | Respektvolle, produktive und entgegenkommende Beziehungen zum CSES-Planungsausschuss und den nationalen Kollaborateuren. Interessen- vertreter | Befähigung der Nutzer durch Reaktion auf Feedback und den Markt. Wir nehmen den Nutzern nicht die Entscheidungsbefugnis bei strittigen Analyse-/Kodierungsentscheidungen. Mitglieder | Entscheidend für unseren Erfolg ist die Förderung der Arbeitszufriedenheit und des persönlichen Wohlbefindens der Sekretariatsmitglieder. Mitglieder | Den Beitrag der Sekretariatsmitglieder anerkennen und ihnen "eine Stimme" geben. Mitglieder | Formelles Trainingsprogramm für alle Sekretariatsmitglieder. Mitglieder | Förderung des beruflichen Aufstiegs von Sekretariatsmitgliedern durch Mentoring, Fortbildung, Förderung

Die Entscheidungskultur eines Projekts hängt mit den angewandten Führungs - und Projektmanagementstilen zusammen. Was den Ersteren betrifft, so setzt CSES grundsätzlich auf eine Mischung aus drei Ansätzen: visionäre, affiliative und partizipative Führung (G oleman, 2017; Goleman et al., 2013). 3 Der visionäre Ansatz gewährleistet, dass die Führungskräfte eine klare Vision festlegen, die mit den langfristigen Zielen und der Entwicklung des Projekts übereinstimmt. Visionäre Führungskräfte stellen sicher, dass die Ziele den Mitarbeitern klar vermitt elt werden. Innovation wird gewürdigt. Visionäre Führungskräfte kümmern sich nicht um Kleinigkeiten. Rückschläge werden als Chance zum Lernen gesehen. Das Erreichen des Gesamtziels steht immer im Mittelpunkt. Von größerer Bedeutung für die Entscheidungsfi ndung sind vor allem die beiden anderen Führungsstile. Der affiliative Rahmen umfasst die Idee "a peoples' first" und basiert auf der Schaffung und Aufrechterhaltung einer einfühlsamen Kultur innerhalb des Projekts. Der Rahmen erkennt die unterschiedlichen Perspektiven, emotionalen Empfindlichkeiten und individuellen Bedürfnisse der Mitarbeiter an - einfach ausgedrückt: Die Gefühle und Umstände der Menschen werden geschätzt. Er stützt sich auf das Konzept der "dienenden Führung" (Servant Leadership), 3 Goleman et al. (2013) befürworten zwar alle sechs Führungsansätze (visionär, zugehörig, partizipativ, Coaching, Tempo vorgeben und Befehl), doch das CSES -Sekretariat (und das Projekt im Allgemeinen) vermeidet den Befehlsrahmen (Direktive). Ein solcher Ansatz entspricht aus mehreren Gründen nich t den CSES -Werten. Erstens fördert CSES Anpassungsfähigkeit und Flexibilität und lehnt pauschale Ansätze ab. CSES sieht die Welt nicht in Schwarz und Weiß, sondern erkennt Grautöne an. Flexibilität ist für uns ein Muss, um die Bedürfnisse unserer Stakehold er zu erfüllen, die sich weiterentwickeln können, und um ein positives Arbeitsumfeld für unsere Mitarbeiter zu schaffen. Zweitens sind die CSES -Mitarbeiter kompetente Personen, die bei der Einstellung ein strenges Auswahlverfahren durchlaufen haben. Darübe r hinaus absolvieren alle Mitarbeiter ein CSES -Training , was bedeutet, dass sie hoch qualifiziert sind, so dass ein direktiver Ansatz kontraproduktiv wäre. Drittens werden Befehlsansätze damit in Verbindung gebracht, dass sie die individuelle Entwicklung u nterdrücken, hierarchische Beziehungen fördern, die nicht zu kollegialem Respekt anregen, und die Kreativität der Mitarbeiter einschränken, was alles potenziell schädlich für die Moral des Teams ist. Außerdem ist dieser Ansatz nicht geeignet, die Zusammena rbeit im Team zu fördern und führt zu einer zu großen Abhängigkeit von einzelnen Führungskräften. Alles in allem trägt dieser Stil nicht zu einer Kultur des kollegialen Dialogs bei, den CSES als wichtigen Bestandteil der Entscheidungsfindung schätzt. Für di e Entscheidungsfindung kann dies bedeuten, dass die Führungskräfte den Kollegen erlauben, auf vielfältige Weise Feedback zu geben (z. B. in einer Gruppendiskussion, privat oder schriftlich). Oder es kann sein, dass die Mitarbeiter bei ihren Entscheidungen bestimmte Eigenheiten oder persönliche Umstände berücksichtigen müssen, die ein Abweichen von der üblichen Vorgehensweise erfordern. Der partizipative (demokratische) Rahmen nutzt die kollektive Weisheit der Teams bei der Entscheidungsfindung, indem er ei n Umfeld schafft, in dem viele Mitglieder des Sekretariats eine Rolle bei der Entscheidungsfindung spielen können.4 Die Kolleginnen und Kollegen können sich jederzeit zu jedem Thema äußern und Änderungen an der Arbeitsweise des Sekretariats vorschlagen un d entwickeln. Bei diesem Ansatz agieren die Führungskräfte als Vermittler, treten zurück und nehmen die Rolle des Zuhörers ein - ganz im Sinne von Admiral James Stockdale5: "So seltsam es klingt, große Führungskräfte gewinnen Autorität, indem sie sie abge ben" (zitiert in Margules, 2011). Sie vertrauen auf die Meinungen, Perspektiven und Erfahrungen ihrer Kollegen. Dieser Ansatz hat den Vorteil, dass er es ermöglicht, die robustesten Lösungen zu entwickeln, da mehrere Perspektiven berücksichtigt werden. Wic htig ist, dass dies den Kollegen eine Stimme gibt und das Engagement der Mitarbeiter fördert, was bedeutet, dass die Mitarbeiter einen größeren Anteil an dem Projekt entwickeln, was die Produktivität verbessert. Der Projektmanagementansatz muss den Führung sansatz in ein praktikables Paket verwandeln. Der CSES -Projektmanager wendet einen Stil an, den man als unterstützenden Projektmanager bezeichnen könnte, und legt den Schwerpunkt auf drei Dinge: Prozesse, Menschen und Technologie. Der Projektmanager bleibt einfühlsam gegenüber der Kultur und den persönlichen Umständen und ist daher so anpassungsfähig wie möglich. Wir fördern ein Umfeld der Motivation und Delegation, das auf regelmäßiger Kommunikation, klaren Zielen und Vertrauen basiert. Um dies zu erreiche n, stellt der Projektleiter Vorlagen bereit, vermittelt bewährte Verfahren, sorgt für einen klaren und rechtzeitigen Informationsfluss und lernt aus Erfahrungen und anderen Projekten. Letzteres ist besonders wichtig für die Entscheidungsfindung - Erfahrung en beeinflussen

text: CSES Module 6: Study Eligibility Checklist based on CSES Methodological Guidelines 27 October 2023 When adjudicating study eligibility for inclusion in CSES Module 6, the following items should be evaluated to ensure they meet the CSES Module 6 Methodological Guidelines. Question numbers starting with “Q” in the “Things to watch out for” section refer to the Module 6 Design Report. If in doubt about a study’s eligibility for inclusion, please bring this to the CSES Secretariat weekly team call or discuss with DH/SQ. ANONYMIZED DATA CSES works with data that is anonymized. Data provided to CSES by Collaborators should not include the following: Name of the respondent or name of the interviewer. Address of the respondent. Telephone number of the respondent. National Identification number of the respondent. Online Identification (e.g., IP address) of the respondent. Location data (e.g., household ZIP code, Geolocation of household) of the respondent. Bank account or social security number of the respondent. Biometric data of the respondent. Suppose the data or respondent IDs within the data contain any or partial information listed above. In that case, the data must be deleted from CSES servers, and Collaborators are asked to re-deposit their data anonymized. Things to watch out for: Lengthy respondent IDs - if in doubt, ask the collaborator whether the ID carries any meaning. Smallest geographical unit in the dataset - electoral districts should be the smallest. Verbatim answers by respondents in the deposited dataset – should not reveal any identities – if in doubt, drop variable from deposited data and make a note in the log file. Whether respondents gave consent to data collection in CSES (Q5). SURVEY LEVEL QUESTIONS FIELDED Studies must ask all survey-level questions unless there is a specific reason for not doing so. Things to watch out for: Deviations in the way question was asked or response categories. Questionnaire version that was fielded (pre-test vs. finalized questionnaire). SAMPLING PROCEDURES Random probability sample required – encouraged at all stages, but the study must be inspired by a random sampling strategy. Things to watch out for: Quota component is allowed (e.g., Brazil 2018, Czechia 2017 & 2020, France 2017). Non-probability panels not allowed (Q17). Example: South Korea 2020. Gaps in the description (Q11-Q13) omitting either steps in sampling or providing insufficient information. A complete description starts with the primary sampling units / initial recruitment of panelists [if applicable] and ends with individual respondent selection (not household selection!) at the final stage. Example for insufficient information: Interviewers in Latvia 2018 were instructed to select the youngest male in a household if present - there could be valid reasons, but still not clear why this happened. Was respondent substitution acceptable (Q13)? If so, ask collaborator

text: CSES and Dropbox: Procedures to access files, ensure data is protected, & files preserved Last Updated: November 23, 2023 1. Who has access to CSES Dropbox? Access to the CSES Dropbox folder is only provided to all active CSES Secretariat members. All Secretariat members are bound by the CSES Pledge of Data Confidentiality, signed by CSES Secretariat members upon commencement of employment. All CSES Secretariat employees are obligated to respect as confidential and anonymous all information derived from their work and never to discuss it for any reason not directly related to the project. 2. Guidelines for Passwords to access CSES Dropbox In devising a password to sign in to CSES Dropbox, CSES Secretariat members are asked to do the following: Create a unique password. Avoid using passwords that you use for other things. Avoid passwords that contain personal references. Avoid passwords that use repetitive keyboard patterns. 3. How to access CSES Dropbox? Access by CSES Secretariat members to CSES Dropbox should be using Two-Factor Authentication (TFA). TFA requires proof of user identity using a combination of two different methods. Besides using a username and password to gain access to Dropbox, CSES Secretariat members will receive a passcode via text message or a mobile app with each login attempt. It is to verify that the individual trying to gain access to CSES Dropbox using a Secretariat member's username, and password credentials is a member of the CSES Secretariat. Dropbox supports the following mobile TFA apps: Duo. Google Authenticator. Authenticator. For more information on setting up TFA for Dropbox, please consult here. CSES Secretariat members are encouraged to enable a backup method for TFA in case their original TFA method is unavailable to them (e.g., no access to mobile phones at the time of sign-in). During the setup of TFA, Dropbox will provide you with ten codes allowing you to sign in in case you ever lose access to your phone. Please store these securely and ensure they are separate from any location, which may let someone figure out your password. The Director of Studies and Project Manager are both administrators on the CSES Dropbox account and can help should you ever lose access. 4. Handling files on CSES Dropbox It is simple for someone to accidentally delete a file or directory in Dropbox without noticing. The deleted item(s) can be restored. So let's follow this policy: Don't delete files from Dropbox's shared "CSES Secretariat" folder unless you're entirely sure of the ramifications. It is advisable to leave any deleting to the Director of Studies or the Project Manager. If a file is deleted accidentally, either restore it (if you have access to it) or let the Director of Studies know,

text: CSES und Dropbox: Verfahren zum Zugriff auf Dateien, zum Schutz von Daten und zur Archivierung von Dateien Zuletzt aktualisiert: 23. November, 2023 1. Wer hat Zugriff auf die CSES-Dropbox? Zugriff auf den CSES-Dropbox-Ordner haben nur alle aktiven Mitglieder des CSES-Sekretariats. Alle Mitglieder des Sekretariats sind an die CSES-Verpflichtungserklärung zur Vertraulichkeit von Daten gebunden, die von den Mitgliedern des CSES-Sekretariats bei Aufnahme ihrer Tätigkeit unterzeichnet wurde. Alle Mitarbeitenden des CSES-Sekretariats sind verpflichtet, alle Informationen, die sich aus ihrer Tätigkeit ergeben, als vertraulich und anonym zu behandeln und sie niemals aus irgendeinem Grund weiterzugeben, der nicht unmittelbar mit dem Projekt zusammenhängt. 2. Richtlinien für Passwörter für den Zugang zur CSES-Dropbox Die Mitglieder des CSES-Sekretariats werden gebeten, bei der Festlegung eines Passworts für die Anmeldung bei CSES-Dropbox wie folgt vorzugehen: Erstellen Sie ein eindeutiges Passwort. Vermeiden Sie die Verwendung von Passwörtern, die Sie auch für andere Zwecke nutzen. Vermeiden Sie Passwörter, die persönliche Bezüge enthalten. Vermeiden Sie Passwörter, die sich wiederholende Tastaturfolgen verwenden. 3. Wie greift man auf die CSES-Dropbox zu? Der Zugriff von Mitgliedern des CSES-Sekretariats auf die CSES-Dropbox sollte über die Zwei-Faktor-Authentifizierung (TFA) erfolgen. TFA erfordert den Nachweis der Benutzeridentität durch eine Kombination von zwei verschiedenen Methoden. Neben der Verwendung eines Benutzernamens und eines Passworts für den Zugang zu Dropbox erhalten die Mitglieder des CSES-Sekretariats bei jedem Anmeldeversuch einen Passcode per SMS oder über eine mobile App. Damit soll sichergestellt werden, dass die Person, die versucht, mit dem Benutzernamen und dem Kennwort eines Sekretariatsmitglieds auf Dropbox zuzugreifen, ein Mitglied des CSES-Sekretariats ist. Dropbox unterstützt die folgenden mobilen TFA-Apps: Duo. Google Authenticator. Authenticator. Weitere Informationen zur Einrichtung von TFA für Dropbox finden Sie hier. Den Mitgliedern des CSES-Sekretariats wird empfohlen, eine Backup-Methode für TFA zu aktivieren, für den Fall, dass ihre ursprüngliche TFA-Methode nicht verfügbar ist (z. B. kein Zugang zu Mobiltelefonen zum Zeitpunkt der Anmeldung). Bei der Einrichtung von TFA erhalten Sie von Dropbox zehn Codes, mit denen Sie sich anmelden können, falls Sie einmal keinen Zugriff auf Ihr Handy haben. Bitte bewahren Sie diese Codes sicher auf und stellen Sie sicher, dass sie nicht an einem Ort aufbewahrt werden, an dem jemand Ihr Passwort herausfinden könnte. Der Studiendirektor und der Projektmanager sind beide Administratoren des CSES-Dropbox-Kontos und können Ihnen helfen, falls Sie den Zugriff verlieren sollten. 4. Umgang mit Dateien in der CSES-Dropbox Es ist leicht möglich, dass jemand versehentlich eine Datei oder ein Verzeichnis in Dropbox löscht, ohne es zu bemerken. Die gelöschten Elemente können wiederhergestellt werden. Befolgen Sie also diese Richtlinie: Löschen Sie keine Dateien aus dem gemeinsamen Dropbox-Ordner "CSES-Sekretariat", es sei denn, Sie sind sich über die Folgen vollständig im Klaren. Es ist ratsam, das Löschen dem Studiendirektor oder dem Projektmanager zu überlassen. Wenn eine Datei versehentlich

Wenn eine Datei versehentlich gelöscht wurde, stellen Sie sie entweder wieder her (wenn Sie Zugang dazu haben) oder informieren Sie den Studiendirektor, der sie wiederherstellen wird. CSES-Archiv Die CSES-Dropbox ist nicht für die langfristige Speicherung von CSES-Dateien gedacht. Um sicherzustellen, dass die CSES-Daten sicher und langfristig aufbewahrt werden, erscheinen nur aktuelle CSES-Module und projektbezogene Angelegenheiten in der CSES-Dropbox und sind für aktive Mitglieder des CSES-Sekretariats zugänglich. Stattdessen werden die Dateien früherer CSES-Module und anderer projektbezogener Angelegenheiten im CSES-Archiv aufbewahrt. Das "Archiv" ist für Referenzdateien gedacht, nicht für Dinge, die aktiv genutzt werden, und ist nur für den CSES-Studiendirektor zugänglich. Ausgewählte Berechtigungen für das CSES-Archiv können vom Studiendirektor auf einer Ad-hoc-Basis erteilt werden. Ausgewählte Berechtigungen für das CSES-Archiv können vom Studiendirektor auf Ad-hoc-Basis für jeweils maximal 30 Tage erteilt werden. Nach diesem Datum erlischt die Genehmigung und es ist eine neue Genehmigung erforderlich. 6. Änderungen an Dateien im CSES-Archiv Wenn Änderungen an Dateien im CSES-Archiv erforderlich sind, stimmen Sie sich bitte mit dem Studiendirektor ab, um sicherzustellen, dass die Änderungen nicht zu Informationsverlusten führen und dass die vorgenommenen Änderungen eindeutig nachvollziehbar sind. //ENDE DER LEITLINIEN

In Module 4 CSES makes use of the ISCED, while it had its own coding scheme in Module 3. In the below table, I tried to put the more or less comparable classification together into one line, see the below table. Table 1: Comparison of level of education in CSES, C2003 to D2003 (Module 3 – Module 4) One of the most striking differences might be the fact that ISCED does not use ‘incomplete’ levels of education as separate categories. However these are present in the ISCED model with more digits. In fact, values have up to three digits, usually differentiating between two subdimensions: ‘programme orientation, and level completion and access to higher ISCED levels’. (ISCED 2011: p. 39). For the three-digits version it means that even if a level has only been started and not completed, the person is coded within the respective level category. If categories should be collapsible, i.e. if we use the one-digit coding in the same way as the three digit coding ISCED is used, we should also code the persons with an ” incomplete” level of education into the same category as the completed/certificated level of schooling. However, in AR1, we did not do this consistently. The detailed brochure (ISCED 2011) also gives advice on how to classify those national schooling levels which fall in between ISCED categories, (‘which do not result in a clear boundary’ p.34), e.g. between ISCED levels 2 and 3. See the below example: ‘151. If use of the classification criteria does not result in a clear boundary between ISCED levels 2 and 3, the following is recommended: i) for programmes spanning ISCED levels 2 and 3 that are organized in stages, the end of the stage closest to nine years after the start of ISCED level 1 should be used as the transition point between ISCED levels 2 and 3; or ii) for programmes spanning ISCED levels 2 and 3 that are not divided into stages, only the grades between the end of ISCED level 1 until the end of nine years of schooling after the start of ISCED level 1 should be classified as ISCED level 2. Doctorate in medicine | Doctorate 1.3 Summary: Some remarks on education To sum up, education is a quite difficult variable to code. In my view, it is now more difficult than before because it is necessary to look more closely at what the ISCED categories mean and what they include. To me, the CSES version of module 3 was thus more straightforward. For example, it seems that the ISCO also includes a person into a specific level, if he/she has not completed it yet. This is not very intuitive. In the more detailed two or three-digit ISCED, the person would be classified into the same level, but with additional digits signifying ‘level incompleted’. I think we should give the variable a more detailed review, when we do AR2, and, maybe also either press collaborators more to this question, or find our internal rules in a more consistent way. At least, there should be no differences in how we apply the ISCED! Occupation 2.1. In my experience, the biggest problem of the occupational variables happens if it is coded not at all alike the ISCO scheme. A secondary problem may happen if it is originally coded with four digits. The collapsing of four-digit codes into three digit ones sometimes leads to three-digit codes ending with a zero. Then, we have to define what that code means, because usually the zero-ending codes have the entry “see election study codes”, e.g. PRODUCTION AND SPECIALIZED SERVICES MANAGERS 130. [SEE ELECTION STUDY NOTES] There are some other examples in which there are a few wild codes. Sometimes it is possible to see what these mean when looking into the questionnaire of the election study, sometimes it is not easy to detect what they mean. In the latter case, ask the collaborator. Also if the codes are completely different, I would first go and ask the collaborator to code these. Based on this review we offer the following eight key recommendations: 1. Macro and district data (1) Continuation of collecting district data which is needed to analyze voting behavior under mixed-member proportional representation system. (2) Continuation of collecting macro data, but the newly introduced 15 variables in the M5 may be candidates for deletion. (3) Searching possibilities of workshops and conference for encouraging use of macro data. 2. Micro data (4) Adding a new variables to measure people’s attitude towards climate change. (5) Adding a new variables to measure respondents’ housing ownership. 3. Meta data (6) Checking use of weight data. (7) Adding a simple ethnicity variable with interviewers being identified as whether they are a member of the majority ethnic group, a minority ethnic group, or if they consider themselves of mixed ethnic descent. (8) Revisiting survey mode. 3 1. Mission of the report and work of the committee The objective of this report is to review and assess three components of Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES) project. The components are consisted of the macro data including district data, micro data composed of answers from survey respondents, and meta data also known as ‘administrative data’ in cses.org. Our charge from Elizabeth J. Zechmeister, the chair of the M6, as the subcommittee is to review micro-level questions (e.g., demographic questions not already covered in Module 6 or core items), meta-data fields (e.g., administrative variables such as interviewer characteristics and date of interview), and macro-level content (e.g., district data, electoral system data) and suggest possible revisions, deletions, or additions for Module 6. Moreover, the new theme of the M6 may need new variables in the 3M data. Then, this report mentions about these three parts: macro with district data, micro data, and meta data in order. 2. These recommendations includes introduction of the new variables and discontinuation of three macro variables about government expenditure in various areas of policy because of little relevance to M5. The chair suggested two issues. “The first is a review of the decision to continue to collect district data. And the third one is that low usage of the district data may be because of lower user community awareness of their availability. The report concluded the retention of the district data, and recommended revisit of the merits of including district data in the CSES to new subcommittee for Module 6. If the researchers want to analyze variation among districts, district-level data is indispensable. On the other hand, sample sizes at each country in the CSES datasets are usually 1000 to 4000. These sizes restrict variables selection for multilevel analysis, which may be the one of the reasons of less usage. But, increasing the sample size is hardly a realistic option for each national survey team. However, abandoning data collection at district has a serious loss. Many countries adopt the SMD as electoral system, and in each district, we often observe different party competition, because every party do not stand in every district and voters face different alternatives for voting. If we do not have district-level data, we will overlook intra-country variation in patterns of party competition and regional variance. Meta data6 Overview of Administrative Variables The CSES’s administrative variables can be divided up in four broad categories: “Identifier”, “Weights”, “Election Logistics”, and “Study Logistics” variables. Identifier Identifier variables describe the dataset and data so that researchers can identify the dataset or subset of the dataset that is pertinent to their research questions. Identifier variables for example include country codes to identify which observations are from a given country, election year codes to identify observations in a given time period, or respondent id numbers to identify respondents within an election study. Some identifier variables are redundant. Election Study (Numeric Polity) and Election Study (Alphabetic Polity) are constructed by combining country code and election year identifiers. Since it is easy and fast to construct these variables, removing them from the study would not improve efficiency particularly. Furthermore, their inclusion makes it easy for researchers to work with multiple waves of the study or to combine the CSES data with other data sources. For these reasons, it should not be a priority to remove these from the study. Weights The CSES includes a variety of weight variables divided up into sample, demographic, and political weights. Sample weights are included so researchers can correct for unequal selection probabilities, while demographic weights ensure that researchers can weigh the data, so the sample’s socio-demographic characteristics more closely resemble the population’s. Finally, political weights provide the researcher with a tool to correct for the sample’s reported voting behavior not fitting with the official vote count. There are three different types: Original Weights, Polity Weights, and Dataset Weights. The Original Sample Weights are the weights reported by the individual election studies. Polity Weights are standardized so that the original weights have a mean of 1 within a given country. Dataset Weights are calculated so that researchers can use all observations in the CSES regardless of country and can correct for not all sample sizes being the same across election studies. The Weights category also includes certain variables that are used to construct the weights. “Factor: Sample Size Adjustment”, for example, reports the ratio of the average sample size to the given election study’s sample size. The Weights variables are fairly technical. Even though researchers could theoretically construct all the weight variables from the set of Original Weights, this might be quite demanding and result in calculation errors. Therefore, removing them could impact the quality of research being done using the CSES. This negative effect would especially hit research using cross-country comparisons since the Dataset Weights are the hardest to calculate. 10 Election Logistics This is the smallest category of administrative variables. The variables describe the type of election taking place and the timing of the election. The timing variables are divided up in “day”, “month”, and “year” variables, which is fairly inefficient. However, this division avoids possible standardization mistakes that could happen when multiple election study

The variables describe the type of election taking place and the timing of the election. The timing variables are divided up in “day”, “month”, and “year” variables, which is fairly inefficient. However, this division avoids possible standardization mistakes that could happen when multiple election study teams differ in their election timing descriptions. Study Logistics The last category of administrative variables describes how the specific election study was administered. This set of variables allows a researcher to see whether the study was conducted by telephone, how long an interview lasted, and whether the study was conducted during or after an electoral period. These variables are important for researchers who use the CSES for cross-country comparisons. If a researcher wants to compare two different countries’ responses to the same question, it could for example be important that both of the country’s samples were asked the particular question over the phone. Comparing Administrative Variables to Other Studies The CSES’s number of identifier variables is above average for the studies surveyed. This seems to be because the CSES wants to make it easy to use the included studies for both national analysis and cross-national analysis. Other cross-national studies, with the exception of the World Values Survey and the LaPOP, do for example not include a unique “study id” variable that combines the year of study and the country the study took place in. Instead, the logic seems to be that researchers can construct these types of variables on their own. This obviously increases the likelihood of a researcher making a mistake and not analyzing the exact observations they are interested in. The CSES does not include a respondent’s region of residence or electoral district of residence under its list of administrative variables. However, these smaller geographic units are included as ordinary variables in the CSES, which means that researchers have a chance to divide respondents up in smaller geographical units for analysis. The CSES’s number and diversity of weight variables is large compared to all other studies 11 surveyed. However, the weight variables make it possible to use the national studies in their original form and also use them for cross-country analyses. Part of the reason the CSES’s weight variables are so numerous is that some of the other studies surveyed are not cross-national. Therefore, the set of weighting variables that are constructed to make sure that individual observations in the CSES can be studied across countries are not present in these other studies. However, even compared to the cross-national studies, the CSES’s number of weight variables is large. Most cross-national studies do not include the original country weights

Therefore, the set of weighting variables that are constructed to make sure that individual observations in the CSES can be studied across countries are not present in these other studies. However, even compared to the cross-national studies, the CSES’s number of weight variables is large. Most cross-national studies do not include the original country weights and the intermediate variables that transform them to cross-national weights. Therefore, it is possible to use the CSES dataset to extract single studies in their original form or to use a multitude of studies for cross-national analysis. National electoral studies unsurprisingly tend to have less information about the elections they are studying than the CSES. The set of election logistics variables makes it clear that the CSES is trying to help researchers who compare certain features of political systems to do so without having to do much outside research. This ensures that an inexperienced researcher does not accidentally include studies that focus on a type of election the researcher is not interested in. The study logistics set of variables are designed so researchers can identify national differences in the way of conducting interviews that could lead to systematically different respondent responses. A lot of other cross-national studies are missing this component. An alternative strategy would be to make sure that all studies included in the CSES conduct their studies in the same way. However, this would mean that some country studies would be forced to change their study logistics. This is not a viable strategy since such a change would make it impossible to ensure consistency in the responses to questions over time. Finally, some studies that use face-to-face interviews, the ANES and the LaPOP , include a battery of interviewer demographics variables. These are included out of a concern for an interviewer’s ethnicity or gender affecting the respondent’s answers to certain questions. The CSES includes the interviewer’s gender but does not include other demographic variables. 12 Table 1. Recommendations Our survey of other election studies suggests that -- far from lacking administrative data found on other studies -- CSES is actually at the forefront of providing researchers with valuable administrative data. We therefore have only three recommendations: 1) If there is a belief that the administrative data requirements are proving too onerous for national election teams, it is certainly the case that CSES provides many, many more potential weights than different surveys. That being said, we find good reason for these weights, and think that by and large they provide useful tools for researchers that 14 increase the value of the data. Nevertheless, it is possible that some of these weights are rarely used. Therefore, if there was to be a CSES wide survey of existing literature to check for usage of different variables or types of data, it might be worth including in that review a measure of how often different weights are applied, with an eye towards possibly not including certain weights if they are never used. To be clear, this is a second best option to continuing to include the weights, and one which we think should only be pursued if there is a mandate to reduce administrative data. 2) The only category of administrative data that we could find for which CSES is lacking information provided by a (limited) number of other studies is in terms of interviewer demographic characteristics. In an era where there is greater attention to both identity politics and transparency surrounding data collection, more information regarding the identity of the interviewer might be useful. However, this is of course complicated by the lack of comparable identity characteristics across countries. However, we would like to suggest that perhaps a simple ethnicity variable could be included, with interviewers being identified as whether they are a member of the majority ethnic group, a minority ethnic group, or if they consider themselves of mixed ethnic descent. This seems like something that could be (a) simple to collect without being (b) overly intrusive and yet (c) provide value to researchers worried about interviewer effects on certain types of questions. The Board could also consider other types of interviewer characteristics (e.g., region of the country, primary language),

text: 1 The Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES) Module 6 3M (micro, meta, macro) Data Subcommittee report Masahiro Yamada (myamada@kwansei.ac.jp) Joshua Tucker (joshua.tucker@nyu.edu) Catherine De Vries (catherine.devries@unibocconi.it) February 2020 2 Executive Summary This report presents a review of the macro, micro, and meta data components of the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES) project in preparation for Module 6. Based on this re view we offer the following eight key recommendations: 1. Macro and district data (1) Continuation of collecting district data which is needed to analyze voting behavior under mixed -member pro portional representation system. (2) Continuation of collecting macro data, but the newly introduced 15 variables in the M5 may be candidates for deletion. (3) Searching possibilities of workshops and conference for encouraging use of macro data. 2. Micro data (4) Adding new variables to measure people’s attitude towards climate change. (5) Adding new variables to me asure respondents’ housing ownership. 3. Meta data (6) Checking use of weight data. (7) Adding a simple ethnicity variable with interviewers being identified as whether they are a member of the majority ethnic group, a minority ethnic group, or if they consider themselves of mixed ethnic descent. (8) Revisiting survey mode. 3 1. Mission of the report and work of the committee The objective of this report is to review and assess three components of Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES) project. The components consist of the macro data including district data, micro data composed of answers from survey respondents, and meta data also known as ‘administrative data’ in cses.org. Our charge from Elizabeth J. Zechmeister, the chair of the M6, as the subcommittee is to review micro -level questions (e.g., demographic questions not already covered in Module 6 or core items), meta- data fields (e.g., administrative variables such as interviewer characteristics and date of interview), and macro - level conten t (e.g., district data, electoral system data) and suggest possible revisions, deletions, or additions for Module 6. Moreover, the new theme of the M6 may require new variables to be added in the 3M data. This report proceeds in three parts focusing on macro with district data, micro data, and meta data respectively . 2. Macro and District -Level Variables The M5 has district- level variables numbered as E4000s, and macro as E5000s. The Module 5 Macro & District Data Subcommittee report1 suggested six recommendations. These recommendations include the introduction of the new variables and discontinuation of three macro variables about government expenditure in various areas of policy because of little relevance to M5. These recommendations include the introduction of the new variables and discontinuation of three macro variables about government expenditure in various areas of policy because of little relevance to M5. The chair suggested two issues. “The first is a review of the decision to continue to collect district data. While election study PIs supply some of these data, most of it is collected by the CSES Secretariat; it can be time - consuming, and your committee should consider whe ther the benefit (e.g., papers published using the data – past or potential) outweighs the cost of using their time for that rather than on other CSES tasks. The second is a set of recommendations regarding the promotion of awareness and use of the CSES macro/district data. 2” In light of these issues, we considered the possibility of omitting 1 https://cses.org/wp - content/uploads/2019/03/CSES5_MacroDistrictSubcommittee_FinalReport.pdf 2 From a mail from Liz to the 3M subcommittee on February 15, 2019. 4 variables. According to the presentation by Stephen Quinlan at the CSES Plenary Session in Philadelphia in August 2016, 4 % of the outputs in the CSES bibliography use district data (Quinlan 2016)3. After 2016, we found two articles using district data, Jung (2017) and Riera and Bol (2017)4. Also, in the Module 5 Macro & District Data Subcommittee report, continuation to collect district data was on the agenda. Th e report indicates three reasons to retain these data. The first one is that d iscontinuation would break a time series link with previous CSES modules. The second is that cessation would also limit the potential for multilevel analyses for those countries where data were available. And the third one is that low usage of the district data may be because of lower user community awareness of their availability. The report concluded the retention of the district data, and recommended revisit of the merits of including district data in the CSES to new subcommittee for Module 6. If the researchers want to analyze variation among districts, district - level data is indispensable. On the other hand, sample sizes at each country in the CSES datasets are usually 1000 to 4000. These sizes restrict variables selection for multilevel analysis, which may be the one of the reasons of less usage. But, increasing the sample size is hardly a realistic option for each national survey team. Yet, abandoning data colle ction at district would mean a serious loss. text: each national survey team. Yet, abandoning data colle ction at district would mean a serious loss. Many countries adopt the SMD as electoral system, and in each district, we often observe different party competition, because every party does not stand in every district and voters face different alternatives for voting. If we do not have district -level data, we will overlook intra -country variation in patterns of party competition and regional variance. Moreover, under mixed -member proportional representation system, no district data makes it hard to analyze split-ticket voting and observe contamination effects between the SMD and the PR system in micro data. Therefore, we also recommend continuation of collecting district data as the M5. Rather, we would like to recommend to add a new variable capturing which districts are included in the sample. The sample does not always include every district because of the sampling process. Yet, the past CSES dataset do es not include such variable. Introducing this variable makes clear which districts are 3 https://cses.org/wp - content/uploads/2019/04/CSES_2016Philadelphia_Bibliography.pdf 4 These are listed at Appendix II of this report. 5 included in the sample and in turn would make the CSES dataset more valuable. If the burden for the secretariat is too high , the information should be included at least in the country report. Concerning macro variables, according to Quinlan (2016), there some variables less used than district data. Among them, ‘communications’, ‘government expenditure’, ‘unemployment’, ‘country’s population’, ‘human development index’ are seldom used (0%). ‘Electoral integrity’, ‘corruption index’, ‘GDP’, ‘inflation’, ‘government debt’ are used in 1% of the total outputs, ‘most important issue in election’ in 2%, ‘democratic ratings of country’ in 3%. These variables may be candidates for deletion. But, the econom ic indices such as ‘government expenditure’, ‘unemployment’, ‘country’s population’, ‘GDP’, ‘inflation’, ‘government debt’ are likely valuable especially for long -term analysis, and the value increases with accumulating long -term data. And ‘communication’ must be needed for comparison for survey environments in each countries. Yet, the newly introduced 15 macro variables for the M5 theme, such as n et migration rates, p opulation by citizenship (foreigners), linguistic fractionalization, religious fractionalization, e thnic fractionalization, Polity Fragmentation Index, Gini coefficient of equalized disposable income, direct democracy , Control of Corruption Index, and five kinds of QOG Expert Judgment of Public Sector, may be candidate for deletion, depending upon core component of the M6. Core questions that tap into political attitudes, electoral behavior and preferences as well as political knowledge and efficacy of respondents. The “core” refer to questions from the main module (questions labelled beginning with “Q” – i.e. question Q1, Q2, Q3, etc.) which should be considered to be repeated for every module of the CSES. B. In addition, when it comes to demographics there has been considerable interest in socio- economic characteristics of individuals in the crisis/post -crisis period. When it comes to the core questions, the questionnaire already covers a lot of ground and questions could be retained in order to guarantee a time series. Yet, one thing that seems blatantly missing from the core questionnaire is any question relating to people’s attitudes towards climate change. Given the importance of this issue globally, this seems like an omission. Perhaps considering to add a question tapping into this could be worthwhile. The American National Election Study for example includes the following question that could be used: “Some people think the federal government needs to regulate business to protect the environment. They think that efforts to protect the environment will also create jobs. Let us say this is point 1 on a 1 -7 scale. Others think that the federal government should not regulate business to protect the environment. They think this regulation will not do much to help the environment and will cost us jobs. Let us say this is point 7 on a 1-7 scale. And of course, some other people have opinions somewhere in be tween, at points 2,3,4,5, or 6.” When it comes to the demographic questions, the questionnaire includes the core sets of demographics used by scholars of electoral behavior , participation and political attitudes. Given that about a third of articles use household income as a key demographic variable, it may be worthwhile considering additional aspects 10 that tap into a respondent’s wealth, such as home ownership or savings for example. Household income might not be a sufficient enough indicator to capture a respondent’s socio -economic status. A question could be included if the respondent rents or owns the house/apartment s/he lives in (and possibly if s/he owns the if she the house/apartment the share of mortgage that still needs to be paid) or if s/he is ab le to put money in savings at the end of the month. 4. text: four broad categories: “Identifier”, “Weights”, “Election Logistics”, and “Study Logistics” variables. Identifier Identifier variables describe the dataset and data so that researchers can identify the dataset or subset of the dataset that is pertinent to their research questions. Identifier variables for example include country codes to identify which observations are from a given country, election year codes to identify observations in a given time period, or respondent id numbers to identify respondents within an election study. Some identifier variables are redundant. For example, there are currently five different variables that make it possible to identify which country a given study was fielded in: Polity CSES Code, Polity UN Code, Polity Name, Election Study (Numeric Polity), and Election Study (Alphabetic Polity). Election Study (Numeric Polity) and Election Study (Alphabetic Polity) are constructed by combining country code and election year identifiers. Since it is easy and fast to construct these variables, removing them from the 6 We are very grateful to Tine Paulsen (https://wp.nyu.edu/tinenpaulsen/ ) for assistance in preparing this section of the report. 11 study would not improve efficiency particularly. Furthermore, their inclusion makes it easy for researchers to work with multiple waves of the study or to combine the CSES data with other data sources. For these reasons, it should not be a priority to remove these from the study. Weights The CSES includes a variety of weight variables divided up into sample, demographic, and political weights. Sample weights are included so researchers can correct for unequal selection probabilities, while demographic weights ensure that researchers can weigh the data, so the sample’s socio -demographic characteristics more closely resemble the population’s. Finally, political weights provide the researcher with a tool to correct for the sample’s reported voting behavior not fitting with the official vote count. There are th ree different types: Original Weights, Polity Weights, and Dataset Weights. The Original Sample Weights are the weights reported by the individual election studies. Polity Weights are standardized so that the original weights have a mean of 1 within a give n country. Dataset Weights are calculated so that researchers can use all observations in the CSES regardless of country and can correct for not all sample sizes being the same across election studies. The Weights category also includes certain variables that are used to construct the weights. “Factor: Sample Size Adjustment”, for example, reports the ratio of the average sample size to the given election study’s sample size. The Weights variables are fairly technical. Even though researchers could theoretically construct all the weight variables from the set of Original Weights, this might be quite demanding and result in calculation errors. Even though researchers could theoretically construct all the weight variables from the set of Original Weights, this might be quite demanding and result in calculation errors. Therefore, removing them could impact the quality of research being done using the CSES. This negative effect would especially hit research using cross- country comparisons since the Dataset Weights are the hardest to calculate. Election Logistics This is the smallest category of administrative variables. The variables describe 12 the type of election taking place and the timing of the election. The timing variables are divided up in “day”, “month”, and “year” variables, which is fairly inefficient. However, this division avoids possible standardization mistakes that could happen when multiple election study teams dif fer in their election timing descriptions. Study Logistics The last category of administrative variables describes how the specific election study was administered. This set of variables allows a researcher to see whether the study was conducted by telephone, how long an interview lasted, and whether the study was conducted during or after an electoral period. These variables are important for researchers who use the CSES for cross- country comparisons. If a researcher wants to compare two different coun tries’ responses to the same question, it could for example be important that both of the country’s samples were asked the particular question over the phone. Comparing Administrative Variables to Other Studies The CSES’s number of identifier variables is above average for the studies surveyed. This seems to be because the CSES wants to make it easy to use the included studies for both national analysis and cross -national analysis. Other cross-national studies, with the exception of the World Values Survey and the LaPOP, do for example not include a unique “study id” variable that combines the year of study and the country the study took place in. Instead, the logic seems to be that researchers can construct these types of variables on their own. This obviously increases the likelihood of a researcher making a mistake and not analyzing the exact observations they are interested in. The CSES does not include a respondent’s region of residence or electoral district of residence under its list of administrative variables. However, these smaller geographic units are included as ordinary variables in the CSES, which means that researchers have a chance to divide respondents up in smaller geographical units for analysis. 13 The CSES’s number and diversity of weight variables is large compared to all other studies surveyed. text: included as ordinary variables in the CSES, which means that researchers have a chance to divide respondents up in smaller geographical units for analysis. 13 The CSES’s number and diversity of weight variables is large compared to all other studies surveyed. However, the weight variables make it possible to use the national studies in their original form and also use them for cross -country analyses. Part of the reason the CSES’s weight variables are so numerous is that some of the other studies surveyed are not cross -national. Therefore, the set of weighting variables that are constructed to make sure that individual observations in the CSES can be studied across countries are not present in these other studies. However, even compared to the cross- national studies, the CSES’s number of weight variables is large. Most cross -national studies do not include the original country weights and the intermediate variables that transform them to cross- national weights. Therefore, it is possible to use the CSES dataset to extract single studies in their original form or to use a multitude of studies for cross- national analysis. National electoral studies unsurprisingly tend to have less information about the elections they are studying than the CSES. The set of election logistics variables makes it clear that the CSES is trying to help researchers who compare certain features of political systems to do so without having to do much outside research. This ensures that an inexperienced researcher does not accidentally include studies that focus on a type of election the researcher is not interested in. The study logistics set of variables are designed so researchers can identify national differences in the way of co nducting interviews that could lead to systematically different respondent responses. A lot of other cross- national studies are missing this component. An alternative strategy would be to make sure that all studies included in the CSES conduct their studie s in the same way. However, this would mean that some country studies would be forced to change their study logistics. This is not a viable strategy since such a change would make it impossible to ensure consistency in the responses to questions over time. Finally, some studies that use face -to-face interviews, the ANES and the LaPOP, include a battery of interviewer demographics variables. These are included out of a concern for an interviewer’s ethnicity or gender affecting the respondent’s answers to certain questions. The CSES includes the interviewer’s gender but does not include other demographic variables. 14 Table 1. Recommendations Our survey of other election studies suggests that -- far from lacking administrative data found on other studies -- CSES is actually at the forefront of providing researchers with valuable administrative data. We therefore have only three recommendations: 16 1) If there is a belief that the administrative data requirements are proving too onerous for national election teams, it is certainly the case that CSES provides many, many more potential weights than different surveys. That being said, we find good reason for these weights, and think that by and large they provide useful tools for researchers that increase the value of the data. Nevertheless, it is possible that some of these weights are rarely used. Therefore, if there was to be a CSES wide survey of existing literature to check for usage of different variables or types of data, it might be worth including in that review a measure of how often different weights are applied, with an eye towards possibly not including certain weights if they are never used. To be clear, this is a second best option to continuing to include the weights, and one which we think should only be pursued if there is a mandate to reduce administrative data. 2) The only category of administrative data that we could find for which CSES is lacking information provided by a (limited) number of other studies is in terms of interviewer demographic charac teristics. However, this is of course complicated by the lack of comparable identity characteristics across countries. However, we would like to suggest that perhaps a simple ethnicity variable could be included, with interviewers being identified as whether they are a member of the majority ethnic group, a minority ethnic group, or if they consider themselves of mixed ethnic descent. This seems like something that could be (a) simple to collect without being (b) overly intrusive and yet (c) provide value to researchers worried about interviewer effects on certain typ es of questions. The Board could also consider other types of interviewer characteristics (e.g., region of the country, primary language), but we suspect the most important would be ethnicity. 17 3) It was not clear to us from the documentation provided how exactly the interviewer mode variable was coded (is that from a list of categories? open ended questions?), but we would suggest that as survey research migrates online, if there are categories that are provided as part of this question, it might be worth re visiting them before Wave 6 to make sure they accurately reflect current modes of survey research. We would also note that the question regarding the gender of the interviewer should probably reflect whatever updates we make in terms of thinking about how to question survey respondents regarding gender identity (i.e., do we want to add a non- binary category?). 18 Appendix I: Current Metadata (Administrative Data) Name Category Website Description Codebook Description (Shortened) Dataset Identifier Dataset This variable reports the CSES module applied in each election study. Electoral Democracy under Pressure” Module 6 subcommittee: Marina Costa Lobo (Chair), Universidade de Lisboa Rüdiger Schmitt -Beck, Universität Mannheim David Sulmont, Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú Markus Wagner, Universität Wien February 2020 Background The CSES Sub committee for Module 6 received 22 proposals for the questionnaire. In the preparation of the Meeting in Vienna, the subcommittee evaluated the proposals, both individually and as a group. The proposals were then presented to the CSES Planning Committee and the merits of each were discussed openly. Following this discussion, a br oad consensus was reached on several topics : the support for different models of democracy, namely distinguishing between participative, representative or technocratic models ; and the representation and participation of women in elections and democratic in stitutions. In this first draft we try to provide an overarching framework that may capture these different topics by revisiting the extant literature on support for democracy. Declining Democracy? The year 2019 marks the 30th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall, a moment which signaled the end of the Cold War, and the dawn of an era of democratization in the world. 30 years on, some have argued that the world is entering a period of “democratic recess ion” (Diamond 2015) or “democratic backsliding” (Bermeo 2016) , others point to the fact that in several countries, alternative regimes to liberal democracy have gained support in public opinion over time 2 (Steenekamp and du Toit 2017) . Despite the fact that this diagnosis has been contested (Levitsky and Way 2015) , the evidence does seem to be gathering strength (Mainwaring and Bizzarro 2019) . According to the most recent Freedom House Report , “2018 recorded the 13th consecutive year of decline in global freedom (…) Between 2005 and 2018, the share of not free countries rose to 26 percent, while the share of free countries declined to 44 percent ” (Freedom House 2019, 1) . What is new about these trends is that t his decline in Freedom is affecting a variety of countries in every single region of the globe, from the United States to Brazil or Austria (The Economist Intelligence Unit 2019, 7) . Latin America has also not escaped this trend (Zechmeister and Lupu 2019; Corporación Latinobarómetro 2019; Lagos 2019) . Mainwaring and Bi zzarro, come to a similar conclusion while surveying the fate of third wave democracies: “Among the 91 new democracies that emerged during the third wave, 34 experienced breakdowns, often in short order. Mainwaring and Bi zzarro, come to a similar conclusion while surveying the fate of third wave democracies: “Among the 91 new democracies that emerged during the third wave, 34 experienced breakdowns, often in short order. In 28 cases, democracy stagnated after the transition, usually at a fairly low level, and in two others it eroded. There have been some successes; 23 regimes achieved major democratic advances between their first year of democracy and 2017.” (Mainwaring and Bizzarro 2019, 100) . Understanding and explaining this decline in democracy is a challenge the CSES should take on . CSES has a global vocation, gather ing election studies from over 50 countries around the world in the Americas, Asia, Europe and Africa. It is really one of the few research projects which has this broad scope, and the only one which focuses on post -electoral attitudes and behavior . Therefore, the CSES is best placed to analyze the causes and consequences of this emerging trend of a decline in democracy around the world , among old and new democracies . In addition, CSES has from the outset, had the goal of understanding how the elector al systems, the electoral process contributes to democracy. For the last 25 years it has built up a longitudinal perspective on the way in which these attitudes shape democracy, which can be put to good use when considering how a module that considers the declining democrac ies should be formulated. Mapping “Declining Democracy ”, its causes and its effects on voting behavior The alarming nature of reports on the state of democracy is not that recent. In fact, it has already led to a substantial amount of scholarly literature on the subject. An increasing number of studies have monitored the widespread dissatisfaction with government performance, as well as distrust of political institutions (Dalton 2004) . Norris (1999) introduced the concept of critical citizens, who are those who, despite being committed to the principles of democracy, nonetheless are increasingly critical of the way democracy works. 3 Indee d, when moving from the country analysis to the individual level analysis of democratic attitudes, a fundamental starting point is the measurement of satisfaction with democracy (SWD). In a seminal study on the meaning of SWD , Linde and Ekman’s found the f ollowing: “Departing from a theoretical multidimensional model of political support, and drawing on large -scale public opinion surveys, (…) the survey item ‘satisfaction with the way democracy works’ is not an indicator of support for the principles of democracy. Rather, it (…) taps the level of support for the way the democratic regime works in practice (…) this item is far from a perfect indicator of support for

text: political support, and drawing on large -scale public opinion surveys, (…) the survey item ‘satisfaction with the way democracy works’ is not an indicator of support for the principles of democracy. Rather, it (…) taps the level of support for the way the democratic regime works in practice (…) this item is far from a perfect indicator of support for the performance of a democratic regime, since it is highly sensitive to diffe rent institutional contexts .” (Linde and Ekman 2003, 391) The authors argue for a cautious approach when analyzing political support and legitimacy, by including multiple indicators. Thus, even though SWD should be an anchor question for Module 6, it is important to reflect on the other indicators which need to be included as well, namely trust in political institutions. Measures of democratic attitudes were proposed by a sizable number of responses to the CSES ’ Call for Questions. Theoretically they made reference s to a variety of themes, most prominently among them the current debate about democratic backsliding, the worldwide crisis of liberal democracy and its challenge through plebiscitarian and executive -dominated populism and the concomitant intensification of political and societal polarization and identity politics. This development bears the potential to erode the normative foundations and institutional architecture of liberal democracy with its emphasis on minority protection and the containment of governme ntal power through the separation of powers and in particular an independent judiciary as well as elected representatives as core agency of authoritative decision -making. Since elections are at the heart of this model of democracy, this is a theme of cruci al relevance for the CSES. Connected to this broader motive are more specific lines of argument where proposals referred to research on process preferences, that is, citizens ’ conceptions of ideal governance. Where should the locus of control ultimately re side, with elected representatives, or rather with experts, businesspeople, or the citizens themselves? The subcommittee proposes a framework to explore th ese issues that can be summarized in the diagram presented in Figure 1. At the center of this framework we place the problem of support and trust of electoral and representative democratic institutions in order to compare it among the different political systems and societies that are represented in the CSES project, and to evaluate its effects on: a) the suppo rt for alternative models of democracy or authoritarian regimes; and b) voting behavior, particularly participation in elections and the preference for radical or populist political parties that might draw support from citizens discontent with representati ve democratic 4 institutions. Figure 1: Module 6 proposed framework Rising levels of dissatisfaction with democracy have been the focus of study, as well as probing the causes for this change in attitudes towards how democracy works in practice. There have been divergent models which have emerged as a possible r eason for dissatisfaction: firstly, the need for more participation, greater involvement of citizens, and generally an opening up of institutions to allow for citizen deliberation (“input” factors) ; others contend that the surge in critical citizens does n ot arise from a greater need for participation, but rather that what is needed is an improvement in the results of democracy (“output” factors) . Yet others would like to propose a reinforcement of the representative democracy process. These can be seen as competing theoretical perspectives on the causes of the emergence of critical citizens: indeed, some scholars argue that explanations for the dissatisfaction with democracy are related to the input side of the political system. If that is the case, then t he solution would be to improve the representative institutions. A rival theoretical explanation contends that political support is largely output driven, and very much dependent on the quality of the outputs which the political institutions are able to deliver to citizens (Norri s 1999; Rothstein 2009; Dahlberg and Holmberg 2014) . Some authors maintain that both the procedural features (the “input” side) and the outcomes of democratic systems (liberty, equality , public services and distribution of material goods) are key elemen ts to evaluate the quality of democracy (Morlino 2004; 2007) . According to Dahlberg, Linde and Holmberg (2015) , the studies which have actually investigated whether 5 causes to dissatisfied democrats are input or output driven are actually very few (Doorenspleet 2012) . Norris’ study on critical citizens noted that these tended to exhibit higher levels of education, and political information. The author was quite optimistic in suggesting that these citizens were holding democratic institutions to higher standards, and making demands on them, to become more representative, thus placing the author firmly on the “input” side of the explanations for democratic dissatisfaction. When considering the improvement of institu tions, the need for better electoral institutions seems to loom large in this “input” driven explanatory model of democratic dissatisfaction. In addition, we know from the literature on democratic

text: standards, and making demands on them, to become more representative, thus placing the author firmly on the “input” side of the explanations for democratic dissatisfaction. When considering the improvement of institu tions, the need for better electoral institutions seems to loom large in this “input” driven explanatory model of democratic dissatisfaction. In addition, we know from the literature on democratic backsliding (Bermeo 2016) , that increasingly, the deterioration of democracy can be detected through electoral manipulation. Thus, the quality of electoral processes needs to be at the center of the input dimension of the investigation into the dissatisfaction with democracy. Not only do electoral processes need to be at the center of the “input” driven model of democratic dissatisfaction. When considering the deficit in the quality of representative democracy, one emerging issue is the degree of participation as well as represent ation of women in political institutions. In some European countries, the role of women in politics has been emerging as a potential cleavage with attitudes towards women important factors of voting behavior . CSES Module 6 will thus innovate in bringing th e deficit of women’s participation as a potential factor of democratic (dis)satisfaction. When considering the “output” factors which may drive support for democracy, several issues need to be considered . Perhaps the most important variable to introduce i s “government performance”, which is a broad concept (Magalhães 2014) . Indeed, it has been argued that performance may be judged by citizens not only in terms of outcomes such as economic growth or a functioning health care system, but also in terms of quality of governance such as effective, non-corrupt institution s (Magalhães 2014; Dahlberg, Linde, and Holmberg 2015; Kotze and Garcia -Rivero 2017) . Going beyond the issues of input or output driven (dis)satisfaction with democracy, it is important to measure support for different models of democracy, namely a plebiscitary vs. a technocratic or a “stealth” model of democracy (Hibbing and Theiss -Morse 2002; del Río, Navarro, and Front 2016; Font, Wojcieszak, and Navarro 2015) . Although to enough research has been undertaken on this front (Bertsou and Pastorella 2017) for lack of the necessary data concerning preferences for either model of democracy. Citizen dissatisfaction due to inputs or output deficits are very much related to preferences rega rding the degree of involvement of citizens, politicians, businesspeople, or experts generally in the political process. 6 Module 6 also aims to integra te the use of social media in the analysis of electoral behavior . Political attitudes, views on democracy, as well as views about politicians may be changing or becoming more polarized through extensive use of social media. The latter may also have an effect on participation.

By probing attitudes to different models of democracy it will be possible to delve into the link between these attitud es, its causes, and consequences for political attitudes and voting behavior . To answer questions such as the following: does a preference for higher citizen participation lead to more voting? How does preference for technocracy correlate for voting for po pulist parties? Despite the fact that SWD is often included in all the major comparative surveys, such as ESS, WVS, EVS, LAPOP and Latinobarometro, it is not the ca se that there has been a global comparative survey on the causes of dissatisfaction with democracy, or with alternative models of democracy such as posited by this Module. In the rest of the document we therefore introduce potential questions. Proposed Questions for CSES Module 6 Support for Representative Democracy and for Alternative Types of Government The subcommittee identified a set of common concerns connecting the various proposals that focused on democratic attitudes. Due to lack of spa ce and concerns about measurement quality none of the proposals could be adopted in full. Instead, we aimed for a parsimonious set of questions that in a coherent and efficient way covers the latent dimensions identifiable in these proposals and fills gaps relevant for the general theme not addressed by them. We anchored the instrument in the standard question about respondents‘ satisfaction with democracy which was suggested by several proposals (Pilet et al. 2019; Ridge 2019) and has anyway been a standard ingredient of the CSES during all previous waves. This instrument is often interpreted as a measure of “specific ” support for democracy. It concerns the way democracy has been implemented in a particular political system and the actual functioning of its political process. It concerns the way democracy has been implemented in a particular political system and the actual functioning of its political process. Thus, it is related to the output dimension of democratic politics. Taking up an impulse from Ridge’s proposal about “democratic commitment” we complemented this question with a set of three items that indi cate more principled, “diffuse ” support of the notion of a 7 democratic political order as such (partly asking for comparative assessments vis à vis non - democratic regimes). Given the CSES ’ focus on elections we found it appropriate to include in this batter y also an instrument that specifically elicits respondents ’ commitment to elections as democratic mode to establish governments. This is in line with Kostadinova’s (2019) proposal on “institutional authoritarianism ”. Finally, to obtain a complete picture of respondents ’ more general stances towards democracy we also found it important to include a measure that registers people’s perceptions of the extent to which their own political system actually qualifies as democratic. To address the more specific level of attitudes towards democratic regimes ’ institutional architecture we included a set of standard questions about confidence in institutions, following the proposal by Pilet et al. However, for lack of space we limited the range of institutions addressed by this question strictly to the institutional core of representative liberal democracy: parliament, government, the judiciar y, and political parties. While parliament, government and parties pertain to elections and representation, including the judiciary makes sure that also the specific role of the courts and the rule of law within the separation of powers is covered. The latter also responds to the proposal by Driscoll and Nelson (2019) , although in a more expansive fashion, since the proposal itself f ocused more narrowly on Supreme Courts within Presidential systems. We propose a set of items aiming to elicit respondent’s process preferences with regard to the locus of power in political decision -making. They are inspired by several proposals, most prominently the very extensive one by Pilet et al. However, not all categories of potentially powerful actors proposed by these collea gues could be adopted in our draft. We concentrated on those that we felt were most interesting from the point of view of a comparative study of global scope and with reference to the overall theme of liberal democracy under challenge. First, to address th e recent populist drive towards strong executive -dominated leadership with diminished accountability towards parliaments and courts we included two items that query respondents ’ views about desirable governmental leadership strength

The third subset again consists of two items. They relate to research about “stealth democracy ” and address authoritative decision - making by businesspersons and experts. The latter also refers to Flores ’ more extensive proposal about “technocratic ” governance. Again, it was not possible to include all agencies proposed by Pilet et al. We decided to exclude association representatives, military officers and religious leaders, among others, from our draft instrument.
