[Slide 9] Data Architecture & Unifying Principle of the CSES IMD 3 [Slide 10] Dataset Naming Criteria: Easily understandable name. Innovative name. Openness in choice of name. Market friendly. 9 different versions. We proposed to name the new CSES Product the CSES Integrated Module Dataset (IMD) which was approved by the PC in November 2017. [Slide 11] Variable Naming CSES Standalone Module Convention: Each variable is assigned a five-character alphanumeric identification. Example: F2003 (Module, Variable Group, Order in Dataset). IMD variables follow Standalone CSES convention closely: Three alphabetical characters and four numerical characters. Example: IMD2003 (Integrated Module Dataset, Variable Group, Order in Dataset). [Slide 12] An integrated file: Constraints Six Modules, i.e., maximum number of data points as of today is six or seven. Various Module specific questions that occur in only one of the CSES Modules. At the polity level, many countries have fielded CSES questionnaire only once [Slide 13] Unifying Principle: “The 3 & 1 rule” 3 applies to the variable level, i.e. a variable is included if it appears at least three times in CSES Modules 1-5: Allows for trend analysis. Ensures that variables included in the CSES IMD are likely to be relevant and asked repeatedly. 1 refers to the polity level: All polities & studies are included: has a political advantage and increases incentives to become part of CSES. Allows for data maximization. [Slide 14] CSES IMD - Stimulus Paper https://cses.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/CSES_IMD_Stimulus-Paper_Final.pdf [Slide 15] Party/Coalition Harmonization in CSES IMD 4 [Slide 16] CSES IMD: Innovation HARMONIZATION OF PARTY/COALITION CODING ACROSS TIME [Slide 17] Recap: Party/Coalition Coding in CSES The CSES uses two different ways to code parties. These appear in different variables. Numerical and alphabetical codes are documented in the parties and leaders part of the Codebook (Part 3). For the first six parties with at least 1% of the vote, ordering of alphabetic codes follows the descending vote share of parties in the main election. This can result in several inconsistencies/anomalies in CSES macro data across modules. Full scope of these issues only emerge when we merge observations/cases at CMP. PURPOSE Macro Consistency Checks explores these issues. Some inconsistencies are legitimate. Others are due to inter-coder or intra-coder challenges or refined understandings. text: Page 1 of 6 CSES Planning Committee Meeting - Leuven, Belgium - January 2025 Handout: Oxford University Press (OUP) Book Series 2020 Volume: Democracy Under Siege? Parties, Voters, and Elections After the Great Recession Authors: Timothy Hellwig, Yesola Kweon, & Jack Vowles Description from OUP: “The Global Financial Crisis of 2008- 2009 was catalyst for the most precipitous economic downturn in eight decades. This book examines how the GFC and ensuing Great Recession affected electoral politics in the world’s developed democracies. The initial wave of research on the crisis concluded it did little to change the established relationships between voters, parties, and elections. Yet nearly a decade since the initial shock, the political landscape has changed in m any ways, the extent to which has not been fully explained by existing studies. Democracy Under Siege? pushes against the received wisdom by advancing a framework for understanding citizen attitudes, preferences, and behavior. It makes two central claims. First, while previous studies of the GFC tend to focus on an immediate impact of the crisis, Hellwig, Kweon, and Vowles argue that economic malaise has a long- lasting impact. In addition to economic shock, the economic recovery has a significant impact on citizens’ assessment of political elites. Second, the authors argue that unanticipated exogenous shocks like the GFC grants party elites an opening for political manoeuvre through public policy and rhetoric. As a result, political elites have a high degree of agency to shape public perceptions and behaviour. Political parties can strategically moderate citizens’ economic uncertainty, mobilise/demobilise voters, and alter individuals’ political preferences. By leveraging data from over 150,000 individuals ac ross over 100 nationally -representative post -election surveys from the 1990s to 2017, this book shows how economic change during a tumultuous era affected economic perceptions, policy demands, political participation, and the vote.” Page 2 of 6 2016 Edited Volume: Globalization and Domestic Politics: Parties, Elections, and Public Opinion Editors: Jack Vowles & Georgios Xezonakis Contributors: Sarah Birch; Stephen D. Fisher; Timothy Hellwig; Jeffrey A. Karp; Mark Andreas Kayser ; Caitlin Milazzo; Stratos Patrikios; Michael Peress; Kathrin Thomas; Erik Tillman; Jack Vowles; Georgios Xezonakis Description from OUP: “Globalization and Domestic Politics addresses how a widely acknowledged and pervasive economic and social process and globalization affect democratic politics among both masses and elites. It inquires into the extent to which, and how, globalization affects the political attitudes and behav ior of ordinary citizens and the policies of political parties. Chapters discuss to what extent globalization affects the salience of left -right politics, the content of party programs and promises, leadership evaluations, economic voting, electoral accountability, the influence of religion in politics, electoral turnout, political efficacy, satisfaction with democracy, and the quality of democracy.

Description from OUP: “A large body of electoral studies and political party research argues that the institutional context defines incentives that shape citizen participation and voting choice. With the unique resources of the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems, this book provides the first systematic evaluation of this topic. A distinguished international team of electoral scholars finds that the institutional context has only a modest impact on citizen political choices compared to individual level factors. Furthermore, the formal institutional characteristics of electoral systems that have been most emphasized by electoral studies researchers have less impact than characteristics of the party system that are separate from formal institutions. text: DRAFT Job Advertisement: Data Visualization Consultant – CSES Survey Data Playground Position: R Shiny Application Developer (Consultant) Project Duration: [ Approximately 80 hours ] Location: Remote We are seeking a data visualization specialist to participate in the development of an interactive application in R Shiny for analyzing survey data. text: Data Playground and C urriculum Tools NSF Proposal Text – Narrative and Budget Justiﬁcation Narrative Finally, it will increase data access and engagement in the project by creating a point -and-click “data playground” for non-specialists to query the data; it will create related pedagogical material via collaborations with the American Political Science Association (APSA) and faculty at diverse teaching - oriented institutions. Innovate over data dissemination. Data access is a core CSES principle. The team releases the project’s harmonized comparative datasets free of charge and in various formats. CSES datasets are made available to the entire research community as soon as they are processed. They can be downloaded, for free, from the CSES website. With this proposal, we seek to extend data access by developing a “data playground” and engaging scholars at non-R1 colleges and institutions in building and disseminating pedagogical tools for this playground. A data playground is an interactive point -and-click means that junior scholars and non-specialists can use to query the data and create related visualizations. Such applications can be built on open-source tools and/or commercial visualization software. Examples include the Tableau -based data query plat form run by LAPOP, the designed-in -house playground run by the British Election Study, and the RStudio/Github -located interactive platform by the National Center for Health Statistics. text: COMPARATIVE STUDY OF ELECTORAL SYSTEMS (CSES) SECRETARIAT MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING 1.Upon signing, this MOU replaces all previous MOUs and is in effect immediately. 2.The CSES project, both intellectually and operationally, is governed by the set of international scholars who compose the CSES Planning Committee. Members of the CSES Planning Committee are elected by the global network of CSES collaborators. 3.The CSES Secretariat is responsible for the implementation and administration of the CSES project, under the guidance of the CSES Planning Committee and its Chair. The CSES Secretariat will be operated in partnership between the Center for Political Studies (CPS) at the University of Michigan and the GESIS -Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences , with both given credit for their contributions in all CSES documents, communications, and the project website. The partners commit to exchanging usage statistics annually and as needed. 4.The common objective of CPS and GESIS in jointly operating the CSES Secretariat is to foster comparative research with and.about the CSES data, and to provide the CSES data to the scientific community in as timely a fashion as possible, according to the best standards for data documentation and dissemination. 5.The CSES Secretariat at GESIS is a separate endeavor from the CSES component within the German Longitudinal Election Study (GLES), which is the charge of the GLES project. 6.The CSES Secretariat comprises the following positions at the listed percent effort devoted to CSES activities: CPS will provide 20% of a Director of Studies out of funding from the American National Science Foundation. GESIS will provide 70% of a post-doctoral Project Leader, 50% of a graduate student Research Associate, and 75% of an Archivist. 7.CSES data products will continue to be disseminated by both CSES and GESIS in their usual ways. 8.The Director of Studies and Project Leader will be ex officio members of the CSES Planning Committee. 9.The President of GESIS is not a member of the CSES Secretariat staff but will have both functional and administrative authority over the GESIS employees. The Director of Studies will provide functional supervision for the Project Leader, Research Associate, and Archivist so long as that supervision is not in conflict with the interests of GESIS. 10.GESIS will fund the annual GESIS Klingemann Prize for the best CSES Scholarship. The annual winner will be decided by a Selection Committee composed of three representatives, with the chair and second representative selected by the CSES Planning Committee and the third representative selected by GESIS. 11.GESIS and CPS will work together to provide adequate funding for appropriate travel for Secretariat staff. GESIS and CPS will coordinate wherever possible to secure funding external to CPS and GESIS to support the activities and expenses of the CSES Secretariat.

text: The Seventh Module of the CSES: Project Description: Page 1 of 15 The S event h Module of the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES) Introduction. At the turn of the 21st century, electoral democracy reached a new apex . Three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall, most countries regularly held fair elections, and the plurality of countries was “free” (Freedom House 2005) . Record -setting numbers of citizens were charged with channeling their input into politics – principally through elections – to secure representation and accountability. Today these gains are in jeopardy. Democracy is in recession: every year since 2005 has seen more global losses than gains in freedom (Freedom House 2021) . What role do citizens play in electoral democracies under stress? How do dynamics at the macro -level – e.g., the composition of the legislature, social media, or the COVID-19 pandemic – register in citizens’ electoral choices and their evaluations of government output, elections, and democracy? Answers to these questions, among others, are made possible through the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES), a project that has succeeded far beyond expectations due to strategic investments and sound management. CSES brings together international collaborat ors to advance the science of surveys, disseminat e harmonized cross-national and cross -temporal comparative data, and make discoveries regarding electoral behavior and outcomes. This proposal seeks to allow the CSES team, first, to complete Module 6, which assesses citizens’ role in representative democracy under pressure , and second, to design Module 7 by crowd-sourcing proposals from the global user community. Concurrent ly, the project will foster dialogue on advances in survey methods, generate original comparative data on electoral attitudes and behavior, and yield new research . Further, the project will disseminate data and policy -relevant findings, strengthen connections between researchers and institutions in over 60 countries, and build capacity in STEM disciplines. Finally, it will increase data access and engagement in the project by creating a point -and-click “data playground” for non-specialists to query the data; it will create related pedagogical material via collaborations with the American Political Science Association (APSA) and faculty at diverse teaching -oriented institutions. Established in 1994, CSES is recognized internationally as a unique and valuable resource for innovating in comparative research on electoral behavior . As the project has grown, so has its value: the project permits analyses across three decades of opinion and an increasing number of diverse country contexts. CSES emerged to solve the challenge of building global collaborations cost-effectively, collecting harmonized scientific survey data, and disseminating user-friendly datasets and research. The project has its origins in a call by Stein Rokkan (1970) for co llaborative cross-nat ional research to systematically investigate the structural and contextual underpinnings of political behavior. Since then , scholars of comparative democratic politics have advanced theoretical understanding s and generated empirical results concerning how societal, political, and economic institutional and structural contexts shape opinion and behavior . CSES is a unique resource for scholars devoted to these efforts: it provides the only publicly-available comparative datasets with micro (survey) and macro (institutions and other contextual features) datasets for the refinement of theory and e mpirical evaluation regarding how electoral behavior varies across and within countries. Soon after its inauguration, CSES received the Przeworski/Lijphart/Verba Dataset Award from the American Political Science Association’s Comparative Politics Section. Th e award citation lauded the project for “the importance and breadth of the questions the data help us to answer, the numbers of hypotheses the data allow us to test, the quality of the information and documentation, [and] public accessibility ” and heralded the project as a “magnificent example of international intellectual collaboration, a model for others to follow .” Today CSES has established itself as the principal data source for systematic research on comparative electoral behavior. Through the collaboration of hundreds of scholars and its dynamic nature , CSES advances the frontier of research on electoral choice in ways not possible through secondary or other data sources. CSES has three core intellectual goals: • understand the nature of political , economic, and social cleavages that generate varied electoral outcomes and party systems ; • illuminate how political, economic , and social structures, especially electoral systems, shape beliefs and behavior , thereby shaping the nature of democratic choice expressed in elections; • shed light on how citizens living under diverse political arrangements evaluate democratic institutions and processes. CSES advances these goals via an innovative design that combines micro and macro data. The micro - level data come from national post-election surveys administered with a common core maintained over time and a distinct theme module that emerges each round from crowd -sourced global input and academic study . The macro data document each country’s electoral -institutional arrangements and other social, political, and economic contextual conditions. This micro -macro design facilitates theoretical and substantiv e advances in understanding, for instance, how electoral institution s directly or indirectly influence individual attitudes and behavior . text: from crowd -sourced global input and academic study . The macro data document each country’s electoral -institutional arrangements and other social, political, and economic contextual conditions. This micro -macro design facilitates theoretical and substantiv e advances in understanding, for instance, how electoral institution s directly or indirectly influence individual attitudes and behavior . Findings from research using CSES data have implications for the conduct of elections and the nature and quality of democratic representation all over the world. The Seventh Module of the CSES: Project Description: Page 3 of 15 Moreover, t he micro -macro design effectively weds two traditions in the field – one centered on individuals and the other centered on contexts and aggrega tes. CSES thus differs from other projects devoted to comparative electoral research in five ways. First, it applies a coordinated, integrated design to analyze electoral behavior in different contexts . This distinguishes it from research comparing the findings of individual or non-harmonized national election studies. Second, the project maximizes innovation by incorporating input from the entire user community into the theme for each round. Third , CSES is a multi-level study relating macro - and micro - characteristics to one another. On a general level, CSES deals with the quality and performance of democracy (Shugart and Carey 1992; Cox 2002). More specific ally, it allows us to determine to what degree electio ns serve the purpose s of popular representation and control of policymakers and which circumstances provide environments for elections to perform those functions well . Fourth, CSES spans three decades , during which countries (and thus the project’s macro data) have changed in numerous ways that permit analys is of how varying democratic contexts affect electoral behavior and vice versa. Fifth , CSES is the only project that generates publicly available comparative election survey data. Advancing discoveries on macro -micro dynamics in electoral behavior is most effective with the kind of comparative datasets that CSES makes possible : comparable samples of citizens observed with comparable instruments. Only through genuinely comparative an alysis can the merits and shortcomings of different democratic arrangements be rigorously evaluated . In the next section , we describe the intellectual underpinnings and the collaborative efforts behind Module 6 , followed by the plan to develop Module 7. Breaking Intellectual Ground with New Modules . The theme for Module 6 ( to be fielded from 2022 - 2026) - Representative Democracy Under Pressure – emerged following a public and widely disseminated call, which generated 25 proposals from around the world. The proposals were reviewed by a CSES Module 6 Planning Committee subcommittee and presented and discussed at multiple Committee meetings. A draft questionnaire was then designed iteratively and pretested in five countries. The resulting questionnaire was reviewed, discussed, and approved in October 2021 at a virtual Plenary Session attended by more than 120 collaborators representing 57 countries. Finally, the questionnaire was posted to the CSES website, and Module 6 data collection officially beg an in early January 202 2. The intellectual motivation for Module 6 emerges from the need to understand how the public engages in democracies that are straining to realize ideal outcomes. The world recently marked the 30th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall, an event that further spread democra cy. Whereas that diffusion led to an apex in global democracy at the turn of the 21st century, these days , scholars argue that the world is in a “democratic recession” (Diamond 2015) or “democratic backsliding” (Bermeo 2016) . Others point to the fact that in several countries, alternative regimes to liberal democracy have gained support in public opinion over time (Steenekamp and du Toit 2017). Even though this diagnosis is contested (Levitsky and Way 2015), the evidence is mounting (Mainwaring and Bizzarro 2019). According to the Freedom House, this past year marked “ the 15th consecutive year of decline in global freedom” (Freedom House 20 21). Although there is important variation within and across countries, this decline in freedom affects every region of the globe, from North America, to Latin America, to Europe, and beyond (The Economist Intelligence Unit 2019 ; Zechmeister and Lupu 2019; Corporación Latinobarómetro 2019; Lagos 2019). The Seventh Module of the CSES: Project Description: Page 7 of 15 The unique design of the CSES is an excellent match to the task of u nderstanding and explaining the role of citizens in contributing or, or buttressing against, declines in democracy . This is because the design leverages global variation to analyze how individuals behave, respond, and think while embedded in distinct contexts around the world. To that end, the CSES Module 6 theme and questionnaire includes three areas of concentration: 1. the functioning of democracy, political trust, and support; 2. representation and democratic procedures; and 3. preferences over alternative forms of government . The initial ideas for Module 6 were in place before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic , yet CSES was able to adapt. This global disaster has placed further stress on governments worldwide and has had significant consequences for citizens’ attitudes toward institutions and elections (e.g., among many, Bol et al. 2021; Lupu and Zechmeister 2021). CSES’ relevance and nimble nature are reflected in its incorporation of the pandemic into Module 6, which contains a set of questions that evaluate pandemic - relevant experience and performance and will permit analyses of t his stressor on electoral democracy . Module 6 will allow researchers to address questions of broad interest to the academic and policy -making communities. For example, there is deb ate over whether global shocks and poor output undermine democratic support for democracy or only, more narrowly, satisfaction with democracy ( see, e.g., Claassen and Magalhaes 2021) . Module 6 permits advances in this agenda with new data and the capacity to investigate how different types of crises (eco nomic, social, pandemic) affect citizens’ views about the merits and limits of various democratic procedures . Further, research has been evolving over the extent to which gaps in descriptive representation b y gender ha ve consequences for political knowledge, engagement, and more (see, e.g. , Dassonneville and McAllister 2018 , among others) . Module 6 permits new advances in this domain by including citizens’ evaluations of gender representation in parliament. Input from the scholarly community in the design of Module 6 also emphasized the need for data to assess the nature and determinants of citizens’ preferences over alternative forms of government, whether democratic or not (see, e.g., Bertsou and Pasto rella 2017) . Module 6 was intentionally designed to generate data that will generate answers to these questions and provide new insights into the role of citizens in democracies under pressure. The team releases the project’s harmonized comparative datasets free of charge and in various formats. CSES datasets are made available to the entire research community as soon as they are processed . They can be downloaded, for free, from the CSES website. With this proposal, we seek to extend data access by developing a “data playground” and engaging scholars at non- R1 colleges and institutions in building and disseminating pedagogical tools for this playground. A data playground is an interactive point-and -click m eans that junior scholars and non-specialists can use to query the data and create related visualizations. Such applications can be built on open -source tools and /or commercial visualization software. Examples include the Tableau -based data query platform run by LAPOP, the designed -in-house playground run by the British Election Study, and the RStudio/Github -located interactive platform by the National Center for Health Statistics. Another way that the project will expand engagement in the project is by support ing the user community via pre -prepared tables and code for open-source statistics software that can serve as alternatives to expensive commercial statistical packages. To that end, we will expand a project GitHub archive of code for analyses and replications. CSES staff will curate and contribute to this archive but , by design, it is open to contributions by any member of the user community. 5. Expand the network of international c ollaborators. The Seventh Module of the CSES: Project Description: Page 15 of 15 Intellectual Merit. This proposal realizes intellectual merit by advancing discoveries regarding electoral behavior and innovating over survey methodology, data generation, and research production. (1) First, CSES advances survey methodology via white papers, expert consultations, global dialogue among survey specialists, workshops, and the dissemination of clear scientific standards. Scholars have used CSES data to develop new tools for comparative data analysis. They have adapted and advanced two -step and hierarchical modeling techniques appropriate for optimal leveraging of the rich empirical information in datasets like CSES with large numbers of micro -level observations across intermediate numbers of macro -level contexts. For e xample, Jusko and Shively (2005) used the data to develop a two-step strategy for analysis of cross-national survey data, and Achen (2005) used the structure of the data to develop a set of considerations for two-step hierarchical estimation. Scholars have also used the data to advance questions of measurement in cross -national research (e.g., Dalton 2008; Golder and Stramski 2010; Powell 2009; Wagner 2021). (2) Second, CSES applies cutting -edge and standardized best-practice standards in the process of data generation, resulting in comparative datasets and research that to date have yielded over 3,300 discoveries (publications) in the domain of electoral behavior . Critical research questions are determined following input from researchers around the globe. Module 6’s theme is Representative Democracy under Pressure. Freedom House and others concur that many democratic institutions are “backsliding ,” yet comparativ ely less is known regarding the role of the public. What deficits do citizens see in their democracies, and with what consequences for attitudes and behavior? CSES Module 6 adds data from 5 0+ countries to advance discoveries on this question. At the same time, the project’s Module 7 planning activities undertake the dynamic crowd-sourcing approach to identify the next critical question for election studies. (3) Third, and related, CSES facilitates research production via user-friendly datasets, workshops, panels, blogs , and an award that recognizes significant findings. Project planning is shaped by a continual process by which the global use of CSES data is tracked and assessed. The project’s research goals are to identify the nature of political and social divides in contemporary democracies, generate new insights into citizens’ electoral decisions, and uncover the nature, determinants, and consequences of citizens’ evaluations of democratic institutions and processes. The project’s research goals are to identify the nature of political and social divides in contemporary democracies, generate new insights into citizens’ electoral decisions, and uncover the nature, determinants, and consequences of citizens’ evaluations of democratic institutions and processes. Broader Impacts. This proposal i s designed to realize the following broader impacts: (1) Data dissemination : CSES designs, collects, cleans, merges, and distributes micro (survey) and macro (institutions and other contextual features) data from up to 60 national election studies across the world . This is the only publicly accessible comparative election studies dataset. Project datasets are downloaded over 500 times monthly. To facilitate data access by students and non -specialists, we will create a “data playground” and pedagogical materia l via collaborations with non- R1 faculty. (2) International collaboration : CSES brings scholars and survey practitioners in 60 -plus countries into cooperation and dialogue. Project-affiliated researchers raise their own funds for data collection, often via national science foundations. Further, CSES engages in outreach to scholars in less developed countries to strengthen institutional connections and support high-quality data collection. The CSES Planning Committee comprises a rotating elected body of researchers from around the world; this group advis es and monitor s project impact. (3) Capacity building in STEM: CSES is a vehicle for training a diverse set of junior scholars in the science of surveys, analysis, and research. CSES is widely used in universi ty course s, and students regularly serve as research assistants for the project . As three examples, Rosario Aguilar, Matias Bargsted, and Karen Long Jusko all worked on the project while completing their PhDs ; they are employed at Newcastle University, the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, and Facebook, respectively. The project provides free, high-quality data that enable scientific research and STEM training in every state in the U S. CSES fosters the creatio n of scientific capital around the world, and in new democracies, in particular – providing advice, venues, and standards to scholars collecting survey data and undertaking research on democratic politics. CSES runs workshops aimed at building capacity in survey analysis, such as the proposed curriculum workshop. (4) Di ssemination of knowledge : Impact is maximized via ungated white papers and blog posts, engagement with events in Washington, DC, and dialogue with national science institutions around the wor ld. In brief, CSES effectively delivers data and tools that generate knowledge regarding how and why citizens do or do not engage in democracy .

Author: Adea Gafuri. Topic: “In the face of the increasing presence of autocratic donors (like China, United Arab Emirates, India, Russia), in developing countries with financial initiatives that entail different practices, it is important to examine citizens’ attitudes toward foreign donors.” Proposal 1 Objective: The project seeks to study “the extent to which citizens demand transparency regarding these projects, channels for communication to express their concerns regarding aid projects, and to what extent they prefer politicians to abide by political conditionality imposed by Western donors or to have no conditions attached to aid.” Proposal 1 Questions: •Knowledge of foreign funded projects. •Preferences for different countries (as funders of projects). •Importance of information on these projects. •Importance of democratic norms as requirement for funds. •Views on how politicians should behave towards donors. •Opposition to donors. Proposal 3 Governing the Anthropocene. Authors: Dennis Abel and Franziska Quoß. Topic: “[P]roposal offers an innovative integration of Earth system justice perspectives into established environmental public opinion research. [It] operationalises Earth system justice attitudes as a major link between environmental attitudes and political outcomes.” Proposal 3 Objective: “Focus on the three boundaries that have been identified as crucial drivers for the destabilisation of the tipping points of the Earth system (...), and are salient enough in all nations that we expect average citizens to have stable opinions and attitudes on them” •Climate change. •Changes in biodiversity. •Air pollution. Proposal 3 Questions: •Climate change, biodiversity, and air pollution attitudes. •Earth system justice attitudes: interspecies justice, intergenerational justice, justice between countries, communities and individuals. •Policy preferences. •Importance of environment for vote. Proposal 4 Climate change. Author: Erik Voeten No formal questions or battery proposed but makes a pitch for including a question on climate change. Updating and managing the CSES Bibliography. Developing a Bibliography Policy for CSES. The CSES Bibliography Project. [Slide 3] The CSES Bibliography 1 [Slide 4] The CSES Bibliography Enumerative bibliography – organized listing of outputs based on a unifying principle. The CSES continuously collects information about the scholarly outputs that utilize our data. Thus, the unifying principle of the CSES bibliography is the use of CSES data in some way. We collect information on published journal articles, conference papers, book chapters, and dissertations for the purposes of providing a detailed bibliography on the CSES website. It is also helpful in funding applications. As of August 2025, we have more than 1,400 scholarly outputs using CSES data. More than 30% are peer-reviewed, published journal articles. [Slide 5] CSES Bibliography on the Website I [Slide 6] CSES Bibliography on the Website II [Slide 7] Updating and Managing the CSES Bibliography 2 [Slide 8] Searching for Scholarly Outputs for the CSES Bibliography I Google Scholar. Journals that usually publish comparative electoral behaviour material: Electoral Studies & Comparative Political Studies. American Journal of Political Science & American Political Science Review. Journal of Elections, Party, and Public Opinion (JEPOP) & Party Politics. For Conference papers/ manuscripts (mostly unpublished) Social Science Research Network (SSRN). All Academic Research Database. Homepages of conferences (e.g.: APSA; MPSA; EPSA; ECPR & EPOP). [Slide 9] Searching for Scholarly Outputs for CSES Bibliography II General searches using the CSES acronym but also use other terms commonly related to CSES, simultaneously: Electoral systems. Comparative voting behaviour. Be cautious using the CSES acronym only – otherwise, you might get : Cambodia Socio-Economic Survey. Center of South East Asian Studies. Conference on Signals and Electronic Systems. For presentations/CSES-related Meetings: Dave or Steve collect some material; Others provide support too. Between two bibliography updates, we store articles/conference presentations on Dropbox at CSES Secretariat II/CSES Bibliography/Bibliography/Add_toEndnote [Slide 10] How to handle publications in the CSES bibliography database? Having identified a relevant item for the CSES bibliography, download the document if possible for our records. If you cannot download the document (i.e., no access), send the link to colleagues and ask if they can get access. Upon downloading, store valid publications in the following name format: One author: cses_Surname_Year.pdf Two authors: cses_Surname_Surname_Year.pdf 2+ authors: cses_Surname_etal_Year.pdf Same author in one year: cses_Surname_Yeara.pdf Our database is stored in an EndNote file Article files are stored on Dropbox in CSES Secretariat II/CSES Bibliography/Bibliography/Article pdfs/pdfs [Slide 11] CSES Bibliography Database in EndNote [Slide 12] Making an Entry/Correction in the EndNote Database The EndNote file is located on Dropbox: CSES Secretariat II/CSES Bibliography/Bibliography/Endnote_database/current_Bib Never change

[Slide 20] Developing a Bibliography Policy for CSES 3 [Slide 21] Developing a CSES Bibliography Policy CSES does not have a formal policy regarding its bibliography. This has created a number of anomalies and discrepancies in how we handle the bibliography. Three vexing questions: Definition of a CSES contribution. Number of times the contribution appears in CSES: Article v Conference paper. Paper presented at multiple conferences. Updating of bibliography by the project – timing, responsibility. [Slide 22] Defining a CSES Contribution What is the exact definition of the use of CSES data? Current rule of thumb: Reference is included if CSES brings added value to the analyses. Comparative analyses possible. Variables in use would not have been in the election study without the CSES. Descriptive analyses also bring added value. But this definition is difficult to assess and might lead to inconsistencies. How do we differentiate between CSES having added value versus a single election study? Other complications: CSES is only mentioned in the article, but the data is not used. CSES was used descriptively only. [Slide 23] Number of Times an Item Appears in Bibliography Papers often make multiple appearances before they are published. An example of the publication cycle of an article: Manuscript/Working Paper. Conference paper (multiple appearances). Online publication/Formal print publication. Current rule of thumb: Add them all to the CSES bibliography. The question has three dimensions: What to count? When to add a contribution to the bibliography? How to present multiple contributions in the bibliography itself? [Slide 24] Examples of CSES Practice Example 1: Two conference papers, one published article, same name Example 3: Two conferences, not exactly the same name Example 4: Article appears twice (online first and paper) Example 2: A Working paper appears after a Journal article [Slide 25] A Potential Way of Remedying the Problem It might be possible to count conference papers at least only once, even if the same paper is presented at two locations: Busch and Quinlan (2015). The Bibliography Project. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Midwest Political Science Association, April 2015. Busch and Quinlan (2015). The Bibliography Project. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Political Science Association, September 2015. In circumstances where a Conference paper goes on to be published in an academic journal, we could retain the current policy of keeping both entries and counting each separately (i.e., conference paper to be counted once and journal article to also be counted once). What particular CSES variables do these articles use? What is the most common topic investigated? Objective: to systematically analyse items in the CSES bibliography by extracting the contents of each contribution through a manual content analysis. [Slide 28] The CSES Bibliography Project What are we interested in extracting? What module of CSES was utilized? What journals are the articles published in? What institutions do the authors come from? What type of analysis is employed? What particular CSES variables are used? Which concepts of political research do the dependent and independent variables in use belong to? [Slide 29] Method Manual content analysis of published journal articles in English up to Summer 2016. A comprehensive coding scheme was created by the team, capturing all relevant information we are interested in. Creation of classification tables that organized all CSES variables into applicable categories, depending on whether they were measured as dependent or independent variables. CSES Bibliography Project. 4. Developing a Bibliography Policy for CSES. [Slide 3] CSES Bibliography 1 [Slide 4] The CSES Bibliography Enumerative bibliography – organized listing of outputs based on a unifying principle. The CSES continuously collects information about the scholarly outputs that utilize our data. Thus the unifying principle of the CSES bibliography is use of CSES data in some way. We collect information on published journal articles, conference papers, book chapters, and dissertations for the purposes of providing a detailed bibliography on the CSES website. It is also helpful in funding applications. As of december 2018, we have 1009 scholarly outputs using CSES data. More than 30% are peer reviewed published journal articles. [Slide 5] CSES Bibliography on website I [Slide 6] CSES Bibliography on website II [Slide 7] Updating and managing the CSES Bibliography 2 [Slide 8] Searching for scholarly outputs for CSES Bibliography I Google Scholar. Journals that usually publish comparative electoral behaviour material: Electoral Studies & Comparative Political Studies. American Journal of Political Science & American Political Science Review. Journal of Elections, Party, and Public Opinion (JEPOP) & Party Politics. For Conference papers/ manuscripts (mostly unpublished) Social Science Research Network (SSRN). All Academic Research Database. Homepages of conferences (e.g.: APSA; MPSA; EPSA; ECPR & EPOP). [Slide 9] Searching for scholarly outputs for CSES Bibliography II General searches using the CSES acronynm but also use other terms commonly related to CSES, simultaneously: Electoral systems. Comparative voting behaviour. Be cautious using CSES acronym only – otherwise you might get : Cambodia Socio-Economic Survey. Center of South East Asian Studies. Conference on Signals and Electronic Systems. For presentations/CSES related Meetings: Dave or Steve collect some material; Others provide support too. Between two bibliography updates we store articles/conference presentations at “Dropbox (CSES)\CSES Secretariat II\Bibliography\Bibliography\Add_toEndnote” [Slide 10] How to handle publications in the CSES bibliography database? Having identified a relevant item for CSES bibliography, download the document if possible for our records. If you cannot download the document (i.e.: no access), send the link to colleagues and ask if they can get access. Upon downloading, store valid publicatons in the following name format: One author: cses_Surname_Year.pdf Two authors: cses_Surname_Surname_Year.pdf 2+ authors: cses_Surname_etal_Year.pdf Same author in one year: cses_Surname_Yeara.pdf Our database is stored in an Endnote file Article files are stored to “Dropbox (CSES)\CSES Secretariat II\Bibliography\pdfs“ [Slide 11] CSES bibliography database in Endnote [Slide 12] Making an entry/correction in Endnote database Endnote file is located on Dropbox: Dropbox (CSES)\CSES Secretariat II\Bibliography\Endnote_current Never change the Endnote file unless you have ownership of it. Make sure the reference uses CSES data

[Slide 20] CSES Bibliography Project 3 [Slide 21] The CSES Bibliography project The CSES continuously collects information about outputs that use the CSES data (E.g.: Journal articles, conference/working papers, book chapters, PhDs etc…) However, we lack detailed information on: What are these articles about? What particular CSES variables do these articles use? What is the most common topic investigated? Objective: to systematically analyse items in CSES bibliography by extracting the contents of each contribution through a manual content analysis. [Slide 22] The CSES Bibliography Project What are we interested in extracting? What module of CSES was utilized? What journals are the articles published in? What institutions do the author‘s come from? What type of analysis is employed? What particular CSES variables are used? Which concepts of political research do the dependent and independent variables in use belong to? [Slide 23] Method Manual content analysis of published journal articles in English up to Summer 2016. A comprehensive coding scheme created by the team capturing all relevant information we are interested in. Creation of classification tables which organized all CSES variables into applicable categories depending on whether they were measured as dependent or independent variables. text: by the project – timing, responsibility. [Slide 33] Defining a CSES contribution What is the exact definition of use of CSES data? Current rule of thumb: Reference is included if CSES brings added value to the analyses. Comparative analyses possible. Variables in use would not have been in the election study without the CSES. But this definition is difficult to assess and might lead to inconsistencies. How do we differentiate between CSES having added value versus single election study? Other complications: CSES only mentioned in the article but data not used. CSES used descriptively only. [Slide 34] Number of times an item appears in bibliography Papers often make multiple appearances before they are published. An example of the publication cycle of an article: Manuscript/Working Paper. Conference paper (multiple appearances). Online publication/Formal print publication. Current rule of thumb: Add them all to CSES bibliography. The question has three dimensions: What to count? When to add a contribution to the bibliography? How to present multiple contributions in the bibliography itself? [Slide 35] Examples of CSES practice Example 1: Two conference papers, one published article, same name name Example 3: Two conferences, not exactly the same name Example 4: Article appears twice (online first and paper) Example 2: Working paper appears after Journal article [Slide 36] A potential way of remedying the problem It might be possible to count conference papers at least only once, even if the same paper is presented at two locations: Busch and Quinlan (2015) The Bibliography Project, Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Midwest Political Science Association April 2015. Busch and Quinlan (2015) The Bibliography Project, Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Political Science Association September 2015. In circumstances where a Conference paper goes on to be published in an academic journal, we could retain the current policy of keeping both entries and counting each separately (i.e.: conference paper to be counted once and journal article to also be counted once). [Slide 37] The CSES Bibliography Slaven Zivkovic Mannheim, 30 September 2019

Data Bridging Identifiers in CSES Products. CSES Data Bridging Webpage. Data Bridging - Challenges. [Slide 3] What is Data Bridging? 1 [Slide 4] What is Data Bridging? I Overall idea: Enabling users to bring together information from CSES with other data sources. Related terms: “[...] data linking means the enrichment of one focal dataset with information from another auxiliary dataset through specific identifiers that can be used to create the link between the data sources.” (Jünger & Breuer 2021) “Data integration refers to the process of bringing together information from multiple data sources in a coherent and consistent manner, making it possible to examine relationships between factors which might not be visible from any one data source alone.” (O’Toole et al. 2025) [Slide 5] What is Data Bridging? II CSES intentionally opted for the term data bridging: CSES provides standard identifiers at the polity/time/party level that facilitate merging of CSES with other projects’ data. However, users must conduct the actual mergers themselves based on the instructions we provide on the CSES website. Merging is just the first step of the data integration process – upon merging data together, researchers will then have to harmonize/ clean/recode data according to their research question. The term “data bridging” aims to bring across these considerations. [Slide 6] What is Data Bridging? III In this scenario, the “ID” Variable acts as a data bridging identifier. [Slide 7] Data Bridging In CSES - Overview CSES products incorporate consistent and internationally recognized identifiers, empowering users to merge them with other projects’ data by polity, time, and party. Identifiers for polities and time present from day one, party identifiers from other projects included since M4 Full Release. Systematic expansion of data bridging efforts in 2020: Inclusion of additional polity, time, and party identifiers from other products further facilitating mergers (first in IMD, with spillovers to M5 and M6) Onset of the CSES Data Bridging Webpage, showing users how they can merge CSES data to 18 other projects Provision of hands-on STATA example syntax, showcasing users how other data can be merged with CSES products by polity and/or party. Solution: Revisit Missing IDs for the Full Release and see whether they have become available by then. text: [Slide 1] CSES Secretariat Training Dissemination & Archiving [Author] [Author‘s Affiliation, Location] [Slide 2] Presentation Outline Where are we? Preliminary steps for dissemination - Errata. Preliminary steps for dissemination – Additional Steps. Release File Creation. Release File Testing. Announcements. Archiving. [Slide 3] Where are we? 1 [Slide 4] Where are we? All Data Processing is complete. We have a Cross-National File (in STATA format) with all checks completed, vetting responses and issues/problems closed off. The Codebook is finalized. We‘re now ready to go into DISSEMINATION MODE: Release of the data file and documentation. Announcement to the user community. Archiving. [Slide 5] Preliminary Steps for Dissemination - Errata 2 [Slide 6] Preparation of an Errata List An errata list (corrigendum) is a list of corrections issued since the last publication of the data. It should contain all the changes that have been made since the preceding release – important for replication purposes and to be transparent about errors discovered in the interim. Not relevant for Advance Release 1 of data, but relevant for all other releases. Collated together by a micro processor who prepares a note for DH and sends it to him before the dissemination phase. [Slide 7] Structure of an Errata List I Introductory blurb, including release dates of the current and previous iteration of the file, the N of studies added and now included in total, plus a list of all new national election studies added in the update. List of data changes in the following order: Variables added to the dataset (if applicable). Separate added variable lists for administrative, micro, and macro data. List of any corrections (i.e., changes) by variable in the order variables appear in the dataset. List of Codebook changes: List of substantive changes made, ordered by the Part of the Codebook in which they appear (i.e., start with changes in Codebook Part 1). [Slide 8] Structure of an Errata List II Each erratum itself follows a specific format, namely: Name of variable/Codebook Part the erratum refers to. Data: Description of previous variable entry (i.e., how respondents or polity have been classified before the change). Data: Description of the implemented change and an explanation of why the change was made. Codebook: Description of additions or corrections made to the respective section. However, since the lower house election is the main election, variables E1016 – E1021_2 have been recoded to reflect the lower house election date. [Slide 20] Release File Creation: Decimals Issue Because we process the data in STATA, we face a unique problem with decimal storage Due to the method by which STATA stores numbers, you may enter the decimal value 0.86 in STATA, and given STATA formats it will appear in STATA as 0.86, but in reality underneath it is being stored as something like: 0.8600002 ...with precision which was not intended to be there [Slide 21] Release File Creation: Decimals Issue So how do we fix this? Use StatTransfer to create a SPSS file out of our STATA file. The precedent decision in CSES is to round all weights to four decimal places (.xxxx) and other variables to two decimal places (.xx) as this is the maximum precision (so far) of the variables. Once the SPSS file has been made, you can hand-edit the number of decimal places for these variables under the Variable View in Data View and then save the file ...but be very careful with the hand-editing! [Slide 36] Release File Checks I If all seems well, release file checks commence. Two additional team members take the ZIP files through the Release Checklist. Start with the most recent STATA original file created before dissemination, run frequencies for several variable types, and turnout/ vote choice model. The STATA original file is then used as a “benchmark” to which other release file formats (STATA release file, SPSS, CSV, R) are compared. Additionally, the full team is granted access to look at other things they are interested to check, including just “playing” with the file. [Slide 37] Release File Checks II Release file checks involve basic checks on the following: basic characteristics (N of cases, N of variables, dataset sorted on respondent ID & polity) Spot-checking (weighted) frequencies on different variable types (strings, integers, decimals, survey variables, macro data) “Eye-balling” files by scrolling through rows and columns of the dataset The goal is to ensure the well-checked Stata file produced during cross-national phase has been transformed to other formats correctly. Templates for Release File Checks across several formats (Stata, SPSS, R) are available on Dropbox. text: ESS 2012 Data Protocol Edition 1.4 October 2013 NORWEGIAN SOCIAL SCIENCE DATA SERVICES Introduction The object of the ESS 2012 Data Protocol is to offer a comprehensive document with specifications and procedures to be used in the production of national ESS data files. The underlying principle is that resources put into the planning phase of an international survey result in national data of higher quality and standardisation, which in turn will advance the release of the integrated (official ESS 2012) data files from the ESS Data web site, http://ess.nsd.uib.no . In general, the Data Protocol gives specificatio ns for the coding of data, the production and delivery of data files and other electronic deliverables. Some of the specifications, for example coding standards, are found elsewhere on the ESS Intranet, https://essdata.nsd.uib.no/ . The Data Protocol defines what the National Teams are required to deposit to the ESS Archive. If the content and quality of the electronic deliverables do not adhere to the specifications in the Data Protocol and the ESS Intranet, the archive reserves the right to ask for new deliverables. Please read all sections of this Data Protocol. The first section A describes how the communication between the archive and the data providers is organised. Section B, “Electronic deliverables”, gives an over view of the files and documents the National Co- ordinators are asked to deliver to the archive. Section B does also describe the more practical issues concerning data delivery, such as common identifiers in the files. Please pay special attention to section B7 “Anonymised data”. Section C of the Data Protocol deals with “princip les of variable definitions”. This section gives detailed information on the usage of missing values, how multiple responses are dealt with, as well as the rationale behind variable names, labels and categories. Please pay special attention to the coding of “Refusals” in section C1. The use of international standards is described in section D. To avoid the use of different versions of the same international standards across countries, the National Teams are required to use the standards made available from the ESS Intranet. Special variable topics like country-specific variables and administrative variables (including Contact form data) are listed, explained and specified in section E, whereas section F contains tables of variable names and definitions for all data files. Section F5 contains a flowchart documenting the routings in the ESS Core part of the questionnaire, and section F6 contains a flowchart documenting the routings in the Contact Form data. Section G refers to programmes for applying labe ls, categories, and formats in SPSS and SAS. The programmes will be made available from the ESS Intranet. Information about National Technical Summaries (NTS) is found in section

ESS 2012 Data Protocol Edition 1.4 October 2013 6 A. Procedures for the collaboration between the National Teams and NSD The ESS Intranet The ESS Intranet at https://essdata.nsd.uib.no/ will be the central meeting place between NSD and the National Teams during the data delivery and data processing phases of the project. One purpose of the ESS Intranet is to give all parties in the project easy access to the common set of tools and utilities that are used in the planning and production of the data files. Another purpose is to make the data processing at NSD as transpar ent as possible. By using the ESS Intranet, the National Teams can control their data delivery, and audit NSD’s data processing. The NSD team and primary contact persons The responsibi li ty for the ESS 2012 data at NSD is shared by a team of persons who are trained in the processing of comparative survey data. Each ESS country will be assigned a primary contact person. This person will have the main responsibili ty for the production of the country’s data files. The NSD team has a project email address, essdata@nsd.uib.no . When you send emails to your contact person, please address them to the project email address. This will ensure that your emails are read even if your contact person is out of office. Consultation process Prior to the fieldwork period consultation processes will be initiated on the measures of partnership status (relationship status and legal marital status), education and religion. The National Teams will be asked to answer specific queries regarding codi ng templates well in advance of the start of the fieldwork. New countries and countries that did not participate in ESS5 will also be approached and asked to answer some questions regarding the use of benchmark data in relation to the Income variable. The purpose of the consultation process is to improve data quality, as well as ease the data processing burden post-fieldwork. Data deposit When electronic deliverables (see section B) are ready for delivery to the archive, the National Teams are kindly asked to use the “Deposit data” op tion on the ESS Intranet. When the transfer is successfully completed, the NSD team will automatica lly be notified by the system. NSD will shortly after get in touch with the National Teams confirming the delivery. ESS 2012 Data Protocol Edition 1.4 October 2013 12 C. Principles of variable definitions C1. Missing values Analysis of item non-response is an important part of quality control of survey items, and consistent use of missing values in the questionnaire and other documentation ensures uniform coding of skips in the interview. The aim is that the ESS data files will contain detailed information on item non-response. The missing values in the data files are defined in the following way: Not applicable: 6, 66, 666 etc., where the respondent has been routed away from the question. This missing value might be coded in the national data files before deposit, but the coding will be overwritten by standardised procedures at NSD. Refusals: 7, 77, 777 etc., where the respondent has explicitly refused. This should be coded by the interviewers whether they use CAPI or PAPI. Important notice: In some questions an explicit refusal code is available. Otherwise, “Refusal” shall not be included in the scale or the list of answer categories pres ented to the interviewer in the questionnaire: 1. Those using CAPI: Place “Refusal” as an opti on for the interviewer, for example on the top menu of the screen where “Don’t know” is usually placed. 2. Those using PAPI and manual registration of the questionnaires: Instruct the interviewers to write (an abbreviation of) “Refusal” at the item. Instruct the registration operators to write in the same number of 7s as there are 8s in “Don’t know”. 3. Those using PAPI and optical scanning of the questionnaires: The questionnaire should have an administrative column with a “refusal” box identifiable for the scanningprogramme. Don't know: 8, 88, 888 etc. These codes are almost always available. They can be included in the list of answering options presented to the interviewers, or placed in administrative columns, menus etc., depending on the routines of the survey organisation. No answer: 9, 99, 999 etc. are codes for missing data not elsewhere explained, for example respondent/interviewer errors and production/syste m errors. This missing value might be coded in the national data files before deposit, but the codi ng will be overwritten by standardised procedures at NSD. Variable names The principles of variable definitions are bound by two factors: the limitations in statistical packages and the concern for user-friendly metadata. These factors limit the length of variable documentation included in the data files. The CST has decided to use mnemonic variable names in the data files. The argument is that about half of the questionnaire (the Core) is replicated in all rounds of the ESS, and that several rotating ESS 2012 Data Protocol Edition 1.4 October 2013 14 modules are replicated. By using mnemonic variable names, different data files contain the same variable names for identical questions, making it easier for the users as well as the producers of cumulative files for several ESS rounds. To ensure consistency in variable names, NSD has set up an internal guideline for abbreviations of frequently used concepts and words in questionnaires. The table below gives one example: Concept Abbreviation Police PLC : : Trust TRST/TST Thus, question B4, “Trust in the police” becomes TRSTPLC. In many statistical packages, the upper limit of variable names is eight characters. In order to allow for versions of a variable, the limit in ESS is seven characters, leaving space for documenting new versions of the variable with characters (A, B, C, etc.) as suffix. For example, between ESS round 1 and 2 the variable WRKCTR "Employment contract unlimited or limited duration" was changed to WRKCTRA, due to a new category that was added. C5. One reason is that the user should be able to grasp the content “in one glance”; another reason is the formatting of outputs from the statistical packages. The ten major groups at the top level of the ISCO-88 structure can still be found in ISCO-08. A number of completely new sub-major groups, minor groups and unit groups have been introduced to ISCO-08, and several ISCO-88 groups at these levels have been merged with other groups or split into several groups. Note that REFVIS1-REFVIS3 must be chronologically consis tent and match the sequence as recorded at OUTNIC1-OUTNIC10. For example, if th e first refusal took place at the 3rd visit (ie. code 02,03 or 04 at OUTNIC3), REFVIS1 should be coded 03. If three refusals are recorded for a sample unit, REFVIS3 (code range 03-10) should always be larger than REFVIS2 (code range 02-10) which in turn should always be larger than REFVIS1 (c ode range 01-10). text: Edition 1.4 October 2013 83 European Social Survey Round 6 SAMPLE DESIGN DATA FILE This is the description of the data file needed regarding the sample design. The file should contain one record f or each selected address, in the case of address-based samples, or for each selected individual, in the case of individual-based (population register) samples – i.e. the com plete gross sample. (In the rare e vent of a des ign in which it is possible to select m ore than one person at an addr ess, extra records will be needed f or any extra per sons thus selected.) Please make sure that you include all ineligible and non-responding units as well as responding ones. The t able below l ists t he v ariables that should be included on the fi le. Please us e t he v ariable names exactly as they appear here. Please include all variables, even though several of them are likely to be blank (missing) for all units. The annex contains ex amples o f how the v ariables should be interpreted f or dif ferent types of sample design. It is suggested that you look closely at these examples. National coordinators may seek advice from their nominated member of the sampling expert panel if necessary. Note on missing values: All variables up to and including “outcome” should be present on the data file. Those v ariables that are not relevant to the sample design ( e.g. 3rd-stage probabilities, in the case of a 2-stage design) should be l eft blank. For missing values on variables that do apply, use code 9 for items that are missing through interviewer or other error. This should apply only to certain items in the case of address-based sampling. We assume that SPSS, STATA or SAS system files will be delivered. NAME of variable MEANING OF VARIABLE (label) and codes IDNO Mandatory . Element number (same as in main data file). All records with the same combination of PSU/SSU should have the same value of PROB2. PROB3 Applies if there are at least 3 stages of selection. Selection probability at third stage (conditional upon first two stages). Numeric, positive, non-zero, 12 decimal places (or as many as necessary to provide at least 4 significant figures for all cases). For some designs, either PROB3 or PROB4 will correspond to the reciprocal of the number of persons aged 15 or over at the address. In this case the value should be blank for ineligibles (OUTCOME=3) and should be 9 for non- responding units (OUTCOME=2) where the number of persons aged 15+ was not established. PROB4 Applies if there are 4 stages of selection. Selection probability at fourth stage (conditional upon first 3 stages). SAMPPOIN Applies only to multi-stage designs where PSUs and sample points are not co- terminous . Sampling point to which the sample element belongs. Integer. Value labels are not needed: sampling points can be anonymous. SSU Applies if there are 3 or more stages and more than one 3rd-stage unit is selected within each 2nd-stage unit . Second stage unit (secondary sampling unit) to which the sample element belongs. Integer. Need only be unique within PSU. STRATEX1 Applies if explicit stratification was used at 1st stage (independent selections from each stratum) . Stage 1 explicit stratum to which the sample element belongs. text: [Leeuw, Edith D. de, and Joop Hox. (2008). Missing Data. Encyclopedia of Survey Research Methods . Retrieved from http://sage-ereference.com/survey/Article_n298.html] Missing Data An important indicator of data quality is the frac tion of missing data. Miss ing data (also called "item non-response") means that for some reason data on particular items or questions are not available for analysis. In practice, many researcher s tend to solve this problem by restricting the analysis to complete cases through "listwise" deletion of all cases with missing data on the variables of interest. However, this results in loss of information, and therefore estimates will be less efficient. Furthermore, there is the possibility of systematic differences between units that respond to a particular question and those that do not respond—that is, item nonresponse error. If this is the case, the basic assumptions necessary for analyzing only complete cases are not met, and the analysis results may be severely biased. Modern strategies to cope with missing data are imputation and direct estimation . Imputation replaces the missing values with plausible estimates to make the data set complete. Direct estimation means that all available (incomplete) data are analyzed using a maximum likelihood approach. The increasing availability of user-f riendly software will undoubtedly stimulate the use of both imputation and di rect estimation techniques. However, a prerequisite for the statistical treatment of missing data is to understand why the data are missing. For instance, a missing value originating from accidentally skipping a question differs from a missing value originating from re luctance of a respondent to reveal sensitive information. Finally, the information that is missing can never be replaced. Thus, the first goal in dealing with missing data is to have none. Prev ention is an important step in dealing with missing data. Reduction of item nonresponse will lead to more information in a data set, to more data to investigate patterns of the remaining it em nonresponse and select the best corrective treatment, and finally to more data on whic h to base imputation and a correct analysis. A Typology Of Missing Data There are several types of missing data patterns, and each pattern can be caused by different factors. The first concern is the randomne ss or nonrandomness of the missing data. Missing At Random Or No t Missing At Random A basic distinction is that data are (a) missi ng completely at random (MCAR), (b) missing at random (MAR), or (c) not missing at random (NMAR). This distinction is important because it refers to quite different processes that require different strategies in data analysis. Data are MCAR if the missingness of a variable is unrelated to its unknown value and also unrelated to the values of

text: are (a) missi ng completely at random (MCAR), (b) missing at random (MAR), or (c) not missing at random (NMAR). This distinction is important because it refers to quite different processes that require different strategies in data analysis. Data are MCAR if the missingness of a variable is unrelated to its unknown value and also unrelated to the values of all other variables. An example is inadvertently skipping a question in a questionnaire. When data are missing completely at random, the missing values are a random sample of all values and are not related to any ob served or unobserved variable. Thus, results of data analyses will not be biased, because there are no systematic differences between respondents and nonrespondents, and problems th at arise are mainly a matter of reduced statistical power. It should be noted that the stan dard solutions in many statistical packages, those of listwise and pairwise deletion, both assume th at the data are MCAR. However, this is a strong and often unrealistic assumption. When the missingness is related to the observed data but not to the (unknown) value of the missing response itself, it is said that the data are MAR. For example, an elderly respondent may have difficulty recalling an event because of memory problems. The resulting missing datum is related to age but not to the event itself. When the data are missing at random, the missingness is a random process conditional on the observed data. If the data are missing at random and if the proper statistical model is used, the missingness is said to be ignorable with respect to inference. For example, in the case of the elderly responde nt, the variable related to the missingness (age) is measured and available for incl usion in the proper analysis. Finally, when the missingness is related to the unknown (missing) answer to the question itself, the data are NMAR. For example, a respondent perc eives the real answer to a sensitive survey question as socially undesirable (e.g. she or he does have drinking problems) and refuses to respond. If the missing data are the NMAR type, the missingness is said to be nonignorable , and no simple solution for treating the missing data exists. A model for NMAR missingness must be postulated and included in th e analysis to prevent bias. Missing Data Patterns Three main patterns can be discerned in item missing data: (1) the data are missing systematically by design (e.g. contingency questi ons); (2) all the data ar e missing after a certain point in the questionnaire (partial completion); and (3) data are missing for some questions for some respondents (item nonresponse). text: Data Patterns Three main patterns can be discerned in item missing data: (1) the data are missing systematically by design (e.g. contingency questi ons); (2) all the data ar e missing after a certain point in the questionnaire (partial completion); and (3) data are missing for some questions for some respondents (item nonresponse). Missing By Design Data are missing by design when the researcher has decided that specific questions will not be posed to specific persons. There are two main reasons for items to be missing by design. First, certain questions may not be applicable to al l respondents and the questionnaire routing skips these questions for these respondents, that is , these are contingency questions. Since the responses to other questions determine the miss ingness, the missingness mechanism is accessible to the analyst and can be in corporated in the analyses. The second reason for items to be missing by design is when a specific design is used to administer different subsets of questions to diffe rent persons. In this case, all questions are applicable to all respondents, but for reasons of efficiency not all questions are posed to all respondents. Specific subsets of questions are pos ed to different groups of respondents, often following a randomized design in an experi ment (i.e. random assignment) that makes the missingness mechanism MCAR. Again, since th e missingness mechanism is accessible, the incomplete data can be handled statistically and the analyses give unbiased results. Partial Completion A partial completion (breakoff) is characterize d by time or place dependency. After a certain point in time or place within the questionnaire, all data are missing. Partial completions mostly occur in telephone interviews and Web surveys. At a certain time point in the interview, the respondent stops and disconnects. As a result, the remainder of the questionnaire is not answered. When the breakoff occurs early in th e questionnaire and only a few questions have been answered, it is usually treated as unit nonresponse. When the breakoff occurs at the end of the questionnaire, the remaining unanswered questi ons are usually treated as item nonresponse. In that case, information on earlier questions and the interview process is used to investigate the missingness mechanism and adjust for it in the analyses. Item Nonresponse Item nonresponse is characterized by blanks in the data for some respondents on some variables. Not every blank in the data matrix originates in the same way. One can distinguish three forms of item non-response: (1) the information is not provided by a respondent for a certain question (e.g. a question is overlooked by accident, an answ er is not known, a refusal to respond); (2) the information provided by a respondent

text: on some variables. Not every blank in the data matrix originates in the same way. One can distinguish three forms of item non-response: (1) the information is not provided by a respondent for a certain question (e.g. a question is overlooked by accident, an answ er is not known, a refusal to respond); (2) the information provided by a respondent for a certain question is not usable (e.g. a given answer is not a possible answer, it falls outside the range of permissible responses, multiple responses are given when only one is al lowed, it cannot be coded, and/or it is unreadable/illegible); and/or (3) usable information is lost (e.g. error in data en try or data processing). The first two of these mechanisms (information is not provided and info rmation is not usable) originate in the data collection phase. The third is the result of errors in the data processing phase. The most problematic form of item nonresponse occurs when a respondent does not provide information, because in this case different miss ing data mechanisms may be at work. When the respondent accidentally overlooks an item, the data are MCAR. The missingness mechanism is ignorable and almost all simple statistical treatm ents may be used, even list-wise deletion. When a respondent is willing but unable to respond—for example, because of memory problems—the missingness depends on an observed variable (age), but not on the answer to the question itself and is thus missing at random. If the data are MA R and if the variable related to the missingness is available, the missingness can be handled adequately with relatively simple solutions. However, when not responding is related to the (unknown) answer to the question itself, the missingness mechanism is NMAR. When a respondent refuses to respond, the missingness is probably NMAR and the mechanism is non-ignorabl e. In this case, simple solutions no longer suffice, and an explicit model for the miss ingness must be included in the analysis. When item nonresponse is due to unusable responses that are coded as missing, it is generally problematic. The reasons for inadequate responses (e.g. outside the range of possible answers or nonsubstantive responses) are related to the ques tion format and the real value of the answer, pointing to NMAR. If the real answer is partly revealed (e.g. through interviewer notes), the missingness mechanism is at least partly known. Finally, losing information because of errors in coding, editing, or storing is usually not systematic and therefore normally MCAR. It arises by accident and is not related to questionnaire and respondent characteristics, so the mechanism is ignorable and the solutions are simple.
