Analyzing Incomplete Data Sets Inspecting The Structure And Patterns Of Missing Data For an optimal treatment of item nonresponse, knowledge of the missing data mechanism is valuable. First, one should investigate whether th e data are MCAR or not. When incomplete data are MCAR, analyses will not be biased, because there are no systematic differences between respondents who completed the question and re spondents who have a missing value for that question. The first step in the analysis of incomplete data is to inspect the data. This can provide very practical information. For instance, one may find that most of the missing values concern only one specific variable (e.g. househol d or personal income). But if that variable is not central to the analysis, the researcher may decide to delete it. The same goes for a single respondent with many missing values. In general, however, missing valu es are scattered throughout the entire data matrix. In that case, a researcher would like to know if the missing data form a pattern and if missingness is related to some of the observed va riables. If one discovers a system in the pattern of missingness, one may include that in the st atistical analyses or imputation procedures. The mere inspection of missing data patterns cannot tell the researchers with certainty whether or not the missingness is independent of the (unknown) value of the variable (question). Extra information is needed to test the MAR hypothesi s and help to determine the causes of item nonresponse. This information may be available in the data set, but ofte n additional information (information from other sources than the actual sample) is needed, such as theory, logic, or auxiliary data from registers, sampling fram es, reinterviews, or other special nonresponse studies. Effective Methods To Analyz e Incomplete Data Sets The default options of statistical software are usually listwise or pair wise deletion or some simple imputation technique such as mean substitution . These solutions are generally inadequate. Listwise deletion removes all unit s that have at least one missing value and is clearly wasteful because it discards information. Pairwise dele tion removes cases only when a variable in a specific calculation is missing. It is less wasteful than listwise deletion, but it can result in inconsistent correlation matrices in multivariat e analyses, because diff erent elements in the correlation matrix may be based on different subs amples. Simplistic imputation techniques (e.g. mean substitution) often produce biased point es timates and will always underestimate the true sampling variances. Listwise and pairwise deletion and simple imputation are likely to be biased, because these methods are all based on the st rong assumption of MCAR, which seldom is warranted. Therefore, the best policy is to preven t missing data as much as possible, and when they occur to employ an analysis strategy that us es (a) all available information to investigate the missing data patterns and (b) an analysis me thod that correctly adjusts for missing data. Only when the data can be considered MCAR do simple solutions like listwise deletion not result in bias. If the fraction of missing data is small, listwise deletion is useful. If the fraction of missing data is large, the MAR-based techniqu es described following are more efficient. When the data are assumed MAR, two distinct analysis approaches can be used: direct estimation and imputation. Direct Estimation Direct estimation means that the incomplete data are fully analyzed using a maximum likelihood approach. Direct estimation requires specialize d software, but this is increasingly becoming available. For instance, several programs fo r structural equation modeling can include incomplete cases in the analysis. Since analysis of (co)variance, multiple regression analysis, and discriminant analysis can all be formulated as a structural equation model, these analyses can now be done using all available information, u nder the assumption of MA R. Another example is using multi-level models for incomplete longitudinal data. Such analyses view the repeated measures as hierarchically nested within cases. Since multi-level models do not assume that all measurement occasions are available for analysis, missing data due to panel dropout (attrition) are not a problem. While direct estimation is powerful, it requires access to and knowledge of specialized software. Imputation fills the gaps in the data set with plausible values, and after the data are made complete, standard software then is used. At th is point, the researcher can simply ignore the missingness problem and proceed to analyze the completed data set using any standard method with which she or he is familiar. Imputation In imputation, the missing values are replaced by "plausible" values. Many imputation methods exist, which mainly differ in the way they define plausible . A problem is that most simple imputation methods, such as replacing missing valu es with the overall mean or using regression to estimate the missing values, result in biased estimates. However, the popular and reasonably simple hot-deck method results in unbiased estimates under the assumption of MAR. In the hot- deck method, the data file is sorted into a number of imputation classes according to a set of auxiliary variables. Missing values are then repl aced by observed values taken at random from other respondents in the same imputation class. There are two fundamental problems associated with imputation. First, using the information in the observed data to pred ict the missing values emphasizes the structure in the completed data. Second, analyzing the completed data set uses a spuriously high number of cases and thus leads to biased significance tests. Donald Rubin proposes to solve both problems by using multiple imputation: Each missing value is replaced by two or more (M) plausible estimates to create M completed data sets. The plausible values must include an error term from an appropriate distribution, which solves the problem of exaggerating the existing structure in the data. Analyzing the M differently completed data sets and combining the estimates into an overall estimate solves the problem of the biased significance test. In the multiple imputation approach, analyzing M data sets and having to combine the results is cumbersome but not especially complex. What is difficult is generating the M data sets in a proper manner. A non-parametric method is to (a) compute for each respondent the propensity to have missing values on a specific variable, (b) group respondents into imputation classes based on this propensity score, and (c) use hot-deck imputation with these imputation classes. Parametric imputation methods assume a model for the data and use Bayesian methods to generate estimates for the missing values. Thes e methods are described in detail by Joseph L. Schafer. When multiple imputation is used, it is important that the model for the data generation is very general and includes those variables th at are important for predicting either missingness or the variables of interest. text: Definitions of missing data Brick and Kalton, 1996: A variety of reasons are causal for missing data in survey research. The four main sources are Total or unit nonresponse: “when no survey data are collected for an element selected for the sample.” ‘Element’ is the unit of analysis of the sample, e.g. a respondent. It is caused by refusal to participate in the survey, noncontacts, and other reasons, e.g. language problems, or being too ill to participate or else. (Brick and Kalton 1996: 215). Noncoverage: “when some elements in the population of inference for the survey are not included in the survey’s sampling frame. These missing elements have no chance of selection for the sample and hence go unrepresented”. (Brick and Kalton 1996: 216). Item nonresponse: “when a sampled element participates in the survey but fails to provide acceptable responses to one or more of the survey items”. Examples are refusals to answer an item because it is sensitive, lack of knowledge, inconsistent answers to other items and deletion of the answer in editing; interviewer failure to ask the specific question or to record the answer. (Brick and Kalton 1996: 216). Partial nonresponse: “when a respondent cuts off the interview in the middle, (…) fails to provide data for one or more of the waves of a panel, or when a respondent in a multiphase survey provides data for some but not all phases of data collection. (Brick and Kalton 1996: 216). The typology of missing data includes the following distinctions of missing data a) missing completely at random (MCAR); b) missing at random (MAR) and c) not missing at random (NMAR). The differentiation is important because the categories need to be coped for with different analytic strategies. MCAR: Missing data are unrelated to its unknown value and unrelated to the values of all other observed or unobserved variables. Making use of analysis with these MCAR data do not lead to biased results due to systematic differences between respondents and non-respondents and pairwise or listwise deletion during analysis procedures is no problem. MAR: Missing data is related to observed data but not to the (unknown) value of the missing response itself. For example, answers to recall questions can be missing due to memory problems related to age. The missing data are ignorable if the proper means of analysis is used. NMAR: Missing data is related to the unknown (missing) answer to the question itself, for example if a question is sensitive and the respondent hence does not want to answer it due to social desirability effects (e.g. being asked about drinking habits). In that case, the missingness is nonignorable, and no simple solution for treating the missing data exists. A model for NMAR missingness must be postulated and included in the analysis to prevent bias. Reasons for missing data /Missing data patterns Missing by Design: some questions are not asked to every respondent, because a) they are not applicable to every person or b) for a subset of questions, the questionnaire includes a random skipping pattern for contingency questions. In the latter example, the questions would be applicable to everybody but respondents are left out randomly for efficiency reasons. In all ‘missing by design’ cases, the reasons why specific respondents are missing, are known and can be handled statistically. Sometimes, question wording is just changed slightly for a specific subset of respondents due to their differences (e.g. married persons are asked the same question as unmarried but with a little different wording). Often these variables can later be combined into one. Partial Completion: The respondent breaks off the interview. If this happens early in the interview, unanswered questions are defined as ‘unit nonresponse’; if it happens late in the interview, it is treated as ‘item nonresponse’. Item Nonresponse: Some variables are left missing due to Random overlooking; answer not being known; refusal The provided answer was not usable, e.g. falls outside the given range of the possible answers; more answers to the question are given than expected; answer is unreadable or illegible Information is lost

It is necessary to investigate the data for possible patterns. For example, only specific variables like ‘income’ may be affected. The researcher may decide to delete that variable from the analysis if it is not central. The same should be done for respondents with many missing answers. There are several useful distinctions we can make. • Random versus selective loss of data . A researcher must ask why the data are missing . In some cases the loss is completely at random (MCAR), i.e. the absence of values on an IV is unrelated to Y or other IVs . Also, as Allison notes (p. 4) “Data on Y are said to be missing at random (MAR) if the probability of missing data on Y is unrelated to the value of Y, after controlling for other variables in the analysis…For example, the MAR assumption would be satisfied if the probability of missing data on income depended on a person’s ma rital status, but within each marital status category, the probability of missing income was unrelated to income.” Unfortunately, in survey research, the loss often is not random . Refusal or inability to respond may be correlated with such things as educat ion, income, interest in the subject, geographic location, etc . Selective loss of data is much more problematic than random loss. • Missing by design; or, not asked or not applicable. These are special cases of random versus selective loss of data. Sometimes data are missing because the researcher deliberately did not ask the question

Sometimes data are missing because the researcher deliberately did not ask the question of that particular respondent . For example, prior to 2010 there wa s a “short” version of the census (answered by everyone ) and a “long” version that wa s only answered by 20% . This can be treated the same as a random loss of data, keeping in mind that the loss may be very high. Other times, skip patterns are used to only ask questions of respondents with particular characteristics . For example, only married individuals might be asked questions about family life. With this selective loss of data, you must keep in mind that the subjects who were asked questions are probably quite different than those who were not (and that the question may not have been asked of others because it w ould not make any sense for them). Missi ng Data Part 1: Overview, Traditional Methods Page 1 In can be quite frustrating to think you've found the perfect question, only to find that 3% of your sample answered it! However, keep in mind that, many times, most subjects actually may be answering the same or similar questions, but at different points in the questionnaire . For example, married individuals may answer question 37 while unmarried individuals are asked the same thing in question 54 (perhaps with a slight change of wording to reflect the differences in mar ital status) . Hence, it may be possible to construct a more or less complete set of data by combining responses from several questions . Often, the collectors or distributors of the data have already done this for you. • Many versus few missing data and their pattern . Is only 1% of the data missing, or 40%? Whatever strategy you follow you may be able to add plausibility to your results (or detect potential biases) by comparing sample members on variables that are not missing . For examp le, in a panel study, some respondents will not be re -interviewed because they could not be found or else refused to participate . You can compare respondents and non- respondents in terms of demographic characteristics such as race, age, income, etc. If there are noteworthy differences, you can point them out, e.g. lower -income individuals appear to be underrepresented in the sample . Similarly, you can compare individuals who answered a question with those who failed to answer. Alternatively, s ometimes you may have external information you can draw on, e.g. you know what percentage of the population is female or black, and you can compare your sample’s characteristics with the known population characteristics. • Dropping variables . When, for one or a few variables, a substantial proportion of cases lack data, the analyst may simply opt to drop the variables . This is no great loss if the variables had little effect on Y anyway . However, you presumably would not have asked the question if you did not think i t was important. Still, this is often the best or at least most practical approach . A great deal of missing data for an item might indicate that a question was poorly worded, or perhaps there were problems with collecting the data. • Dropping subjects, i.e. listwise (also called casewise) deletion of missing data. Particularly if the missing data is limited to a small number of the subjects, you may just opt to eliminate those cases from the analysis . That is, if a subject is missing data on any of the variables used in the analysis, it is dropped completely . The remaining cases, however, may not be representative of the population. Even if data is missing on a random basis, a listwise deletion of cases could result in a substantial reduction in sample size, if many cases were missing data on at least one variable . My guess is that listwise deletion is the most common approach for handling missing data, and it often works well, but you should be aware of its Missi ng Data Part 1: Overview, Traditional Methods Page 2 limitations if using it. Another thing to be careful of, when using listwise deletion, is to make sure that your selected samples remain comparable when you are doing a series of analyses . Suppose, for example, you do one regression where the IVs are X1, X2, and X3. You do a subsequent analysi s with those same three variables plus X4. The inclusion of X4 (if it has missing data) could cause the sample size to decline. This could affect your tests of statistical significance . You might, for example, conclude that the effect of X3 becomes insigni ficant once X4 is controlled for – but this could be very misleading if the change in significance was the result of a decline in sample size, rather than because of any effect X4 has . Also, if the X4 cases are missing on a nonrandom basis, your understanding of how variable effects are interrelated could also get distorted . For example, suppose X1- X3 are asked of all respondents, but X4 is only asked of women. You might see huge changes in the estimated effects of X1 -X3 once X4 was added. This might occur only because the samples analyzed are different, e.g. if you only analyzed women throughout the effects of X1- X3 might change little once X4 was added. In Stata, there are various ways to keep your sample consistent. The if statement on the reg command will limit the analysis to cases with nonzero values on touse (i .e. the cases with data on all 5 variables). Yet another possibility is to use the e(sample) function. In effect, cases are coded 1 if they were used in the analysis, 0 otherwise. Such a matrix is computed by using for each pair of variables (Xi, Xj) as many cases as have values for both variables . That is, when data is missing for either (or both) variables for a subject, the case is excluded from the computation of rij . In general, then, different correlation Missi ng Data Part 1: Overview, Traditional Methods Page 3 coefficients are not necessarily based on the same subject s or the same number of subjects. This procedure is sensible if (and only if) the data are randomly missing . In this case, each correlation, mean, and standard deviation is an unbiased estimate of the corresponding population parameter . If data are not mi ssing at random, several problems can develop:  The pieces put together for the regression analysis refer to systematically different subsets of the population, e.g. the cases used in computing r 12 may be very different than the cases used in computing r 34. Results cannot be interpreted coherently for the entire population or even some discernible subpopulation.  One can obtain a missing- data correlation matrix whose values are mutually inconsistent, i.e. it would be mathematically impossible to obtain such a matrix with any complete population (e.g. such a matrix might produce a multiple R² of - .3!) It may be even worse, though, if you do get a consistent matrix . With an impossible matrix, you'll receive some sort of warning that the results are implausible, but with a consistent matrix the results might seem OK even though they are total nonsense. Also, even if data are missing randomly, pairwise deletion is only practical for statistical analyses where a correlation matrix can be analyzed, e.g. OLS regressio n. It does not work for techniques like logistic regression

Suppose the variable Religion is coded 1 = Catholic, 2 = Protestant, 3 = Other . Suppose some respondents fail to answer this question. Rather than just exclude these subjects, we could just set up a fourth category, 4 = Missing Data (or no response) . We could then proceed as usual, constructing three dummy variables from the four category variable of religion. This method has been popular for years – but according to Allison & others , it produces biased estimates. • Substituted (plugged in) values , i.e. (Single) Imputation. A common strategy, particularly if the missing data are not too numerous, is to substitute some sort of plausible guess [imputation] for the missing data . Common choices include:  The overall mean  An appropriate subgroup mean (e.g. the mean for blacks or for whites)  A regression estimate (i.e. for the non- MD cases, regress X on oth er variables . Use the resulting regression equation to compute X when X is missing) Unfortunately, these strategies tend to reduce variability and can artificially increase R² and decrease standard errors . According to Allison, “All of these [single] imputation methods suffer from a fundamental problem: Analyzing imputed data as though it were complete data produces standard errors that are underestimated and test statistics that are overestimated. Conventional analytic techniques simply do not adjust for the fact that the imputation process involves uncertainty about the missing values.” Missi ng Data Part 1: Overview, Traditional Methods Page 4 • Substituted (plugged in) value plus missing data indicator . Cohen and Cohen (1975) advocated a procedure that Allison calls “Dummy variable adjustment”. This strategy proceeds as follows:  Plug in some arbitrary value for all MD cases (typically 0, or the variable's mean)  Include in the regression a dummy variable coded 1 if data in the original variable was missing (i.e. a value has been plugged in for MD), 0 otherwise . text: calls “Dummy variable adjustment”. This strategy proceeds as follows:  Plug in some arbitrary value for all MD cases (typically 0, or the variable's mean)  Include in the regression a dummy variable coded 1 if data in the original variable was missing (i.e. a value has been plugged in for MD), 0 otherwise . This approach keeps cases in that would otherwise be dropped. The t -test of the coefficient for the missing data dichotomy then (supposedly) indicates whether or not data are missing at random. HOWEVER, while this technique has been used for many years ( including, unfortunately, in earlier versions of this class !) Allison and others have recently been critical of it . Allison calls this technique “remarkably simple and intuitively appealing.” But unfortunately, “the method generally produces biased estimates of the coefficients.” See his book for examples . In the 2003 edition of their book, Cohen and Cohen no longer advocate missing data dummies and acknowledge that they have not been widely used. NOTE!!! Buried in footnote 5 of Allison’s book is a very important point that is often overlooked (Thanks to Richard Campbell from Illinois -Chicago for pointing this out to me) : While the dummy variable adjustment method is clearly unacceptable when data are truly missing, it may still be appropriate in cas es where the unobserved value simply does not exist . For example, married respondents may be asked to rate the quality of their marriage, but that question has no meaning for unmarried respondents . Suppose we assume that there is one linear equation for married couples and another equation for unmarried couples . The married equation is identical to the unmarried equation except that it has (a) a term corresponding to the effect of marital quality on the dependent variable and (b) a different intercept . It’s easy to show that the dummy variable adjustment method produces optimal estimates in this situation. So, for example, you might have questions about mother’s education and father’s education, but the father is unknown or was never part of the family . Or, you might have spouse’s education, but there is no spouse . In such situations, the dummy variable adjustment method may be appropriate . Conversely, if there is a true value for father’s education but it is missing, Allison says the dummy variable adjustment method should not be used. What would you recommend for her—substitution of the mean for MD cases, or substitution of the mean plus including missing data dichotomies? W hy? In the past I recommended using the Cohen and Cohen method: substitute the mean for the MD cases, and then add a missing data dichotomy. A significant coefficient for the dichotomy supposedly indicated that data were missing on a non- random basis. That method has now been discredited however. The researcher probably needs to better understand the reasons data are missing before deciding on a strategy. For example, are data missing because the question was not appropriate for the respondent (e.g. questions about marital satisfaction should not be asked of people who are not married)? Are they missing because some subjects refused to talk about sensitive topics? Were there problems with the questionnaire or with the data collection? However, if the data ar e missing because they are non- existent (e.g. the question pertains to the spouse but there is no spouse) the Cohen and Cohen dummy variable adjustment method may be appropriate. text: Definition of missing data – Spreadsheet Four causes of missing data In general, missing data in survey research can be any kind of partial or full non-response to a survey. Brick and Kalton (1996) differentiate between four causes of missing data which relate to different stages of development of a survey: Non-coverage (non-inclusion of an element of the target population in the sampling frame), Total Nonresponse (complete refusal of a respondent, non-contact, or inability to participate), Partial Completion (ending the interview before it was fully answered). If this happens after half of the interview, this is usually counted as ‘unite non-response’. Otherwise, it is rather counted as ‘item non-response’. Item Non-response (some single items were left unobserved for some of the respondents). Reasons can further be differentiated between being refused or unknown by the respondent, or randomly overlooked, the answer being not usable because it fell outside the given answer range, more than one answer being given when only one was expected, answer is unreadable or illegible. Information is lost in data entry stage or processing stage (by mistake) A special case of item non-response are Missings by design (some questions being non-applicable to the surveyed person, or element; or some contingency questions being asked to random respondents for efficiency reasons). Occurrences of these missing data in the CSES’ staff working procedures Due to non-coverage and total nonresponse being topics in the design and interviewing stage of a survey, they are mostly taken care for by the collaborators and their field institutions. However, for transparency and quality reasons, these are topics which are also considered in sections of the design report. CSES processors hence need to control if the specific questions on sampling frames and total nonresponse were appropriately answered and estimate if any issues were dealt with properly. Source 4, the item non-response is the causes of missing data, which the CSES team deals with mostly during data processing. We do not really control for 3, although we could do this. When dealing with item non-response, we need to assign the appropriate missing codes of either ‘not applicable’ or ‘missing’, refused or don’t know. We could even think of more if that was useful, but we should keep in mind the usefulness for the analyst. In Lavrakas, Paul J., Encyclopedia of Survey Research Methods. Sage: London/Thousand Oaks CA. pp. 467-471. Appendix 1 (builds on Leeuw and Hox (2008). Definitions of missings related to their randomness Taking the perspective of the analyst, Leeuw and Hox emphasize the distinction between different kinds of randomness of missings. The typology of missing data includes the following distinctions of missing data a) missing completely at random (MCAR); b) missing at random (MAR) and c) not missing at random (NMAR). The differentiation is important because the categories need to be coped for with different analytic strategies: deletion from analyses is only appropriate for MCAR. MCAR: Missing data are unrelated to its unknown value and unrelated to the values of all other observed or unobserved variables. Making use of analysis with these MCAR data do not lead to biased results due to systematic differences between respondents and non-respondents and pairwise or listwise deletion during analysis procedures is no problem. MAR: Missing data is related to observed data but not to the (unknown) value of the missing response itself. For example, answers to recall questions can be missing due to memory problems related to age. The missing data are ignorable if the proper kind of analysis is used. NMAR: Missing data is related to the unknown (missing) answer to the question itself, for example if a question is sensitive and the respondent hence does not want to answer it due to social desirability effects (e.g. being asked about drinking habits). In that case, the missingness is nonignorable, and no simple solution for treating the missing data exists. A model for NMAR missingness must be postulated and included in the analysis to prevent bias.

text: Missing vs. Non-Applicable. report on coding inconsistencies in the CSES, M4 (20170411) Macro variables Introduction The CSES Secretariat found that the CSES can advance on the consistency with which we differentiate between ‘non-applicable’ and ‘missing’ data and on the application of respective codes in the CSES (M4) data. In an effort to get a better understanding of the differences between missing data and non-applicable data, I wrote the document “Missing_vs_NonApplicable.docx, which takes a review on scientific explanations about the subject and outlines to a working definition for the CSES team. The current document is a follow-up which builds on the Missing vs Non-Applicable differentiation. It shows some of the issues which are currently present in the CSES M4 macro part of the data. Definitions Not applicable We now define ‘Not applicable’ with missing-by-design: This denotes to every situation in which a valid code could not be given due to the intentional design of the questionnaire. In the case of the CSES, I suspect three main sources for this kind of expected non-applicability: 1.) filter instructions which lead to non-inclusions of variables for specific groups of respondents (e.g. variables investigating on spouses are non-applicable for persons without a partner or spouse), 2.) non-applicability of specific variables for election studies due to the kind of election, (e.g. ‘variables on presidential election’ are not applicable for parliamentary systems). 3.) Variables about a number of ‘important parties’ which exceeds the real number of important parties in the specific country (e.g. in Australia, we only have micro variables about parties A-E, due to the small number of effective parties in the party system. Variables for party F-I should hence be coded non-applicable in the case of Australia.) Missing To the contrary of ‘not applicable’, missing means that a value is missing in cases in which a valid answer would have been expected. This is true in every situation in which there is no answer code for the variable due to some kind of error. The ‘missing’ code supplements situations in which a respondent did not answer voluntarily (refused to answer) or said that they ‘don’t know’ the answer. Only in cases in which an answer would have been expected by design, (and this excludes the not applicable cases), but is neither a ‘refusal’ nor ‘don’t know’ answer, the code should denote to ‘missing’. I will now turn to each of the problems one-by-one. Variables about party xth which is not present in country: No collaborator asks respondents about e.g. a sixth party if it is not meaningful. A sixth party is only meaningful if it is either important in terms of its percentage of votes, or due to other reasons (our additional parties H/I). If a party is left-out throughout the micro questionnaire, we should hence think of it as being ‘missed out by design’. This would be different, if a collaborator indeed did not ask about an important party in some of the variables – for example, if the British Election study would exclude a left-right question about the Labour Party, even though Labour Party was party B due to its vote percentage in the current election. text: 1 Missing by Design: Questionnaire Skip Logic Kathryn Valdés, SRI International, Menlo Park, CA ABSTRACT The primary purpose of a questionnaire is to gather information needed to answer important research qu estions. Researchers must rely upon the kindness and coopera tion of respondents—all of whom have varying degree s of time, patience, and motivation—to provide this info rmation. With this in mind, every effort is made t o design questionnaires that will collect data as efficientl y and painlessly as possible. A common way to reduce respondent burden is to empl oy skip logic, i.e. to conditionally ask questions based upon prior responses or other sources of information. Fo r example, if the subject is 14 years of age, there is no point in asking questions about having a driver's license or registering to vote; he or she is too young to do those activities and these questions would not apply. In another ex ample, if the respondent has indicated that he or s he has never attended a 4-year college or university, it is not necessary to ask questions about college experience s. Survey designs that decrease respondent burden incr ease the effort on the part of the programmer or an alyst. As the n's change from item to item, the befuddled pro grammer has to make sense of the conditional skip l ogic in order to track the cases through the logical flow of data . In checking the validity of the data, errors can be found in programming, in the respondents' ability to complet e the questionnaire, or in the skip logic itself. Using SAS ®, there are some approaches that can make this tracking and validation of data a bit easier. Reducing respond ent burden is all well and good; happily, a few good lines of SAS code can reduce the programmer's burden as well. INTRODUCTION In any area of research, it is a rarity to receive pristine data. One of the first requirements befor e starting any analysis is to familiarize oneself with the content s and formats of the data, the various idiosyncrasi es, the pitfalls, and the richness of the data. More often than not we have found researching data inconsistencies and doing data validation takes far more time than doing the analy sis. Skip logic presents additional challenges in data validation. There are different types of skip logic—as there ar e different types of data collection instruments—ea ch presenting its own unique challenge for programming. We will look at the various types of instrumentation and sk ip logic and identify programming approaches that may help in mu ddling through these challenges. Finally, we will take an example questionnaire and go through the

TYPES OF DATA COLLECTION INSTRUMENTS There are many types of data collection instruments used for research, however we will concern ourselv es only with questionnaires. There are also many ways to admini ster a questionnaire; the choice in which type of q uestionnaire to use usually depends upon the study and how respo ndents can be contacted. Often questionnaires are paper and pencil forms—or hardcopy forms—that are mailed to a respondent or d istributed in a location such as a classroom. The completed f orms are converted to data either by transcribing t he responses into electronic format, i.e. data entry, or by usin g scanning technology. On scanable forms there are places for notations or marks to be made next to the possible responses which will be read and converted to data using a scanning system. With a hardcopy format, the respo ndent reads the questions and follows instructions as to how to complete his or her responses. We have found from hard earned experience that the simpler these instr uctions are the better the subsequent data are likely to be. T herefore, in designing hard copy questionnaires, we attempt to make the skip logic very simple and easy for a resp ondent to follow. Another questionnaire format is an interview form w here the respondent is asked questions and an inter viewer enters the responses. As with the hardcopy questio nnaire completed by the respondent, if the intervie wer must read and enter responses onto a paper form, skip logic m ust be simple and easy to follow. Add a computer t o the mix and all manner of complexities can be introduced. CATI (computer assisted telephone interviewing) is programmed to display specific questions on an interviewer’s s creen based on logical conditions. Many conditions may have to be met in order for a question to be displayed, but that complex logic is never seen by the interviewe r; only the programmers have that privilege (or burden). The i nterviewer simply reads the questions as they appea r on the screen while the CATI programs drive the display. In addition to the hardcopy and interview forms, an other type of questionnaire is one that is administ ered online. With an online form, the respondent logs onto a sit

However, if the administration of the q uestionnaire is scripted and displayed by some type of programming logic running in the background then—as with the CA TI interview—the skip logic can be very complex; th e respondent sees only questions being displayed with out being aware of the programming behind the displ ay. 2 Often the type of format to use is not dictated by the researchers’ preference but by which means a re spondent may be reached. SOURCES OF ERRORS The source of errors in skip logic can be from any direction, which makes tracking the logic all the m ore challenging. There could be errors in design: the skip logic in the data collection instrument itself may be faulty or the instructions in the questionnaire could be so confusing that res pondents find them difficult to follow. In self-ad ministered questionnaires, the respondent may not pay close at tention to either the instructions or the text of t he questions and as a result he or she might not complete the questi ons appropriately. In CATI or scripted on-line sur veys, the question generating program logic and code may have errors. Finally—perish the thought, how could thi s be—the SAS program logic replicating the skip logic may be faulty. Determining the source of the error is ch allenging, and depending upon when the error is discovered, may no t be reversible. By the time all the data are coll ected only the SAS program can be corrected; it is too late to fix any of the other sources of errors. TYPES OF MISSING

TYPES OF MISSING DATA Survey data has different types of missing values. We routinely use user-defined missing values to id entify why items are missing giving us the ability to track re sponses. If a respondent gives a response of “don’ t know,” we assign a “.d”, if it is “not applicable,” we assign a “.a”, and if the response is “refused,” we assig n a “.r”. These missing values indicate that the respondent was ask ed this question but could or would not answer it. If the respondent skips questions, we assign a “.s”. This indicates that the questions were not asked and ar e legitimately missing because they were skipped. If items are mi ssing for no determined reason, we either leave the m as a system missing or assign a “.z” to indicate that we reviewed the missing response but cannot decipher why it is missing. We do not include missing values in analy sis, but having missing values clearly marked helps us understand varying n's when we are validating the d ata. VALIDATION OF SKIP LOGIC IN QUESTIONNAIRES WITH WRI TTEN SKIP INSTRUCTIONS We have no control over how well a respondent compl etes a questionnaire. We can only hope to provide h im or her with concise, easy to understand instructions and t hat he or she reads, understands, and follows these instructions. This does not always happen. Whether the design of the instrument is at fault or the lack attention p aid to it by the respondent is the problem, it is up to the programm er to try and determine as best as he or she can wh at the respondent meant to say. Any respondent may choose to not answer a given set of questions. The programmer must determine if re sponses are missing because the respondent chose not to ans wer those questions or because those questions are meant to be skipped. This can be particularly difficult if the lead question is missing as well. An example o f a lead question is, “Have you ever had a paid job?” If the respondent marks yes, the instruction next to the yes response says, “Please continue with the next question” and the subsequent questions ask about that job. When the data are all neatly collected and the SAS programmer makes a mistake in following the skip logic, it is only a matter of correcting the programming code and rerunning the p rogram against the data. However, if a programming error is made in the question generation, one of two things can happen. The first is not particularly problema tic for the data but annoying to the respondent: too many questions that do not apply are asked and the respondent’s ti me is wasted. The second possibility is not at all notic eable to the respondent but can be devastating to t he data, too few questions are asked and key information is not coll ected. If the number of non-missing and mi ssing values are the same before the SAS logic is a pplied and after it is applied, it is a very good sign. If th ere are unassigned missing values after assigning t he user-defined missing values for skipped, it could be an indicati on that the respondents are not being asked questio ns that should be asked. Unaccounted for missing values are an in dication of a problem. If there are more missing v alues after assigning values to skipped than before, it could b e that the respondent is being asked questions that should have been skipped. In either case, if the number of mis sing and non-missing values before and after the lo gic is applied do not agree it might be the SAS program that is in error. The challenge is to determine the source a nd cause of the error: is it the question generating logic or the S AS code replicating that logic? Identifying the source of the problem can be a bit tricky, particularly when there are compound skips being applied to one single question. While testing, we go through the questionnaire and assign a letter to each skip within a section. In Skip E, we have a nested skip that will be resolved in another sec tion. Since D looks like there are no errors, I would assume the problem is in Skip A. We have one person who is mi ssing the lead question but answered the subsequent question, so perhaps the lead question should be set to yes. There is also a problem with someone answering the questions that should be skipped; either the lead question n eeds to be corrected or the subsequent questions need to be se t to skipped. The next step would be to print out individual case s to look at the data. The errors are resolved to the degree possible. If, for example, someone says no to the lead question, do the subsequent responses indicate that the lead question is in error? That the lead question is co rrect? That these items should indeed be skipped? Unfortunately, this can be a case-by-case examination. If it is d etermined that the items should be skipped, nothing further need be done as the skip logic program will set the appropr iate items to ".s" for skipped. If not, the lead q uestion has to be corrected so that the items are not logically overw ritten with ".s" in the next step. Once the corrections are determined, there are mult iple ways to apply them to the data. When there ar e a lot of similar corrections, or for coding of verbatim resp onses in other specify items, we often use Excel to enter the data and then update the SAS data with the resulting imp ort of the Excel transaction data. We use the upda te statement on the data step rather than merge as update only r eplaces items when it finds a non-missing value whe reas merge overwrites everything with both missing and valid v alues. In the end, the goal is to have data that has valid responses and, if values are missing, missing values are identified and accounted for. W e need to know who is asked a question and why or w hy not. Using SAS macros and procedures, reaching that goal can be attainable no matter what the source of dat a and the associated challenges. We might not have control o ver the strength and clarity of the questionnaire d esign, the respondents who complete the questionnaires, or the programs that generate the series of questions tha t are asked, but we do have the power to track the responses thr ough the questionnaire logic. Hopefully we can be involved in the early stages. Early programmer/analyst involve ment can aid in good questionnaire design, which in creases the respondents’ ability to understand and follow instr uctions, and help ensure that the programmed skip l ogic driving the question generation is correct. Unfortunately, it is too late to make any corrections when the da ta are collected. All those unaccounted for missing values would be s et to “.z” and this is one case where a lot of “z”s would not be a good thing.
